en: Homage to that Self of All, in whom is everything, from whom is everything, who is everything, who is everywhere, and who is eternally composed of all things. (RA 1.1)
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, adorned with various jewels,
filled with diverse trees and creepers, and free from hidden attachments— the God of gods, the blue-throated, three-eyed one, seated in comfort— (RA 1.2).
Having bowed her head, the goddess Pārvatī inquired:
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who burn the body of Kāma!
O destroyer of Kulakaula, Mahākaula, Siddhakaula, and the rest!
By your grace, everything has been heard and fully comprehended;
if I am worthy of your favor, and if I am dear to you.
It has been indicated in all the tantras; yet, O Lord, this liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) which has not been revealed—of what nature is it? You should tell me.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! Excellent, O daughter of the mountain!
Well asked by you, O Goddess, out of a desire for the welfare of devotees:
[the knowledge] of the identity with Śiva of one whose body is free from old age and death.
O Great Goddess, liberation while living is difficult even for the gods to attain. (RA_1.8) That liberation which occurs upon the fall of the physical body is a liberation devoid of purpose;
O Goddess, when the body has fallen, even a donkey is liberated. (RA_1.9)
If liberation occurs through the agitation of the *bhaga*, why do donkeys, goats, and bulls not attain it? O Mother of the Gaṇas, why are they not liberated?
Therefore, one should protect the *piṇḍa* by means of juices and elixirs (*rasāyana*).
If liberation comes from the consumption of semen, urine, and excrement, O Great Goddess, why are dogs and pigs not liberated? Furthermore,
even in the Six Darśanas, liberation is shown to occur through the casting away of the physical body.

O Goddess of the Gods, that too is like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand; it is not perceived through direct perception, nor can it be described. Nevertheless, I shall tell you its true nature:
the practitioner of mantra who is free from sin should never hold onto the physical body.
O Goddess of the gods, even for the gods, the maintenance of the body is difficult to attain;
how much more so for humans who dwell upon the surface of the earth?
When Dharma is lost, where is Dharma? When Dharma is lost, where is ritual action?
When action is lost, whence can there be yoga? When yoga is lost, whence can there be a destination?
When the destination is lost, whence can there be liberation? When liberation is lost, there is nothing at all.
Thus spoke the Illustrious Goddess.
"But as for the nature of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), O God of gods, it has been heard by me;
tell me the means to attain it, if you have compassion for me.
Śrī Bhairava said:

O Goddess of gods, by means of the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), the maintenance of the body (*piṇḍadhāraṇa*) is attained, as well as mercury and the vital wind (*pavana*). The yoga of action is considered to be twofold:
when swooned (*mūrchita*), it removes disease; when dead (*mṛta*), it restores life itself.
When bound, it brings about the power of moving through the sky; O Bhairavī, [this is achieved by] the mercury and the vital air.

Liberation comes from knowledge, O Mistress of the Gods; knowledge comes from the retention of the vital air. Therein, O Goddess, the body becomes firm; where there is stability, mercury is the master.
O Goddess, before long a body that is free from old age and death arises, according to the meditation of the mind; it is obtained through the application of the vital essence (*rasa*).
O Goddess, he attains truth, preceded by wisdom and higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).
His mantras are successful even if he consumes [the food of] a death-impurity;
for as long as there is no descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and as long as the bonds (*pāśa*) have not been severed,
how could his intellect arise regarding the death-impurity?
For those who are constantly addicted to liquor and meat, and who take pleasure in the female and male organs—

those whose intellect is ruined— for them the knowledge of the essential taste is very difficult to attain. For those devoid of the Kula teachings and those who do not desire the True Vision, [it is likewise unattainable].

The elixir is not accomplished, O Goddess; they drink at a mirage. I consider him of noble birth who would eat beef and drink the wine of the immortals (*amaravāruṇī*); others are base, knowing only the [common] elixir.
The embryo is not for the sake of mere tradition; the embryo is ordained as the *rasa*.
By means of that, one attains accomplishment (*siddhi*); there is no accomplishment without the *sūtaka*.
As long as one does not consume the seed of Hara, the mercury-essence (*pārada-rasa*), [one cannot attain it].
How can there be liberation for such a person? How can he maintain his physical body?
(RA 1.28) Those whose wisdom is devoted to liquor and meat, deluded by the *māyā* of Śiva, prattle on: "We are liberated; we shall go to the abode of Śiva. (RA 1.29)

And in the yoga of sustaining the *piṇḍa*, those of dull intellect who are devoid of desire [attain] the state of moving and non-moving beings colored by fragmentary knowledge, O Goddess of Gods; and by this,
the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) and the state of Śiva (*śivatva*) are obtained within one's own body.
"But regarding such knowledge of rasa, O beloved, practice it constantly.
Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord of the Gods, [tell me] the descent of Rasendra and its majesty."
"I wish to hear it, O Lord of Gods; you ought to speak it according to the truth.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Well asked, O highly fortunate one! You have asked about that which is more secret than the secret."
Meditation is that which bestows grace and is beneficial to the worlds.
You are the mother of all beings, and I am the eternal father.
And that essence of the two, O Goddess, which arises from the great union—

O Goddess, because it arises spontaneously (*svairataḥ*), it is celebrated as *pārada*; and that which is proclaimed as *pārada* is the Great Radiance (*mahaḥ*) for the sake of others by the most excellent practitioners.
This elixir (*sūta*), O Goddess, is equal to me, having arisen from my very own limbs.
Because it is the essence of my body, it is therefore called "rasa" (essence).
From seeing, touching, eating, remembering, worshipping, and giving it, a sixfold fruit is observed. (RA 1.36–37)
The Kedāra and other such *liṅgas*— whatever [sacred sites] exist upon the earth—
the merit that is obtained from seeing them is attained simply by seeing the mercury (*rasa*).
This mercury is contained within sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron.
One who has fainted during the worship of Śiva [revives] for the sake of attaining proximity to Śiva. O Supreme Goddess, by consuming it, the mercury destroys the three types of sin;
likewise, it destroys the three types of suffering and the diseases arising from the three humors.

It is difficult to attain even for those well-versed in the Veda; yet, O Maheśvarī, the supreme state is attained by means of the mercury residing within the pericarp of the sky of the heart. By its mere remembrance, one is instantly liberated from the sins accumulated over many lifetimes.
The fruit that results from the perfect worship of thousands of self-manifested (*svayambhū*) liṅgas is multiplied ten million times by worshipping a mercury-liṅga (*rasaliṅga*).
The inferior [form] is the "bird-argument" (*khagavāda*), while the middling is the "cavity-argument" (*vilavāda*).

The discourse on mantras is supreme, but the discourse on alchemy (*rasavāda*) is most excellent. Those who, while fully understanding the *mantra-tantras*, disparage the application of alchemy, all go to hell after their store of merit has been exhausted.

The science of alchemy (*rasavidyā*) is the supreme knowledge; because it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, it is extremely difficult to find even throughout the three worlds. Therefore, it should be imparted by those endowed with virtuous qualities.
Some say that [the elixir] exists; some say that it does not exist.

Success shall belong to the believer; for him, success is achieved upon this earth. But through the disposition of a nihilist—who says "it is not, it is not"—there is no success in what is dear, even in hundreds of millions of births.
He who is liberated through the knowledge of Brahman— even if he is a sinner who reviles the *rasanā*—
I shall not be his protector, even after hundreds of millions of births.
O Goddess, such a person is born as a dog for as long as a thousand births.
For three million births he is born as a cat;
for a hundred thousand births he is born as a donkey; for a hundred thousand births he is a crow;
for a hundred thousand births he is a worm; and for a hundred thousand births he is a cock.

One who reviles the tongue is a sinner who will be born as a vulture for a hundred thousand lifetimes. He who engages in conversation or physical contact with those who revile the tongue shall remain tormented by suffering for as many as a thousand births.
In terms of taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation, mercury (*sūtaka*) is like nectar;
therefore, O beloved, mercury removes birth, old age, and disease.
One should first propitiate the Guru with a purified inner self.
The Marīcis bestow the tradition when the Guru is pleased.
(RA 1.54) That person of deluded mind who performs ritual action without service to the Guru finds that his action is fruitless, like wealth obtained in a dream. (RA 1.55)
Whatever visible rite one performs, its fruit is obtained at every step;
however, one should cause the discourse on *rasa* to be performed by a satisfied Guru, O Dear One.
This is the instruction on the means of accomplishment, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon both [the teacher and the disciple].
The *Rasārṇava* is a great tantra; it is extremely difficult to obtain. It is to be kept secret through the grace of the guru, and should be acquired for the sake of attaining the fruit of success.
Having acquired the practices of alchemy (*rasakarma*) herein, one should not practice arrogance.

And having been authorized by the Guru, and having obtained permission, one should accomplish Rasabhairava by resorting to the body of Bhairavī, who is the goad of mercury (*rasāṅkuśī*). Thus has the origin of mercury and its majesty been described, O Mistress of the Gods.
Tell that to me, O Goddess of Gods; what else do you wish to hear?
The Second Chapter: [The Procedure for Initiation].
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"And who is the giver of the instruction on mercury? Tell me, O Lord, how one may become such;
and how, O God, does a disciple become intent upon the practice of mercury?
Śrī Bhairava said:
Free from longing and free from egoism, devoid of greed and deceit,
always devoted to the path of his lineage, and intent on honoring his guru; self-controlled, knowing how to instruct disciples, capable, and free from envy.
He was a knower of the Dharma, truthful in speech, and skillful; he was virtuous, endowed with good qualities, and pure.

He was an expert in the treatises on the various *rasas*, proficient in the pavilion for *rasa* alchemy, and knowledgeable in the procedures for the initiation into *rasa*, as well as in mechanical devices, medicinal herbs, and great elixirs.
The enumeration of passion is the seed-essence; the union of the couple is the *viḍ* (fecal matter);
coloring is the *sāraṇā* oil; the petals are the *krāmaṇas*. [One attains] excellence of color and softness through the digestion (*jāraṇā*) of the bound [mercury] of the child and the youth.
He who knows both Khecarī and Bhūcarī is considered a Guru.
(RA 2.6) He is one who understands place, time, and action; he is endowed with compassion and courtesy; he is free from greed and deceit, and is devoted to the practice of mantra. (RA 2.7)
Endowed with the characteristics of the ocean, profound and affectionate toward his guru, always delighting in the worship of the deities, the fire, the circle of yoginīs, and the [spiritual] family;
a disciplined disciple who knows the tantras, truthful and firm in his vows. (RA 2.8)
O Goddess, those men whose hands are marked with signs such as a water-jar, a hoe, a banner, or a conch shell should be employed in the attainment of treasures;
they are powerful, possessed of great strength, and have eyes that are black and red.

Those with crooked noses are always cruel; they are recommended for the practice of mining. One should employ those with fleshless heads, red hair, who are tireless, firm, and have warm feet in the art of alchemy.
First, O Goddess, one should examine the practitioners— Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras— in due order, ensuring they are well-composed,
have conquered their senses, endure hardships, and are endowed with constant diligence.
O beloved, those who are brave, learned, praiseworthy, and accomplished practitioners [are to be favored]. However,
those who are devoid of the initiation into the *rasa*, who lack the aforementioned characteristics,
who are subversive and devoted to evil— these one should avoid with great effort.

One should avoid that woman who is of evil conduct and wicked behavior, who is harsh, fond of quarreling, gluttonous, and evil-minded; one who has sunken eyes, is merciless, and who reviles the sacred word. (RA 2.15)
O lady of excellent hips, even if the entire circle of the earth were filled with such women as these, there would not be a woman like her who is a binder of passion (*rasabandhakī*).
A *kākiṇī* is a low-born woman; likewise, she is one who wears a golden girdle (*kāñcikācinī*).

A woman who is in her season during the dark fortnight is known as a *kākiṇī*. A woman who is in her season during both fortnights is considered a *kīkaṇī*. A woman who is in her season during the bright fortnight is a *kāñcikācinī*.
Endowed with fresh youth, beautiful in form, with a lovely smile and fine hair, that woman who always delights in a diet of milk,
who is ever fond of pleasant speech, and who takes pleasure in the stories of the Śiva scriptures.
Her face has the shape of a lotus; her gaze has the form of a blue water-lily. Her teeth are like diamonds; her lower lip is like coral. O Goddess, both her breasts are high, full, and symmetrical.

Her vulva is like the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree; her labia are even, and her feet are fleshy and smooth, with circular whorls of hair. She is dark-complexioned yet slender at the waist, and she is devoted to Śiva.

She should be known as Padminī, serene and with eyes like those of a deer. Whether on the full moon or the new moon day, she who becomes menstruating every fortnight is the sixfold one named Kākinī; she was previously described as the bestower of the essence.

But for him with whom Mahādeva is pleased, O Goddess of the gods, success in alchemy is achieved by that very [grace]; he should perform the works of mercury. For his intellect is stainless and certain in the accomplishment of mercury.
Therefore, both the guru and the disciple—having been previously described—shall become partakers of accomplishment.
The Śrī Devī said:
"By what means does the practitioner obtain a woman with such characteristics?"
Where there is form, O Mahādeva, no characteristic is found here.
Where a characteristic is found, no cultivation is found here; or else, for that which is devoid of form, by what means could form proceed?
"O Maheśvara, tell me, O Lord, where those three characteristics have been seen by you— that from which this [universe] is born— and what that means is.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain:
the birth from the father Sadāśiva, and that which occurred within the womb of Caṇḍikā. O Goddess, the intellect of those [women] shall become stainless in the accomplishment of the rasa.
One should cause the Tvaritā mantra to be given; one should recite it free from pride.
She who recites the mantra one hundred thousand times becomes endowed with auspicious marks.
Having bound the khecarī mudrā, one should recite the Pheṭkārabhairavī mantra.

"This Caṇḍikā is my mother; I was born from Kālikā, the destroyer of Tripura"—thus she should remember herself. She can indeed declare the past, the present, and the future throughout the three worlds.
His companions are such as his destiny shall be.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Great God, vessel of all knowledge!
"I ask, however, about the initiation of rasa (*rasadīkṣā*), for the benefit of practitioners indeed.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Bhairavī, to that state; I shall describe to you what is unprecedented."

Now listen to the procedure for the initiation of mercury (*rasadīkṣā*), which has been declared [by me]. (RA_2.37) In that place where the king is devoted to policy, powerful, and intent on dharma, and the minister knows the true essence of dharma and is endowed with devotion and faith; (RA_2.38)
In that regard, one should have this ritual performed: "Where people who are devotees of Maheśvara [practice] the binding of mercury and the elixir, in that place one should have it performed.
One should have it performed in a secluded place where no sacrificial animal is present.
In a well-concealed and beautiful place, free from all disturbances;
provided with walls and moats, protected by doors and bolts; in a secluded, pure, and pleasing spot, filled with various flowering trees.
It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned by ruddy geese, endowed with clusters of divine medicinal herbs, possessed of water and dark-green meadows,
and decorated with groves of white water-lilies, blue lotuses, *kahlāra* lilies, and plantains.
O Supreme Goddess, one should have a painted mansion-garden constructed.
In its center, O Mistress of the Gods, there should be a hall joined with intoxicated elephants,
provided with windows, and from which smoke issues upward.
It was adorned with red banners, equipped with all necessary implements,
and provided with well-distributed medicinal herbs, parched grain, wood, and lotuses from the forest; it had the deities of the directions painted upon it, and Vināyaka was duly worshipped there.

It is established by Umā and Īśa, and protected by the world-protectors. One should have a pavilion constructed with either one or two stories during the bright fortnight, O Goddess, when the moon and stars are in a favorable position.
On an auspicious lunar day and at a favorable moment, when the ascendant is aspected by a benefic planet,
having bathed, wearing white garments, and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
one should worship young girls with honey, clarified butter, curd, milk, and sesame seeds.

O Goddess of the Gods, upon that sacrificial altar constructed with bricks, which has been smeared with the dung of a tawny cow, surrounded by golden jars, strewn with barley and white mustard seeds, and adorned with perfumes and garlands— [therein one should worship].

Having carved a stone slab, O beloved, one should place the seal of the stone slab using the *rasāṅkuśa* mantra itself, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the fingers, the heart, and other parts. Therein, O beloved, one should install a mercury-liṅga together with gold.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, [this] is declared to be the root mantra of the King of Mercury (sūtarāja). O Dear One, one should invoke the goddess Rasāṅkuśī therein with the root mantra; having worshipped the guardians of the directions outside the square in their proper sequence, one should proceed.
Having stationed Nandin and Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgirīṭa and Mahābala,
Kumbhakarṇa and Sugrīva, and Bhṛṅgīka and Dṛḍhāyudha at the four gates,
one should worship them on the right and left sides.
Having first worshipped Śukra in the east, [one should worship] Skanda in the southeastern quarter;
then Rudra in the south, Pavana likewise in the southwest,
Śiva in the western part, and one should place Pāvaka in the northwest.
Umā is in the northern quarter, while Vyāpakā is in the domain of Īśa.
Also [there are] Lepikā and Kṣepikā, as well as Kṣārikā, Rañjikā, Lohaṭī, Bandhakārī, Bhūcarī, and Mṛtyunāśinī.
Vibhūti and Khecarī— these ten Dūtīs are to be worshipped in sequence upon the eight petals of the lotus, starting from the top petal and proceeding downwards.
[The five minerals are] Mākṣika, Vimala, Śaila, Capala, and likewise Rasaka.
Sasyaka, Gandha, and Tāla [are located] according to the sequence starting from the east. The Rudras have eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes;
their crowns are adorned with the crescent moon; they have blue necks and the bull as their emblem.
O Maheśānī, all eight Vidyeśvaras, each bearing their respective colors, are likewise to be worshipped in the second eight-petalled lotus; specifically, first,
the four Śaktis [are to be worshipped] in the pericarp, starting from the east.
Mālinī and Hemaśakti; Parāśakti is known as Balā, and Aparā is Vajraśakti. Kānti is to be known as both Parā and Aparā. And in the midst of those Śaktis is the omniscient Rasabhairava.
Resembling pure crystal, he has five faces and three eyes;
his fierce, tawny eyes blaze, as do his tongue, his face, his eyebrows, and his hair. He is difficult to behold, seated upon a corpse.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, with his crest formed by the crescent moon,
wearing a tiger skin, having a serpent as his sacred thread, and possessing a bull as his emblem—
the god with eighteen arms, his face slightly smiling.
One should worship the complete Śiva with the thirty-two-syllable mantra.
Now, listen to me as I recite the mantra of Raseśvara:
Oṃ hrīṃ krīṃ to Raseśvara, the Great Time, the One of Great Power, Aghora Bhairava, Vajravīra, Krodhakaṅkāla, kṣlauḥ kṣlaḥ. (RA 2.66–2.68)
On his lap [he saw] the Great Goddess, adorned with jewel ornaments,
radiant as refined gold, wearing yellow garments, and possessing three eyes;
she was graced by a pearl parasol held between two white chowries.
Holding a goad and a rosary in her two right hands,
and a noose and the gesture of fearlessness in her two left hands; she who has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament, the Great Goddess Rasāṅkuśī, blue-necked and full of compassion.
One should worship for the sake of attaining mastery over mercury (*rasasiddhi*) by means of the Vidyā consisting of the five seed-syllables:
*vāgbhava*, *bhuvaneśī*, and *śrībīja*, O Sovereign of the Gods;
as well as *mādana* and the *śaktibīja*. This Vidyā is exceedingly difficult to obtain.

Having performed the worship according to the prescribed ritual with incense, lamps, food offerings, flowers, betel, and sandalwood; with the resonant chanting of peace-texts (*śāntipāṭha*), and with the sounds of hymns and auspicious verses accompanied by the ringing of bells.
One should offer the bali-oblation with the Aghora mantra for the pacification of all obstacles,
diligently to the bhūtas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas—
conjoined with the Aghora mantra, beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
O Goddess, it accomplishes all rites and destroys obstacles and calamities. Having recited the *rasāṅkuśī* mantra according to one's capacity,
O Mistress of the Gods, one should prepare a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a vulva-diagram (*yonicakra*) and a girdle.
There, O Goddess, having performed the fire-oblation in due order with ghee and sesame seeds, one should place a water-pot filled with milk and provided with fruit,
endowed with the five jewels, and wrapped in cloths.
There, having consecrated [the vessel] individually with each of the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*),

and having worshipped the *arghya* vessel— filled with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and adorned with sprouts— and having sprinkled the practitioner with water from the *vardhanī* jar; (RA 2.79–2.80)
In this manner, one hundred and eight [times]; having consecrated [the disciple] according to the rule with the water from the arghya vessel, the knower of mantras,
O Goddess, should impart the Vidyā and cause the practitioner of mercury to recite it.

He should satisfy the prince, the yoginīs, and the yogins with appropriate food and drink, and he should certainly hold a vigil there. Thus initiated, the practitioner [should proceed] under Kṣuranāyikā.

There, upon the thread consisting of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should bind the *rasāṅkuśī* mudrā and recite one hundred thousand times, O Dear One, the Vidyā which consists of the five seed-syllables and is endowed with the five colors, being composed of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

O Goddess of the Gods, for him Rasabhairava is accomplished without obstacle. The supreme recitation consists of [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, performed at the conclusion of the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Non-violence is the sandalwood paste; truth is the flower; non-stealing is the incense.
Celibacy is the great lamp; the bell is non-acceptance of gifts;
the milk-rice porridge, O Great Goddess, consists of compassion for all beings.
Concealing these, one should worship the Goddess; he shall become a vessel for spiritual accomplishment.

One should recite this one thousand or even one hundred times at the three junctions of the day. By the grace of its command, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the elixir that moves through the sky arises, and for him alone, the divine medicinal herbs are perfected.
Having mounted the unrestrained [elephant] like a rutting elephant in the forest,
one who knows the goad of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) perishes upon encountering the sovereign mercury (*rasendra*).
One should contemplate [the subject] together with the science from a teacher who possesses the authentic tradition.

But regarding the application of the elixir (*rasa*), for one who desires accomplishment in every respect: (RA 2.91) Now, for the introduction of the inquiry, one should meditate with a concentrated mind on the previously mentioned Rasabhairava; one should practice while absorbed in that. (RA 2.92)

Having fixed the mind upon the stainless *anāhata* at the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), and having first performed the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) followed immediately by the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantra of the Lord of Tastes (*rasendra*) according to one's capacity. (RA 2.93)
Having again made a square, one should draw a hexagonal mandala in the center,
measuring one cubit or two cubits, using pure rice grains.
On a place smeared with fragrant substances, one should worship it with sandalwood and other offerings.
O Goddess, one should place the previously mentioned Rasabhairava in the pericarp;
in the hexagon, one should assign the group of six deities beginning with Mahākāla:
Mahākāla, Mahābala, Aghora, and Vajravīraka.
One should place Krodha and Kaṅkāla and worship them with the garland-mantras:

OṂ HRĪṂ KRAUṂ KṢLAIṂ KṢLAṂ HRĪṂ HRĪṂ HRĪṂ HRŪḤ HUṂ PHAṬ! To Raseśvara, to Mahākālabhairava, to him of fierce form, whose eyes are black and tawny: descend, descend! cause to descend, cause to descend! speak, speak! cause to speak, cause to speak! declare the auspicious and inauspicious, declare it, declare it! perform great protection, perform it, perform it! grant the perfection of mercury!
Thus are the garland mantras:
Oṃ mahākālabhairavāya hṛdayāya namaḥ;
Oṃ mahābalabhairavāya śirase svāhā.
Oṃ aghorabhairavāya śikhāyai vauṣaṭ; Oṃ vajravīrabhairavāya kavacāya huṃ;
Oṃ krodhabhairavāya netrāya vauṣaṭ.
Oṃ kaṅkālabhairavāya astrāya phaṭ svāhā; thus are the placements of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) performed everywhere, ending with svāhā.
In this manner, one should first perform the placement of the fingers;
these are the root mantras for the worship of the six limbs.
Thus, with the syllables of the placement and the *kuṭas*, one should worship with perfumes and flowers.

One should place a full water-pot in the center, along with a shallow bowl filled with rice. Upon that, one should set a ghee lamp and consecrate the wick with mantras. Then, having brought a maiden or a very handsome youth, [one should proceed].

One, two, three, four, or five—whatever may be obtained—one should bring together and worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings. (RA 2.100) One should place the mantra upon each individual [deity], as well as the deities beginning with the Heart. (RA 2.101)

Then, having gazed upon that lamp, all those young maidens see the deity in the lamp; and the young men [see] the auspicious or inauspicious, as well as success or failure. Thus do the young maidens speak.

"Having understood the introduction to the question, one should proceed with the work of mercury (*rasakarma*). O Goddess of the God of Gods, he who has previously purified his self through the Lord of Mercury (*rasendra*) and has been born after dying seven times [in this practice] shall not abandon the purification of mercury."
Having thus understood what is auspicious and inauspicious, and being endowed with the grace of the deity,
one should worship the Goddess Rasāṅkuśī in the pavilion as before;
and having also fully honored the preceptor with incense, garlands, sandalwood, and other offerings.

Having offered the bali-oblation with the Aghora mantra, one should then perform the ritual action. The medicinal herbs are in the eastern part of the pavilion; extraction by liquid and sweating are in the south-east; the smelting of metal is in the southern part; and grinding and so forth are in the south-west.
The act of liquefaction (*drutikriyā*) takes place in the western [direction]; blowing (*dhamana*) in the north-western, O Dear One;
the excellence of the colors (*varṇotkarṣa*) in the northern; and the piercing of the essence (*rasavedhana*) in the north-eastern.
Having placed the seat of the Guru in the center, O Leader of the Gods.
The ritual acts beginning with *niyāmana* and ending with *krāmaṇa*, O fair-faced one,
should be performed by the practitioner using the mantra *rasāṅkuśa*.
O Goddess of the gods, that *Rasabhairava* who was previously described—
*Sadyojāta* is his knee; *Vāmadeva* is his secret organ. *Aghora* is his heart; his face is known as *Tatpuruṣa*.
*Īśāna* extends up to the middle of the eyebrows; the half-moon is his forehead.
O Goddess of the gods, the *bindu* is above that; the *nāda* is situated above the *bindu*, between the forehead and the head. *Śakti* is established in that very place.
*Vyāpinī* resides in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*); above that, however, is *unmanā*.

The Unmanifested (unmanā) [attains] the state of the Unmanifested (unmanībhāva), the imperishable station of the Unmanifested (unmanāpada). Above that is the supreme reality, abiding in the void, higher than the highest.
It is the void, the void, and again the void—the triple-void (triśūnya) which is free from affliction.
Nabhas, gagana, and vyoman; kha and ākāśa are the absolute, partless, stainless, eternal, waveless, and free from disease.
It is beyond conceptual proliferation, without support, devoid of qualities, yet the sphere of all qualities.

One should always meditate on such a form: Rasabhairava within one's own body. And when one meditates with unwavering focus, when the mind is motionless in the midst of the fire, then the mercury is likewise bound and rendered immobile.
And when the meditative absorption wavers, the essence does not remain in the fire.
Outside the mandala at night, one should worship the yakṣas, gandharvas, piśācas, and likewise the rākṣasas with liquor, fish, meat, and so forth.

Obstacles to the performance of rites and obstacles to the fruits thereof arise in their respective ways by the millions; therefore, for the sake of pacifying them, one should first worship Vaṭukeśvara and the sixfold grace-bestowing deities, and then proceed with the practice.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the ritual action, one should honor the child with eight sets of eight favors and employ him; for the accomplished substance bestows accomplishment.
However, once accomplished, it may destroy the debate; therefore, one should abandon that place.

One should wander for alms like a bee (*mādhukarī-bhikṣā*). When the great elixir (*mahārasa*) is well-perfected, an obstacle may arise from negligence; once the binding of the elixir (*rasabandha*) has been accomplished, the pacification of the elixir (*rasaśānti*) must be performed. One should not cause agitation of the elixir (*rasakṣobha*).

O Goddess, one should not show the *rasa*; one should not let it fall into the hand of a woman, nor should one speak of the secret to a woman; for one must conceal the substance from them. One should not act with the wealth of others, nor should one touch the wives of others.

One should never eat another's food, nor should one place trust in others. One should not give to those of wicked intent, nor to a beggar under the guise of a social gathering. On the eighth day, on the full moon, on the new moon, and on the anniversaries of the Yugas...
During the solstices, the equinoxes, and especially on the fourteenth day,
one should perform the Rasa festival according to one's means.
O Goddess, he who performs the Rasa festival in this manner, endowed with devotion, [attains the supreme state].
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and various other evils are destroyed.
Wherever practitioners perform worship according to this rite,
neither disease nor misfortune prevails there, nor do epidemics arise.
Having thus established this kind of worship with the *rasas* according to the ritual procedure,
the subsequent rite should then be performed by those who desire their own welfare.
However, for one who acts otherwise, success does not arise.
There is ruin and the fear of evil; for the destruction of the intellect arises [from it].
There is contempt and a multitude of diseases, as well as doubt at every step, due to laziness, excessive greed, and the talk of others.
"Even when consciousness has arisen, the Kulakas carry it away, O beloved.
Initiated into the works of mercury (*rasakarma*), one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*);
tell me that, O Goddess of Gods. What else do you wish to hear?"
The Third Chapter [The Depositing of Mantras]. The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, Protector of the World, Master of the Universe!
"Explain the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), which assists in the work of mercury (*rasakarma*).
The venerable Bhairava said: 'I shall further proclaim another [practice], the mantra-form of Rasāṅkuśī.'"
But the fifth house, O Goddess, is difficult to attain even for gods and dānavas.
There are four principal houses; the fifth is the Haṃsa-house, where accomplishment beginning with the letter *ma* resides in the fifth house.

Form is that which rests upon the *liṅga*; the *māyā* is the possessor of the *liṅga*, and she is to be known by means of the sky (*ākāśa*). The line of the *bhaga*, however, is in the fifth [syllable].
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, the seed-syllable is the unsurpassed sound.
The syllable *hrīṃ* and the syllable *krīṃ*, followed immediately by the *haṃsa*-intellect; the Lord of Practitioners should take up this great mantra, the noose of Time (*kālapāśa*),
as the gatekeeper for that [great] undertaking, along with *rasāṅkuśī*.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times for that person; then the great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*) proceeds.
One should cause the feces of a young child to be taken by means of that very [mantra];
O Supreme Goddess, one should cause the ashes of the funeral pyre to be taken by that same [means].

That field is the supreme place; there the Lord of Essences (Rasendra) resides. One should sweep the place with a broom. O Goddess, she known as Kubjikā is the Khecarī of thirty-two syllables, established within the five Nadīs.

Then there are four Siddhas; eighteen persons are traditionally taught as being joined with the five objects. Furthermore, the meditation is fivefold, conjoined with the six Yoginīs, and endowed with the sequence of twenty-seven.
Endowed with eighty-one squares and joined with the five coverings—
by this sequential yoga, one should worship the broom;
by this one should sweep the field where the Lord of Mercury (rasendra) resides.
As for the anointing, it should be performed right there. One should have Caṇḍaghaṇṭā made;
that goddess, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, is established in the eastern house.
The goddess Caṇḍabhairavikā is situated in the southern house.
One should take cow dung for the purpose of smearing, O fair-faced one.
The goddess Caṇḍakāpālinī is stationed in the northern house;
having taken water from there, one should smear the mandala ground with it.
One should place the seventeen-syllable Kālī-mantra upon a flat stone;
one should employ the thirty-two-syllable Ghoramantra upon the crusher. O Goddess, being consecrated by the Kālapāśa-mantra, one should take up the sour gruel.
In this way, the Khecarī clan brings about union with virtuous action. Those eighty-eight thousand divine Khecarīs who reside there all become his servants; they grind medicinal herbs for him.
For all of them, however, there is but one mantra, joined with four syllables: "So 'haṃ haṃsaḥ. That is the *vidyā* of the *khecarīs*, and by name it is the *Kulakhecarī*.
Having placed black mustard seeds and rock salt, one should consecrate sour gruel there with that *vidyā*, the *Kulakhecarī*; [this] is the king of mantras, the *Rasāṅkuśī*.
One should recite the *astravidyā* there, which was known previously by Bhārgava.
Having thoroughly ground the molasses-brick, O Dear One, [one should take] that ground essence.
What need is there to mention the King of Mantras? One should not apply the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the Three-Headed One; rather, one should then hold it with haste.
One should apply the great mantra named Ḍāmara to the channels;
one should apply the great vidyā of the Cintāmaṇi to the armors;
and one should apply the great mantra of Caṇḍikā to the vessel.
O lady of excellent hips, one should place the ninefold Vidyā upon husks and cow dung.
One should place the goddess Tripurābhairavī upon black mustard and sour gruel; O you who are worshipped by heroes, Kālarātri is to be placed upon molasses.
One should place the three-eyed one with three peaks; O Goddess, one should place the fire in the water. There are eighty-four Caṇḍikās.
O Dear One, the Kṣetrapāla and the Aghora-weapon are to be placed in the square.
One should employ the Mahāpāśupata weapon in the crucible.
O Goddess, one should employ this collection of mantras in the place of mercury;
then, O Beloved, the fruit is accomplished for that practitioner.
One should recite the great mantra Rasāṅkuśa within the heart;
as for the other mantras of the Yoginīs, one should cause all women to recite them. However, that king of mantras, Rasāṅkuśa, must not be disclosed by him.
One should likewise guard the secret of women, as well as the *praṇava*,
from the violation of the great pledge (*mahāsamaya*), just as one guards the heart of women. Those mantras beginning with Kubjikā which have been revealed by me—
They have agitated the three worlds, yet they do not honor me, O beloved.

By means of the knowledge of the "liquid-hook" (rasāṅkuśa), the three worlds shall come under one's control. Having understood this as the "mantra-deposition" (mantranyāsa), one who knows the measure of the furnace-fire of the yantra—
Performing the operations of mercury (*rasakarma*), the practitioner attains accomplishment.
The Fourth Chapter: [Description of the Yantra, Crucible, and Fire].
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, what can even one who knows the mantras do without knowing the yantras, the crucibles, the fires, and the measures? You should tell these to me.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Metals, minor metals, and base metals; cloth, sour gruel, and *viḍa* salt;
bellows, iron vessels, and furnaces; a mortar, a stone, and a pestle; a crucible, a curved tube, cow dung, resin, and fuel.
And clay-made implements, as well as pestles and mortars; sand-sieves, cloth-strainers, tongs, earthen vessels, and iron ladles; weights, balances, and the touchstone.
A bamboo tube or a metal tube; saline earth, charcoal, and likewise medicinal herbs;
oils, acids, salts, alkalis, poisons, and secondary poisons—having thus gathered these materials, he should apply the ritual procedure.

With a liquid substance filling half the belly of a vessel, and with the mouth of that vessel turned sideways, one should heat the mercury suspended by a thread resting on the bottom; this is known as the *dolāyantra* (swing apparatus). (RA 4.7)
Having prepared two iron crucibles measuring twelve finger-breadths in size—
one provided with a slight opening— place the mercury together with sulfur inside one crucible and insert that [first] crucible into the other.

Water should be placed beneath the *sūtaka*; fire is applied above and below. O auspicious lady, one should diligently provide a copious amount of garlic juice, strained through cloth with care, having first soaked the mercury and sulfur.

Having placed [the substance] inside a vessel, turn it upward; prepare another sturdy vessel and carefully seal the joint with clay and cloth. Inside that vessel, one should always apply the *kapota*-type *puṭa* using a fire of one *karṣa*.
One should place a fire of dried cow-dung or even a fierce fire beneath the apparatus.
One should proceed in this manner for three days; thereafter, one should release the apparatus into hot water or onto a heated hearth, but one should not perform the procedure when it is cold.
In this process, the mercury is not consumed, nor does it go anywhere;

by means of this sequential application, one should perform the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of the sulphur-born [mercury]. Fire is above and water is below, while the collection of the mercury (*rasa*) is in the middle.
O Goddess, this is the crucible apparatus (*mūṣāyantra*); it causes the digestion (*jārayet*) of *gagana* and other substances.
I shall now describe the womb-apparatus (*garbhayantra*), which is the cause for producing a paste (*piṣṭikā*) and ash (*bhasma*).
One should take a firm crucible made of clay, four finger-breadths in length.
It should be three finger-breadths in width at the middle; one should fashion the opening circular.
There should be twenty parts of iron and one part of guggulu. Having ground it very finely, one should add water again and again.

Then one should apply a coating to the crucible and place the paste at its base. One should apply gentle heat on the ground using a fire of husks for one day and night or three nights; thus the mercury will turn into ash.

In the processes of digestion (*jāraṇa*) and killing (*māraṇa*), as well as in the coloring (*rañjana*) of the king of mercury (*rasarāja*), there is one supreme machine (*yantra*) which is the ultimate secret; therein the medicinal herbs possess great power.
Yet, this [mercury], when devoid of medicinal herbs, is bound by force through the machine.
The impurity (*sūtaka*) pervades everywhere, except for that which bears the characteristics of a mountain. For even a clod of earth, when drawn by the deities, moves;
therefore, the power of the machine must not be disregarded by one who possesses discernment.
Through the conjunction of mantra and medicinal herbs, this mantra indeed brings about perfect accomplishment;
here the Aghora mantra should be recited. At the conclusion of the recitation, one should worship the mercury.
This practice must be performed in a secluded place, for it has been observed that [if done otherwise] it becomes fruitless.

There is no exhaustion of the fragrance; there shall be no exhaustion of the taste; rather, the exhaustion of the apparatus is to be recognized. When the operation on the apparatus is altered due to the unavailability of magnetite (*kāntaloha*), one should have the apparatus made of iron. (RA 4.25)
Without knowing the signs of the fire, there would be a loss of half the mercury even for one who knows the method for the loss of the apparatus; [otherwise], there would be a loss of a fourth part.
In two months, there would be a second part lost; in three [months], a third part would be lost.
For he endures even a great fire wherever he is directed to stand. Having filled one shallow bowl with sand, one should place another bowl upon it; there, one should cook it slowly over a mild fire.
Likewise, with the five alkalis, urines, and salts,
*viḍa* is then known as *haṃsapāka* by those skilled in the meaning of the machines and procedures.
There are clays that are black, red, yellow, and white in color.

The first is the best, the last is the youngest; the middle one is considered the middling. O beautiful goddess, clay mixed with burnt grain husks, or even that made from a curved stalk for the preparation of the crucible, is recommended.

The kilns are burnt, the husks are burnt; the clay of the anthill is burnt, and the dung of goats and horses is burnt until it has turned black. So too are the leaves of the *vāsaka* plant, together with the clay of the anthill.
One should grind it with fire-water until it reaches a state of smoothness.
One should knead [the clay] with that and bind the crucible (*koṣṭhikā*) with a curved neck.
Charcoal, burnt husks, and burnt anthill earth [are to be used].

Cīra, charcoal, and dross; even by a diamond it is not split. Six parts of burnt charcoal and one part of black clay—cīra, charcoal, and dross—this is proclaimed as the diamond crucible (*vajramūṣā*).

Having burnt husks equal in measure to the cloth, and adding four parts of clay mixed with *kupī* stone, it is proclaimed as the "excellent crucible" (*varamūṣā*). The crucible is traditionally held to be of two kinds: the transparent (*prakāśā*) and the blind (*andhamūṣā*).
O Goddess of the Gods, the *prakāśamūṣā* is shaped like a shallow bowl;
it is highly praised by experts for the extraction of substances.
However, the *andhamūṣā* should be made resembling the shape of a cow's udder.
It is joined with a lid and has its head slightly raised. Likewise, in leaf-paste, in dye, and in the blending of two substances, it is the same:
when it is perforated and dull, it is deep and suitable for drawing out the essence.

Two parts of sesame ash combined with one part of brick should be known as the ash crucible; it is beneficial for the purification of silver. Two parts of Mokṣakṣāra combined with one part of brick [should be used].

The portions of clay are for the purpose of purifying silver; they are excellent, O woman of excellent complexion. Mixed with the red group [of substances], saturated with the red group, and smeared with the red group, they are beautiful in all purifications.
Mixed with the white group, flooded with the white group, and having an ointment made from the white group; she is beautiful in white purifications.
Mixed with the fecal group, she desires steadfastness in the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*).
One should perform the extraction using a coating of the red group [of minerals].
One should apply a coating to the crucible with poison, borax, and *guñjā* seeds;
this should be done in an open space, or alternatively, by applying charcoal.
Having placed the substance in that crucible, the wise one should cause it to melt;
O Goddess, the coating consists of red clay, sea salt, earth, and sulfur.
While the gold is being melted, there is a yellow luster, while in silver it is white.
O Sovereign of the Gods, she appears blue-like in bell-metal (*śulva*) and black in steel (*tīkṣṇa*).
In tin (*vaṅga*), she has the luster of a flame and the color of a dove; in lead (*nāga*), she is like soiled smoke;
O Goddess, she is greyish-white in stone (*śaila*) and tawny in iron (*āyasa*).
In the magnet (*ayaskānta*), it is smoke-colored; in the loadstone (*sasyaka*), it becomes red;
in the diamond (*vajra*), there are various kinds of flames; and in the *khasattva*, it has a pale white luster. When there are no sparks, nor bubbles, nor a mass of lines, nor sound—
When it has entered the crucible, it becomes stable like a jewel; then they declare the metal to be purified.
First, the additive (*pratīvāpa*) should be applied, and immediately after that, the pouring-in (*niṣeka*);
indeed, the additive is known as the covering, while the pouring-in is understood as the immersion.

They desire that consecration which is performed as a ritual bathing (*snapana*). Immersion (*vāpa*), pouring out (*niṣeka*), and bathing (*snapana*)—when [the mind] has become swift and pure, they indeed desire heat alone; they do not desire cold.
When there is a white radiance accompanied by sound, that is to be known as the "Iron-Turning" (*lohāvarta*) Vaiśvānara fire; then the stainless *sattva* falls [into it].
It is sixteen finger-breadths wide and one cubit in length, auspicious.
O lady of excellent complexion, for the purpose of bringing down the elements and sentient beings,
one should blow upon the crucible with air; the crucible, made of bamboo, khadira, mādhūka, or badarī wood, should be filled with firm charcoal.

One should kindle the fire by means of a bellows through the path of the flame. (RA 4.57) The furnace should have a wide opening and a contracted interior space, with a long internal lattice-work constructed on its surface;
it should be equal in size to a crane’s neck, and a curved tube (*vaṅkanāla*) should be provided. There should be a hollow lotus-shaped pipe made of clay, long and cylindrical. (Ras 4.58)
In an earthen vessel, or a metal bowl, or one made of magnetite, or on stone, or crystal, or even on a pearl-stone;
the presser must be made very firm, four finger-breadths in height.
And that mountain should be made of iron or else of magnetite;
one should perform the purification by means of the mantra known as Aghora-āstra or the Mahāpāśupata, and with that very [mantra], one should purify the ground.
One should ignite all kinds of fuel, especially substances that burn, by means of that [fire]; one should purify the *khalla* with that very same [fire],
purify the mercury (*rasa*) with it, and set it aside on an auspicious day.

And having placed it upon the crucible, one should meditate upon the form of Śiva. O Goddess of the Gods, having obtained the grace of the deity, one who knows the measure of the fire in the crucible-furnace should also know the medicinal herbs for the sake of attaining success in alchemy (*rasasiddhi*).
The dimensions of the yantra, the crucible, and the fire have been described, O Mistress of the Gods;
tell me that, O Queen of Devas. What else do you wish to hear?
(RA_4.65) The Fifth Chapter: [Determination of Medicinal Herbs].

The Goddess said: O Lord of the Gods, you ought to tell me of the medicinal herb by which these rites, beginning with subjugation (*niyāmana*) and ending with transference (*krāmaṇa*), are accomplished.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Sarpākṣa, Vahni, Karkoṭī, Kañcukī, Jalabindujā, Śatāvarī, Bhṛṅgarāja, Śarapuṅkhā, and Punarnavā.
Maṇḍūkaparṇī is matsyākṣī; brahmadaṇḍī is śikhaṇḍinī;
anantā is kākajaṅghā; and kākamācī is kapotikā. Viṣṇukrāntā is sahacarā; sahādevī is mahābalā.
Balā, nāgabalā, and kṛṣṇā; cakramarda and kuruṅgiṇī;
pāṭhā, āmalakī, and nīlī; jvālinī, padmacāriṇī, phaṇin, trijihvā, and gojihvā; kokilākṣa and ghanadhvani. (RA 5.4–5)
Ākhuparṇī, triparṇī, dviparṇī, ekaparṇikā, tittiḍī, kṣīriṇī, rāsnā, meṣaśṛṅgī, kukkuṭī,
kṛṣṇaparṇī, tulasī, śvetā, and girikarṇikā.

These are the medicinal herbs that provide restraint; they are provided with flowers, roots, and leaves. O lady of excellent vows, one should perform a fomentation bath (*dolāsveda*) using these roots.
[They are] Caṇḍālī, Rākṣasī, Vyāghrī, Khaḍgārī, and Gajakarṇikā.
Śaṅkhapuṣpī is agnidhamanī; lāṅgalī is bālamocakā. Raktasnuhī is raktaśṛṅgī; raktikā is nīlacitraka;
śṛgālajihvā is bṛhatī; and vajrā is cakrī as well as rājikā.
Ekavīrā is *narakasā*; Rudantī is *brahmacāriṇī*; Uccaṭā is the root of *māninī*; Kumārī is *raktacitraka*. Lakṣmī is *śākhoṭaka*, and Kañcukī is *meṣaśṛṅgikā*.
Himāvatī is the *somalatā* plant; Modā is *vyāghranakhī*, and Śamī is [the other]. (RA_5.11) Kāñcanī is *vanarājī*; Kākamācī is *keśinī*.
Ajamārī is *koṭarākṣī*, and Hanūmatī is *aṅganāyikā*. (RA_5.12)
Narajīvā, hemapuṣpī, kākamuṇḍī, kālikā, toyavallī, gajārī, haṃsāṅghrī, kuhukamvikā, tāmbūlī, sūryabhaktā, and rasanirjīvakārikā. (RA 5.13)
Bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*) and *gosandhī*; *devadālī*, *indravāruṇī*, *vākucī*, and the seeds of *brahma*; cotton and black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīraka*);
*kaṅgunī*, black *kanaka*, white *arka*, and that which is born from ants (*pipīlijam*).
*dantinī* and *yavaciñcā*; *karkoṭī* and *kāravallikā*;
(*RA_5.15*) *gojihvā* and *kākajaṅghā*; *mahākālī*, *śambarī*, *śvetaguñjā*, and *sitāṅkola*; *paṭolī* and *bilva*.
Each individual medicinal seed shall slay Rasabhairava.
Raktasnuhī, Somalatā, Rudantī, Raktacitraka, Śākhoṭakī, Dagdharuhā, Modinī, and Vṛddhadāruka.
Triśūlī is the black cat’s claw (*kṛṣṇamārjārī*). Cakrikā, kṣīrakukkuṭī, devadālī, and śaṅkhapuṣpī [are synonyms]. Kākamācī is hanūmatī.
Nīlajyotis is tṛṇajyotis. Utkaṭā is hemavallarī.
Tridaṇḍī and Brahmadaṇḍī; Cakrāṅkī and Sthalapadminī;
Nāgajihvā and Nāgakarṇī; Vīrā and Vartulaparṇikā;
Arkapattrī and Vaṃśapattrī; Tāmraparṇī and likewise Īśvarī.

O Indurī, O Goddess of the lords of gods! O Dear One, [these] bind the mercury. By means of substances—whether stationary or moving—that possess intense smell, taste, and touch, the mercury is killed and indeed bound through sweating and rubbing.
Sūryāvarta, kadalī, vandhyā, kośātakī, vajrakanda, udakakaṇā, kākamācī, śigruka,
and devadālī— O Mistress of the Gods, these are proclaimed as the drāvikās.
Yogins remove the defects of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and of mercury (*pārada*). [The following herbs are used:
*kākamācī*, *ghanarava*, *kāsamarda*, *kṛtāñjali*, *varāhakarṇī*, *saṭirī*, *haṃsadāvī*, and *śatāvarī*.
Tāmbūlī, nāginī, brahmī, haṃsapādī, lakṣaṇā, arjunī, and kṣīranālī; kāravello, arkapattrikā, vyāghrī, cavī, and kuravaka—these are the *krāmika* plants, O Goddess worshipped by the gods. (RA 5.25)
Brahmadaṇḍa, Sudaṇḍa, and Lohadaṇḍa as the third—these are suitable for *rasāyana* [alchemy/elixirs]; they correspond to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. Bhūpāṭalī, Kaumārī, Siṃhavallī, and Śūkarī.
Hemaparṇī and paṭolī, as well as nāgavallī and bhṛṅgarāja—these are declared to be the eight roots (mūlikās). Listen, O beloved, to the five jewels (pañcaratna):
the goddess Mantrasiddhāsanā, and likewise Kaṅkālakhecarī.
Indirā, Kṣamāpālī, and Niśācarī as the fifth— O Goddess, these five jewels are excellent for the purification and digestion of mercury,
and each one individually, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, is praised for the fixation of mercury.

One should seize it with the goad of mercury (*rasāṅkuśa*). O observer of good vows, at the union of mercury and Bhairava, it bestows the five jewels and the accomplishment of moving through the sky (*khecarī-siddhi*). The three alkalis are *ṭaṅkaṇa* salt, barley ash (*yavakṣāra*), and *sarjikā*.
Sesame, apāmārga, kadalī, palāśa, śigru,
mocikā, radish, ginger, and tamarind are proclaimed to be the alkalies of trees (*vṛkṣakṣāra*).
Sour vetasa, jambīra, citron, and the sour chickpea (*amlacaṇaka*) are also [sour substances].
The orange and the tamarind are the best among the group of sour vegetables, such as the *cāṅgerī*. Sea salt, rock salt, *cūlikā* salt,
*sauvarcala* salt, and *kāca* salt are proclaimed as the five salts.
*Saktuka*, *kālakūṭa*, likewise *sitamustā*,
*śṛṅgī*, and *kṛṣṇaviṣa*— these five are indeed the great poisons (*mahāviṣa*). Also *snuhī*, *arka*, *unmattaka*, *karavīra*, and *lāṅgalī*.
There are five principal poisonous plants: indeed, the excellent oils are those produced from safflower, *kaṅguṇī*, *naktā*, sesame, and mustard;
and the urine of elephants, horses, goats, and women, with cow’s urine as the fifth.

Bile is of five kinds, derived from fish, cow, horse, man, and peacock. (RA_5.36) Fat is of five kinds, derived from fish, sheep, snake, elephant, and peacock. (RA_5.37) The excrement of pigeons, blue jays, vultures, peacocks, and roosters [is also used]. (RA_5.38)
Mañjiṣṭhā, saffron, lac, khadira, and likewise āsana—this, O Goddess of Gods, is the red group. Now hear the yellow group:
kusumbha, kiṃśuka, rātrī, pataṅga, and madayantikā.

The white group consists of lime, tortoise shell, conch, pearl oyster, and cowrie shells. Guñjā, ṭaṅkaṇa, honey, clarified butter, and molasses constitute the five liquefiers. Glass, ṭaṅkaṇa, and sauvīra—these three, O Dear One, are the purifiers.
All alkaline substances remove impurities; all acidic ones are awakening agents;
poisons destroy darkness; and unctuous substances produce softness. Thus the groups of medicinal herbs have been declared, which grant success in the union with mercury.
They perform the ritual action through union with that; and the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are the great essences (*mahārasāḥ*). Tell me that, O Goddess of Gods! What else do you wish to hear?
The Sixth Chapter: [The Determination of the Characteristics and Purification of Abhraka and Other Substances]
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva! What are the characteristics of the *śaktis* regarding their fitness for the work of mercury (*rasa*)? Let the purification (*saṃskāra*) thereof be told.
The illustrious Bhairava said: Once, when the goddess Girijā beheld the captivating Hara,
she released her vital energy (vīrya), which then became auspicious abhraka.
Yellow, black, white, and red arise from the union with the earth.
Listen now to [the description of] mica (*abhra*), magnetite (*kāntapāṣāṇa*), diamond (*vajra*), and *vaikrāntaka*.
Mica is of four kinds: *pināka*, *dardura*, *nāga*, and *vajra*.
When fire has entered a *pināka* reed, there arises a crackling sound (*ciṭiciṭi*).
When fire has entered a frog, the sound is like that of a cock.
But when fire has entered a snake, O Goddess, it emits hissing breaths.
But when the thunderbolt has entered the fire, it remains like a thunderbolt, O beloved.
The *pinākābhra* causes leprosy; the *dardura* brings death.
The *nāga*, constantly residing within the body, produces disease and fistula (*bhagaṃdara*).

O Dear One, vajra-abhraka should be employed for both alchemy (*rasa*) and elixirs (*rasāyana*), according to its various color distinctions; that abhraka is of four kinds. Red and yellow are for gold, while black is for both gold and the body.
And in the process of transmutation (*tārakarma*), one should always discard glass and slag. O Leader of the Gods,
previously,
mica (*abhraka*) was processed with the water of *agasti* flowers and with the juice of white water-lilies (*kumuda*).
With *kapittha*, *induka*, and *jambīra*; with *meghanāda* and *punarnavā*; with *yavaciñcā*, sour gruel, and sour *karavīra*; with red lotuses;
with forest ginger, *sūraṇa*, and *bhūdhātrī*; with the root of *bhiṇḍī* and *amlavetasa*.
O Goddess, one should steam [the substance] for three days with the bile of a ram and a rabbit, with horn-oil, the juice of *śamī*,
with *vajravallī*, *kṣīrakanda*, black pepper, and *sumukha*;
thus it becomes free from defects.
First, having prepared "grain-cloud" (*dhānyābhraka*)—
thirty *palas* of extremely fine space-dust (*vyomarajas*) smooth as butter— and two *palas* of small fish,
one *pala* of sesame powder, three *palas* of *guñjā*, and one-quarter *pala* of *ṭaṅkaṇa* salt.
That bolus, bound with wheat and impregnated with the five products of the cow,
is placed in a crucible furnace; by blowing with bellows and a fierce fire,
the essence of mica falls out, as do all other essences.
Repeatedly processed with the exudations of sweating medicinal herbs and repeatedly subjected to *puṭapāka* cooking,

it becomes "dead" (*mṛta*) when cooked many times in the *puṭas* of *pañcanicula*. Having formed it into a mass, one should provide the moisture-free, stainless essence (*sattva*) which is like the sky.
With *umā* fruits and flowers, soaked in sixty-day-old sour gruel and crushed with a stalk of flax (*umadaṇḍa*),
movement clearly dissolves.
Having placed *agnijāra* in a new jar, one should keep it above the earth.
The sky quickly melts, possessing a luster equal to a pearl.
O Goddess, the powder of *kañcukī* processed a hundred times with the juice of *kañcukī* will cause the sky and all metals to melt.
Having been kept in fermented rice water (*dhānyāmlaka*), it remains in a solution of *nicula* alkaline water; it attains a liquid state, appearing as if its taste and color have vanished.
Having ground it with the juice of *agastya* flowers and *sūraṇa* tubers...
The mercury that has entered the crucible remains for a month;
it becomes like a liquid essence. O Goddess, when mica is sprinkled with goat’s urine and sown with the powder of *kapitinduka*, it becomes like water.
The powder of mica produced by rubbing it with the seed-powder of *kākinī* and sprinkled with the milk of *snuhī* for seven days becomes liquefied when heated.
The five parts of *apāmārga* and well-ground mica [should be used].
One should place it in an earthen vessel so that it becomes water. Then,
having ground abhraka powder together with *kapālī*, black pepper, and realgar,
it should be sown [into the liquid] and further combined with the juice of *agastya*.
The juice of *mārjārapādī*, crushed with sour fruits and roots,
should be placed inside a *mātuluṅga* fruit and buried in the midst of rice; it will liquefy in just a fortnight when combined with *śilā* and rock salt.

Having been processed in a single vessel for seven days, one should throw it into the juice of *muni* mixed with *dārvī* and black pepper, and saturated with the juice of *maurvī*. Combined with *sauvarcala* salt and *meghā*, it is saturated with the juice of *vajravallī*.
When heated in a closed crucible, it becomes like water.
(RA 6.29) The powder of mica produced from clouds, when treated with an equal amount of the ash of *vegāphala* and in the milk of the *kuliśa*, melts at that very moment when heated. (RA 6.30)
Having ground "space" (mercury) combined with black salt in the juices of *vajravallī*, one should cook it in a crucible sealed with a shallow bowl; it will melt like water.
Again, [it is processed] with beef, rock salt, and *arka* (calotropis), joined with the juice of munīyā.
The interior of a plantain bulb should melt for three days in a fire of cow dung.
Having taken a leaf of black mica (*kṛṣṇābhra*), one should smear it with *pīlu* oil and heat it in the sun for seven days; then, having placed it in sour liquid (*āmle*) for three days—
Vajra, arka, citraka, and alkali; likewise tumbī alkali, arjuna, sarja alkali, yava alkali, and ṣṭaṅkaṇa shall be the eighth.
And also kṣīrakanda juice, as well as vajrakanda juice.

One should apply a coating of the group of alkaline substances combined with the three types of *vṛhatī*. When that mica-leaf (*patrābhra*) is smeared with this paste and heated in a bronze vessel by means of the sun's heat for three days, it becomes liquefied.
Alternatively, one should soak a leaf of mica within the milk of *kañcukī* using that same [substance], until it becomes a powder;
then one should collect the mica leaves after immersing them in sour liquid for three days.
One should smear it with that paste and place it in a bell-metal vessel for seven days under the heat of the sun; liquefaction occurs instantly.
[This is done] with the powder of *kākāṇḍī* fruit and likewise with the five fluxing agents (*drāvaka*).
The powder of mica, when heated and placed within a crucible, melts. Magnetite (*kāntaloha*) is of four kinds:
*bhrāmaka*, *cumbaka*, *karṣaka*, and likewise *drāvaka*; *romakānta* is the fifth.

One, two, three, four, or five; that [mandala] faces in every direction and is yellow, black, and likewise red. It may consist of these three colors individually. In sequence, the deities therein are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.

When drunk, it is piercing by touch; the black variety is best for alchemy (*rasāyana*), while the red-colored one, O highly fortunate lady, is praised for the binding of mercury (*rasabandha*). The *bhrāmaka* type is the lowest, while the *cumbaka* is middling, my dear.

O Goddess, the *karṣaka* is the best, and the *drāvaka* is the best of the best. One should cause the mass of iron to revolve; that is the *kānta*, O beloved, which is the *bhrāmaka*. One should kiss the *cumbaka*, the *kānta*; one should attract [the metal], O beloved, with the *karṣaka*.

That which directly liquefies metal is a flux; it may end with buttermilk (*takra*) or end with *romaka* salt, so that the emergence of hair-like scales occurs. The inferior [flux] has one opening, while the middling has two or three openings.

The four-faced and five-faced types are excellent; the all-facing type is the most superior. The *bhrāmaka* and *cumbaka* types are praised for the destruction of diseases, as well as for alchemy (*rasa*) and elixirs (*rasāyana*); the *karṣaka* and *drāvaka* types are beneficial.
The charioteer is an elephant intoxicated with rut; the beloved is called the goad.
Having dug up the field, it must be seized with great effort.
O beautiful goddess, one should avoid that which is scattered by wind and heat.
One should saturate a magnet situated outside with goat's blood.
Having wrapped it in a cloth smeared with goat's blood,
and having enveloped it in a goat skin, one should place it on the ground as before.

Extracted over seven months, one should place it in a water-pitcher. It should always be worshipped with red flowers, and when honored with red garlands, ointments, liquor, and meat, it should be employed for alchemy (*rasāyana*).
It is refined with goat's blood; by this sequential yoga, it becomes a *bhrāmaka* and a *cumbaka*. It becomes a *drāvaka*, O Dear One.
I shall describe the refinement of quicksilver (*sūtaloḥa*) which bestows supreme bliss.
And upon entering a living body, it bestows physical comfort and strength. Without *kāntaloha*, mercury never enters the body;
[but with it] it pierces and pervades quickly, like a drop of oil upon water.

Without the *sūta* it is not beloved; without the excellent *sūta* it is not beloved; when united with both the beloved and the *sūta*, the preparation sustains the body. Having taken *yavakṣāra*, one should place it in a smooth vessel.
With the powder of black pepper and mica, one should form a pill-bond; the magnetite (*kāntaloha*) will melt when blown [with a bellows]. There is no need for deliberation here.
Having ground thirty parts of magnetic magnetite with the water of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), [one should proceed as before].

With that very [substance], the washing should be performed. As for the five *niṣkas* of *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax), one should place it in a worn-out cloth, combine it with honey and clarified butter, and seal it (*puṭet*); having kept it for the duration of a month, purification occurs therein, O beloved. (RA 6.59–60)
The root of *sināḍikā*, weighing ten *niṣkas*,

should be combined with a decoction of the three fruits (*phalatraya*) and thoroughly rubbed in a mortar. It should then be placed evenly in three crucibles (*trimūṣā*), each measuring eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*).
A coating of mercury should be applied; its cost is one *niṣka*.

Then, having fashioned a five-faced mold (*śivapañcamukhī*) corresponding to the crucible, and having firmly attached it to the hand of the machine, [one should place] the *khoṭaka* upon the surface of the stone.
Having mixed it with oil, one then obtains *kāntanāga* through the sequential application of the process of mica (*abhraka*); one should also accomplish the precipitation of the flux (*drutipāta*).
When the Ocean of Milk was being churned by the gods and demons with Mount Mandara, [this occurred].

That nectar was drunk by the gods, and they attained immortality. O Goddess, as they drank, drops fell upon the surface of the earth; having dried, they attained the nature of vajras, possessing various colors and great power.
Certain drops were produced: pure grains, as well as Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, in many such ways.
They were white, red, yellow, and black—thus fourfold.
Men, women, and likewise eunuchs follow in sequence.
Those who are rounded, full of fruit, radiant, and very large should be understood as men; those devoid of lines and dots [are women]. (RA 6.68–69)

Those joined with lines and dots are female; those that are fragmented, triangular, broad, or long are to be known as neuter. Those possessing *sattva* are endowed with strength; in the case of metals, they have the nature of permeating.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, male *vajras* quickly effect the binding of mercury;
female *vajras* produce luster for the body, though they possess little power; and neuter *vajras* are devoid of potency and enter into the metal with difficulty. (RA 6.71–72)
In all undertakings, Kṣatriyas are to be avoided; in the work of mercury (*rasakarma*), they are proclaimed to be of the highest, middling, and lowest [qualities].
O Dear One, [the veins] are thick, very thick, middling, subtle, and even subtler.

Through cracking, burning, and splitting, those [mercury preparations] that are free from defects, free from calamities, and full of potency are the best; they are stainless and exceedingly powerful. Indeed, in the practice of *rasāyana*, such a mercury bestows upon the practitioner the qualities of *aṇimā* and the other supernatural powers.
The Kṣatriya [attains] the destruction of death; he removes wrinkles, gray hair, and disease. The Vaiśya likewise becomes a maker of wealth; he brings the body to firmness.
The Śūdra effects the alleviation of illness and brings about the stabilization of youth.
The weak are for the weak, women for women; men are beneficial for all.
As is one's birth, so is one's energy; as is one's nature, so are one's qualities;
as is one's taste, so is one's character; and as is one's character, so is one’s mate.
O Dear One, the *kuliśas* produce a color corresponding to their excellence:
the *śyāmā*, *śamī*, *ghanarava*, *vaṣā*, *mattakodrava*, *ākhukarṇī*, the *munitaru*, *kulattha*, and *amlavetasa*.

The juice of these [plants] is also [used for] *meṣaśṛṅgī*. One should purify the *vajra* [diamond] from the root *sūraṇa* for three days; it attains purity, O Goddess of the Gods. *Meṣaśṛṅga* is the bone of a serpent, and *kūrmapṛṣṭha* is bitumen (*śilājatu*).
Milk, the juice of *snukkīlāla*, and *kāntapāṣāṇa*—
and also *vajraka* and *vaikrānta*— one should place these within it, O beloved, and having applied a *puṭa* in a fierce fire, [heat it] until the end of the *puṭa* has been reached.

One should grind *kulattha* and *kodrava* with horse urine and pour it over a heated anvil until it has been reduced to ash. This is the *Kāpālika* yoga, the supreme method for the slaying of a diamond (*vajra*).
Having applied a paste of honey, *meṣaśṛṅga*, realgar, sulphur, borax, *vaikrānta*, and also *tālaka*, soaked in the milk of *vajrī*,
inside the crucible, one should cause it to be rotated [in the furnace] for one full cycle.
Diamonds die there, and they unite perfectly in pairs. One should grind together sulphur, realgar, the mouth of a magnet, and the teeth of a rabbit with *vetasāmla*.

With this perfected paste, one should apply a coating to the crucible; when heated within a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), the diamond (*vajra*) dies in an instant. The diamond mixed with that very [substance] [is transformed] into silver and gold; of this there is no doubt.
Tālaka, gandhaka, kānta, tāpya, camphor, ṭaṅkaṇa, the stone of the *ciñcā* tree, and the horn of a ram, ground together with female menstrual blood and applied as a coating to the crucible,
cause the diamond (*vajra*) to die instantly when heated.
The five parts of the *śarapuṅkha* plant should be ground with menstrual blood;
or else, the seed of the *peṭārī* should be ground with rice-water.
Alternatively, three *karṣa*s of the root of cotton (*kārpāsa*) should be ground with rice-water.
Or the root of *āraktarākā*, ground with breast milk;
or one should grind *vajrakanda* with the milk of a *vajrī* cow, O observer of good vows.
When that paste is enclosed in a crucible and heated, even diamond (*vajra*) itself becomes reduced to ash.
In a great river-oyster shell, it should be infused for one day with the milk of *uttaravāruṇī*. O observer of excellent vows,
it should be encased with this paste of *tāla*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, and *vajravallī*.
When heated in an andhamūṣā crucible, the vajra dies instantly.
O Goddess, one should place the vajra in the midst of the paste of kāntaloha and grind it with fragrant oil; thus, O Sovereign Lady, the vajra dies.
Diamond, when sprinkled with water from *kulattha* beans mixed with *kāsīsa*, *saurāṣṭrī*, *tālaka*, and the alkali of *apāmārga*, becomes dead (*mṛta*).
[It should be] enveloped in *amṛtā*, the root of *timira*, seeds, bark, and milk.
A thunderbolt made from the horn of a ram, when coated with clay, is killed by means of *puṭa* fumigations. *Peṭārī*, *haṃsapādī*, *vajravallī*, *sūraṇa*,
and the sprouts of the *aśvattha* tree, O Goddess— all these, when ground with breast milk, [achieve the same].

With this prepared paste (*siddhakalka*), [the substance] is wrapped, placed inside a *bṛhatī* fruit, and coated on the outside with clay; it dies [i.e., is reduced to ash] in seven roastings (*puṭa*).
[This is done] with white moon-streaked flower-water, sulphur, the three [substances], and honey.
O Goddess, the diamond (*vajra*), when wrapped [in these], becomes dead through the process of *puṭapāka*.
Having ground together the *aśvattha*, jujube, *bhiṇḍī*, honey, and the bone of a crab with the milk of *snuhī*, a Brahmin [metal] becomes dead through the *puṭa* [process].

With the milk of *karavīra* and *arka*, along with *meṣaśṛṅga*, realgar (*hiṅgula*), and *udumbara*, [this preparation], when subjected to *puṭapāka*, effects the killing of a Kṣatriya. *Bālā*, *atibalā*, sulfur (*gandhaka*), and the bone of a crab (*karkaṭāsthi*)...

By means of *uttaravāruṇī* with milk, through the process of *puṭapāka*, a Vaiśya is killed. (RA 6.104) By means of *kaṇḍūla*, *sūraṇa*, *śilā*, garlic, and the milky sap of the *nyagrodha* and the conch shell, even a Śūdra dies in an instant. (RA 6.105)
The thick [parts] become soft through many thick folds; the fruit-skins and so forth vanish and become as if well-steamed.
Having ground the five parts of the *āmalaka* and the pale-yellow *indravāruṇī*, softness is produced. (RA 6.106)
The vajra wrapped with this [substance] dies after seven coatings.
O Goddess, one should place the vajra of the life-force of the *mātṛvāhaka* in the middle during steaming on a swing for three days; it will become equal to a leaf of *guṇa*.
O Goddess, one should place the *vajra* in the midst of castor-oil plants;
O Goddess, when one month has passed, it becomes equal to the leaf of the *guṇa* plant.
O Goddess, one should place the *vajra* in the midst of the paste of *kānta*.
One should grind together cotton, neem leaves, and jujube leaves; having wrapped this in a ball of *kāntaloha*,
one should place it between the knees, covered on the outside with a betel leaf.
Within two watches (*yāma*), that *vajra* certainly becomes soft;
at that very moment the *vajra* dies, [dissolving] into the *tārā* within the gold—of this there is no doubt. It should be placed inside the fruit of a *jambīra* and enclosed within a cloth pouch.
One should boil it in a decoction of *kodrava* for three days according to this sequence; thus that *vajra* becomes a solidified mass (*khoṭa*), which instantly mingles with gold.
It should be smeared with *nāgavallī* and wrapped in its leaf itself.

The watch [of time] situated between the knees certainly becomes soft. At the base of the vajra-creeper, one should insert a soft vajra and apply a seal with effort; it is reduced to ashes in that very instant.
For it quickly brings about bondage from pleasure; yet at that very moment, it liberates the being.
They are the pacifiers of all death and the bestowers of all accomplishments. Having placed the vajra, pierced through, in the midst of a chain of bones—
When that has been steamed in a water-vessel, it will attain a liquid state for seven days.
Having added the three alkalis, asafoetida, sour chickpea flour, and *amlavetasa*, along with the milk of *jvālāmukhī* and the juice of the flesh of the land-tortoise; (RA_6.118)

O Goddess, when the diamond (vajra) has been crushed with these [substances] and likewise steamed in a dolāyantra with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, it becomes like mercury. Alternatively, mica (*abhraka*), pearl, and coral may also be steamed in this manner.
Honey and blue flowers, great yellow emeralds,
lapis lazuli, crystal, and so forth— just as these melt into water,
so too is the mass of metal seen when heated until it takes on the color of fire.
If it is infused just once by a single person, the dead shall become like water. However,
a pearl infused for seven days with *vetasāmla* and placed inside the interior of a *jambīra* fruit should be deposited within a heap of grain.
By means of *puṭapāka* [fumigation], that powder becomes like water.
Listen, O highly fortunate goddess, to the great elixir known as *vaikrānta*.
The lord of the Daityas, Mahiṣa, was perfected; he was born from the body of Hara.
The goddess Bhagavatī Durgā crushed him with her trident. His blood fell wherever it landed upon the earth; in each of those places, there appeared vaikrānta, a great mineral of adamantine form.
It exists to the south of the Vindhya mountains and does not exist at all to the north;
it completely cuts through metals, and for that reason it is known as vaikrāntaka.
It is white, yellow, red, blue, and has the luster of a pigeon.
One [complexion] resembles a peacock’s tail, and another has the luster of emerald. Black bestows the perfection of the body; yellow when [the subject is] yellow, white when white;
red grants the accomplishment of all aims, as does that which has the luster of emerald.
The remaining two are fruitless and should be avoided. Thus, *vaikrānta* is of seven kinds.
O Goddess, in whatever field this *vaikrānta* is situated, the best of practitioners, having worshipped Bhairava and Vināyaka there, should take it. (RA 6.128–129)
Vaikrānta, finely ground into powder and honored by gods and demons,
should be placed within the core of a *vyāghrī* root; having been heated in a crucible and kept there,
one should steam it over a gentle fire with horse urine for seven days.
Then one should dry it in the shade; this is the excellent *vaikrānta*.
Alternatively, one should steam it for seven days with salt, alkali, urine, sour liquids, black oil, and a decoction of *kulattha* and *kodrava* beans.

Vaikrānta is indeed the powder of the barren woman; one should grind it in equal parts and saturate it with goat’s urine. Having dried it in the shade and then smelted it in a closed crucible, the essence of the crucible is produced.

Powdered *vaikrānta* stone, processed with the alkaline water of *mokṣa*, *moraṭa*, and *pālāśa*, and saturated with cow’s urine; combined with a paste of *vajrakanda* roots, lac, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and mixed with the juice of *meṣaśṛṅgī*.
When the essence has been fused in a silent crucible and heated, it releases its potency.
