One should grind vaikrānta and vajrakanda with vajra-water and buffalo butter; then, having formed a mass with honey, [it is ready].
Having purified it, one should blow upon the *sattva*; it falls like an *indragopa* insect.
O Goddess, from the juice of the *ketakī*, *kāṅkṣī*, and *maṇimanthaka*, together with *sakhecarī*, *vaikrānta*—which resembles mercury—is produced through sweating. (RA 6.136–137)
"Gold, silver, copper, or the dust of kāntaloha—
by this method of sweating, they melt like water. Thus has been stated the characteristics and so forth of the four [substances], beginning with abhraka.
"Tell that to me, O Goddess of Gods; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Characteristics and Purification of Abhraka and Other Substances," in the *Rasārṇava*, the compendium of alchemy (*rasasaṃhitā*), within the dialogue between the illustrious Pārvatī and Parameśvara.
[Chapter Seven: The Determination of the Characteristics and Purification of Major and Minor Metals, Irons, Gems, and their Melting and Killing.]
The Goddess said:
"Together with their characteristics and refinements, command me regarding the great essences (*mahārasas*),
and anything else of that kind, O God, which is beneficial for the science of alchemy (*rasavidyā*)."
Śrī Bhairava said:
Mākṣika, vimala, śaila, capala, rasaka, sasyaka, darada, and srotoñjana— these are the eight [minerals].
And thus there are eight great flavors; listen first to these.
But Kṛṣṇa, having heard the *Bhārata*, entered into yogic sleep;
his sole was pierced by a hunter who mistook it for a deer.
Those drops of blood that fell there upon the ground, having the appearance of nimba fruits, became indeed stones of honey. There,
the honey-stone was of two kinds, distinguished by its yellow and white divisions.

O Goddess, *vimala* is of three kinds: white, yellow, and red. Likewise, *mākṣika* [is purified] in sesame oil, sour gruel, and buttermilk; in cow urine, the juice of plantain, and decoctions of *kulattha* and *kodrava*. Thus is *vimala*.
O woman of excellent complexion, one should repeatedly sweat the *śūraṇa* tuber;
it should be provided with three *puṭa* applications combined with alkali, acids, salt, oil, and clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), and thus that pair becomes purified.
Honey-powder, processed with breast milk and repeatedly saturated with the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, releases its essence when well-heated, having been treated with *ṭaṅka* and *kaṅkuṣṭha*.
It is then thoroughly drenched in the juice of plantain root, *tulasī*, and sour orange.

Endowed with seven layers of sevenfold [enclosures], combined with the five fluxing agents (*pañcadrāvaka*), and moistened with breast milk, when heated, the *mākṣika* mineral releases its essence. [It is processed] with honey, *gandharvataila*, cow’s urine, and clarified butter.
Honey repeatedly processed with the essence of the core of plantain roots releases its essence when heated in a crucible—
a soft substance resembling copper.
Having added the juice of *devadālī* along with one-fourth part of borax, [it is processed].
Having made the mouse manifest, one should blow upon it while keeping the desired *sattva* in view.
What wonder is there in this? A well-cooked *sūraṇa* tuber, heated in a *puṭa* with *vātāri* oil inside a casing of plantain juice, attains excellent purification when burnt by the *puṭa*.

It should be soaked in cow urine and the milk of *snuhī*, and then processed with castor oil for one day. Having been ground and formed into pills, one should blow it like ore to extract the essence (*sattva*). This same procedure applies to *sasyaka* as well.
Tāpya, āvartaka, dhātumākṣika, and madhudhātuka are synonyms for mākṣika.
It is bitter and sweet, cures urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, consumption, and skin diseases;
it removes phlegm and bile, is strengthening, is a vehicle for other substances, and is a rejuvenative elixir.

Since even fevers, derangements of the humors (*saṃnipāta*), and poverty perish by the mere mention of its name even at a distance of a hundred *yojanas*, who then would not employ this "piercer of metals"? (Rasārṇava 7.15) [The metal] is purified with the juice of *śigru* and with *kāṅkṣī*, *kāsīsa*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
Combined with *vajrakanda* and processed with the juices of plantain,

and joined with the lye of *mokṣaka*, this essence (*sattva*)— when smelted in a sealed crucible (*mūkamūṣā*)— becomes like the moon and sun; it bestows [the desired result], of this there is no doubt.
"Fallen and unfallen"— O Goddess, this twofold classification of mountains is also proclaimed in other texts, as it has been celebrated by many gods.
In the summer heat, the mountain ranges, scorched by the sun's glare, [yield] the essence of their minerals.
And they emit an exudation; that is celebrated as *śilājatu*.
Like a stone, the mineral ore (*dhātuka*) is heated; it is called *śailaja*, *girisānuja*, *jatvadrija*, and *giri* or *śaila*—thus has it been proclaimed and recited by you.
Śilājatu is purified by being heated with alkaline substances, sour liquids, cow’s urine,
or even with cow’s ghee; having placed it in an iron vessel, one should diligently purify it with the juices of the three myrobalans and fresh ginger.
Having pulverized a mountain and having duly bound a pill with *dhānyāmla*, fermented grain-liquor, and various poisons, one should cause the fickle one to fall as if he were a stone.
A fickle one who is fair, white, ruddy, or black is highly recommended.
That which has the luster of gold and the luster of a star is especially a binder of mercury.
The remaining two are middling and like lac; however, those two that melt quickly are fruitless.
It melts in fire like tin; therefore, it is called *capala* (the volatile).
If one binds the *capala* with a cloth and it leaps across the ocean, the cloth will immediately wrap around it; therefore, it is known as *capala*.
One should refine the *capala* on a mountain peak using the *puṭapāka* method.

It indeed effects bodily binding; specifically, it effects the binding of mercury (*rasabandhana*). Capala causes piercing (*vedha*) by means of capala; that which is dense and mobile is like a cloud. Capala is considered to be a smooth engraver (*lekhana*) that produces bodily strength and iron.
Rasaka is of three kinds according to its resemblance to earth, molasses, or stone. That which is yellow and has the appearance of earth is the best *mṛttikā-rasaka*;
that which resembles molasses is to be known as middling; and that which resembles stone is the lowest.
Having stirred the *rasaka* with the exudation of bitter *alābu*, one should cook it;
thus purified and freed from defects, it becomes yellow in color. What wonder is there in this—that the *rasaka* is transformed by the juice of a menstruating woman’s flower?

Having processed it in sequence with mercury, he makes the copper red; by means of the *tripuṭa* [process], he makes it gold. Even when situated in fire, the great power whose nature is *sattva* does not diminish. Having ground the *rasaka* and bound it in cloth, the wise one [proceeds].

O Goddess of the Gods, one should cause it to be placed in the urine of women for seven nights. One should then repeatedly saturate the *rasaka* with the juices and leaves of red and yellow flowers, as well as with alkaline substances,
oils, and acids.
Combined with wool, lac, turmeric, *pathyā*, *bhūlatā*, and soot,
and placed within a sealed crucible (*mūkamūṣā*), when heated together with borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*),
it will undoubtedly release a metal essence (*sattva*) resembling mercury.

Gobhadra is *rasakastuttha*. Kṣitikiṭṭa is *rasodbhava*; kharpara is the enemy of eye diseases. Rītikṛt dyes copper. (RA 7.37) *Rasaka* is a colorant; it is dry, generates wind (*vāta*), and destroys phlegm (*śleṣman*).

That essence destroys the three humors and eliminates defects of the eyes. Having drunk the kālakūṭa poison, Garuḍa was unable to endure even the nectar; likewise, he consumed the venom of the poisonous snake as if it were ambrosia.

When it has emerged spontaneously from the two beaks, that *sasyaka* becomes *kālika*. That *sasyaka* of his should be processed into a single substance with female urine, or with menstrual blood and rabbit blood; one should let it remain for one day.
O Maheśānī, its powder, combined with *pādasaubhāgya* and placed within *karañja* oil, should be left for one day.
Placed in the middle of an *andhamūṣā* crucible, one should heat it for three *kokila* intervals.
A beautiful substance resembling an *indragopaka* insect falls;
from that, the *sasyaka* gem, when smelted, becomes single-colored,
free from black spots (*kālikā*), red, and shaped like the throat of a peacock.

Sasyaka is mayūratuttha; it generates fire, destroys [the effects of] time, is suitable for *rasāyana*, and acts as an arrestor of aging. Sasyaka attains purification when processed with the group of red substances (*raktavarga*).
Cinnabar is said to be of three kinds: *carmāra*, *śukatuṇḍaka*, and *haṃsapāda* as the third; each subsequent one is superior in quality.
Furthermore, cinnabar is of two types, distinguished by being either powdered (*cūrṇa*) or liquid mercury (*pārada*).
Having cooked it for three days each in beef, buffalo urine, curd, sour gruel, sesame oil, and [cow's urine], one should saturate it with peacock bile. Then,
one should cause mercury (darada) to fall into a water reservoir using a *pātanāyantra*.
But the *sattva* is like mercury; it is produced here, of this there is no doubt.
The *laghukandarasa* is a barbarian [substance]; *hiṅgula* is powdered mercury;
that which is born from the coloring of gems is indeed called *carmāragandhika*.

Mercurial cinnabar (*hiṅgula*) is indeed bitter and hot; born from mercury and sulfur, it is divine, removing iron-based ailments and leprosy, and it kindles divine strength, intellect, and the digestive fire.
What is surprising here? Well-refined cinnabar [is treated] many times with goat’s milk and with groups of acidic substances.

White gold, when heated by intense heat, directly assumes the luster of excellent saffron. O Goddess worshipped by the gods, river-born gold has the shape of an anthill’s peak; when broken it has the brilliance of a blue lotus, but when rubbed it has the hue of red ochre.
Having been processed many times in cow dung, juice, urine, clarified butter, honey, and fat, that [metal] quickly binds the *sūtaka*.
Thus the great minerals (*mahārasa*) have been described; listen now to the semi-minerals (*uparasa*), O beloved.
Gandhaka, tālaka, śilā, saurāṣṭrī, khagagairika,
rājāvarta, and kaṅkuṣṭha— these eight are known as the minor minerals (uparasas).
O Goddess, in the past, in Śvetadvīpa, which was adorned with all kinds of jewels...
On the delightful shore of the Ocean of Milk, which consists of all desirable things,
[he was surrounded] by preeminent Vidyādharīs, by women,
by beloved Siddha-women, and likewise by hosts of Apsarases.
"O beloved, in the past you sported with celestial nymphs and others,
with various songs and dances, as well as with many kinds of musical instruments. While you were thus sporting, your *rajas* became manifest."

"O lady of beautiful hips, that pollen was exceedingly fragrant and captivating. Due to the great abundance of that pollen, your garment turned red; having left that garment there, you bathed well in the Ocean of Milk."
Surrounded by celestial nymphs and accompanied by the gods, you went to the city;
meanwhile, your garment of dust was carried away by the waves into the midst of the ocean. Thus, O blessed lady, your blood has entered the Ocean of Milk.
During the churning of the Ocean of Milk, this [substance] arose together with the nectar;
by its own fragrance, it gladdened all those gods and dānavas.
Then, the hosts of gods said: "Let this be named Gandhaka."
"For the purpose of binding the mercury, may it serve for its digestion;
may all those qualities which have been proclaimed for pārada be present here as well"—
thus was it spoken of old by the delighted hosts of gods, O Queen of the Suras.
Therefore, this is known as *gandhaka* on the surface of the earth.
And it is of three kinds, O Goddess: the best resembles the beak of a parrot; the middling is yellow in color; and the inferior is white in color, my dear.
Having dissolved [the substance] with *karañja* seeds and egg-oil, one should sprinkle it three times separately into goat’s milk and the resin of the *unmatta* plant. Then,
one should saturate it with the powder of *jvālinī* seeds and with fish bile.

Or, having been infused for seven days with the juice of *bhṛṅga* flowers, it is washed with water; then heated over embers of *badara* wood and rolled upon a vessel of iron smeared with ghee over a gentle fire,
on top of a cloth soaked in ghee.
Sulphur, when washed with the exudate of the *bhṛṅga* tree, becomes beneficial.
For sulphur is by its very nature liquid in form;
one should purify sulphur in milk as well as in the juice of fresh ginger.

And in the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, as well as in the juice of *nimbuka*, purified seven times, the sulphur becomes stainless. *Tālaka* consists of *paṭala* and *piṇḍa*; of these two, the former is superior.
A wise person should subject talaka to sudation one hundred times with the juices of *snuk*-milk,
*kaṭukālābu*,
sesame, mustard, and *śigru*, as well as lac, salt, and jaggery, each applied separately.

With these combined with *ṭaṅkaṇa*, the *tālaka* will melt in the *bhūdhara* [crucible]. The wise one should grind *vyādhighāta*, *phalīkṣāra*, *madhuka*, and *kuṣmāṇḍaka* for seven days with juices produced from *punarnavā*.

Having given all [the ingredients] in the proportion of one part each, one should then apply a "gaja" (elephant-shaped) *puṭa* in a dropping-furnace (*pātanayantra*). The essence will fall from the *sutālaka*.
Red mineral (*raktā śilā*), however, when cooked with beef and the sour juice of *luṅga*, [is effective].
One should saturate it with the juices and bile of red and yellow flowers. Then, one should saturate the *saurāṣṭrī*— which consists of white, black, and powdered fragments—
with cow-bile one hundred times.
Having heated it, one should cause the *sattva* to fall; this is the extremely secret method of transference (*krāmaṇa*).
O Dear One, there are three kinds of *kāsīsa*: white, black, and yellow.
Having ground the *kāsīsa*, however, with the juice of *kāsamarda*...

One should saturate it with the juices of *rājakośātakī* and with bile. Gairika is of three kinds, distinguished as red, golden, and pure; one should saturate each of these separately with the juices, decoctions, and bile of the red group of substances.
By this sequential method, one should smelt pure red ochre until it gradually becomes white and then red; thus the excellent *sattva* falls out.
O Goddess, *rājāvarta* is of two kinds, distinguished by its form as a pellet (*gulikā*) or a powder (*cūrṇa*).
O Goddess of the lords of gods, one should cook that powder in an iron vessel combined with buffalo milk and mixed with cow’s ghee.
O Mistress of the gods, that same powder should be mixed with the oil of *kunaṭī*.

By means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) associated with good fortune, one should cause it to be formed into a solid mass and smelted with charcoal from *khadira* wood; thus the beautiful essence (*sattva*) is released. O Dear One, that [essence] has the luster of coral and consists of pure essence (*sattvamaya*).

With the juice of *sūryāvarta* and water-drops, with the juices of the roots of fire-plant (*vahniśigru*) and plantain (*kadalī*), with the essence of the plantain-root, with the juices of *vandhyā* and *kośātakī*,
and likewise with the juices of *kākamācī*, *devadālī*, and *vajrakanda*.

By these— either individually or collectively— namely alkali, acid, oil, rock salt, the great minerals (*mahārasa*), and the secondary minerals (*uparasa*)— when impregnated (*bhāvita*), they attain purification. [Also] lac, salt,
*saubhāgya*, *dhūmasāra*, and the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*).
The root of *śigru*, beeswax, *pathyā*, *guggulu*, and mineral pigments;
combined with *sarjikā*, resinous exudate of the *sarja* tree, oil-cake, and *ūrṇā*; along with the five: the excrement of a pigeon, small fish, and *drāvaka*. (RA 7.91–92)
Sesame, mustard, wheat, mung beans, and chickpea flour,
combined with goat’s milk, is proclaimed as *vajrapiṇḍī*.
By means of this *vajrapiṇḍī*, joined with the fifth [ingredient] from buffalo [milk],...

The great essences, being delighted and processed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), are blown upon with a fierce fire in the crucible; O observer of good vows, they release their essence. Thus, from stones, from living beings, and from earth, the essence is produced.
Thus the secondary minerals have been described; now hear of other metals hereafter. Gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead—these are the six kinds of metal, which, as before, are imperishable.
In that regard, O Queen of the Gods, at the outset, the essence is known to be of two types of iron:
*tīkṣṇa* and *śulva* for ordinary purposes; whereas *vaṅga* and *nāga* are considered impure (*pūtiku*).
Likewise, there is that which is produced from mercury (*rasaja*), that which is produced from the earth (*kṣetraja*), and that which is produced from a mixture of metals (*lohasaṃkaraja*).

Gold is born of three kinds; a fourth is not found. O Goddess, gold is of two types: that which is reddish and that which is yellow. When heated it is red, when cut it is white, and on the touchstone it has the luster of saffron.
Gold that is respectful, soft, and lustrous, free from dross and copper, and enriched with the sixteen colors, is recommended for both the body and metalwork.
Clay [treated] with the acids of citron for five days [is likewise used].
Gold is purified by means of *puṭapāka* using ash and salt.
O Dear One, silver is of two kinds: white and black-and-white.
Silver that is heavy, glossy, soft, and white is considered the best.
Melted by the king of alkalis (*kṣārarāja*), silver (*tāra*) that desires purity is cast three times into the midst of *piśācī* oil.
And copper is said to be of two kinds, O Mistress of the Gods: red and black.
It should be glossy, capable of withstanding repeated hammering, with red leaves, and of the finest quality.
Having been smeared with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, salt, alkali, and sour substances,
the copper leaf should then be immersed in the juice of *nirguṇḍī*.
Rohaṇa, vājara, and thirdly paḍālaka—
these three types of sharp iron are known as kāntaloha. That which is blue or black, glossy, with a fine edge, and auspicious is [the best].
Guḍūcī and haṃsapādī, naktamāla and the three fruits (phalatraya),
gopālakī for the milks, and tumburu as a subduer of iron—
these one should boil in their decoction for the removal of the defects of the mountain ore.
Tin is to be known as being of two kinds, distinguished by its white and black varieties.
That which is white, light, soft, and glossy is called the best lead (*vaṅga*). Lead (*nāga*), however, O Goddess, is of one kind; it melts quickly and is soft and heavy.

By means of the powder of buffalo bone, through sowing [it] and sprinkling with its urine, tin likewise becomes purified; so too does lead by means of elephant bone and urine. Gaurī-phala, kṣuraka, rajanī, and tumburu—
The seeds of *kuberākṣa* and of *mallikā*, O beautiful one—
by means of an application of the ash of *palāśa* and dried *apāmārga*, together with the milk of *snuk*, through sevenfold soaking, they purify the serpent.
Then, one should cast tin into it through the application of the milky sap of *snuhī*.
[One should also process it] with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, *halinī*, the bulbous root of *kañcukī*,
*citraka*, *guñjā*, *karañja*, *dhuttūra*, *hayagandhā*, and the foot of *tālaka*.
When the roots of *naktamāla*, *iṅgudī*, *śakra*, and *vāruṇī* are ground together with buffalo buttermilk and left to soak for seven nights,
sprinkling [the liquid] over all types of metal destroys their impurities; of this there is no doubt.

Gold that has been repeatedly saturated with the juices of the powder of *devadālī* fruit can be liquefied by the addition [of other substances]; it will never become hard again. By its power, one may likewise liquefy all metallic essences (*sattva*).
O Goddess, by adding an equal portion of *suragopa* and the dust of *suradālī* to the *āvāpa*,
one makes gold appear like water.
[One also prepares it] with frog-bone, fat, *ṭaṅka*, *hayalālā*, and *indragopaka*.

Gold, by means of a secondary addition (*prativāpa*), remains fluid for a very long time. Ashes of the *jvālinī* plant, strained after being soaked twenty-one times in cow’s urine, should be dried; by the addition of these, even hard iron (*tīkṣṇa*) placed in a crucible will melt.

By being processed twenty-one times with the ash of *nicula* and the juices of *ketakī*, even a sharp substance will attain fluidity through the addition of these ingredients. [Likewise,] by being processed for seven days in a conch shell with the juice of ripe *dhātrī* fruit...

Again, by means of the inner chamber (*kañcukītoya*), it is infused for seven days. O Goddess, when that sharp powder is placed between a pair of shallow bowls (*śarāva*) and firmly sealed, it is produced in the form of mercury (*rasa*).
Tālaka, sulphur, realgar, orpiment, red ochre, ferrous sulfate, alum, yellow orpiment, blue vitriol, mica,
and likewise the excrement of dogs, jackals, hyenas, and cocks.
One should take equal parts of the excrement of a peacock, a vulture, and a cat; having processed this paste three times with the milky sap of *snuhī* and the juice of *devadālī*,
one should coat iron leaves with it using an eighth part [of the paste].
One should heat it until the metal becomes molten; then one should sprinkle it with these very [substances].
One should grind the roots of *aṅkola* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and then apply it as a coating to the metal. O Dear One, one should maintain it while it remains in the fire.

Then one should apply another coating with fish bile whose essence has been extracted, O Goddess of Gods; one should hold it over the fire, O Beloved. Then one should again perform the application [of a coating] derived from the root of *lāṅgalī*.

Iron that has been melted with three coatings becomes stainless, like clear water. O Goddess, powdered tortoise shell, ram’s horn, and bitumen, when used as a secondary additive (*prativāpa*), make it as firm as powerful water.
One should prepare an alkali from *arka*, *apāmārga*, *musalī*, *nicula*, *citraka*, as well as *kadalī*, *potakī*, and *dālī*.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should strain it six times into buffalo urine.
By means of *āvāpa*, one should cause this dust produced from minerals such as *abhra* to liquefy;
specifically, the root of *dantī* will cause it to liquefy, just as water does. Dust produced from *vaikrānta* should be saturated with the juice of *uttaravāruṇī*.
By means of a secondary additive (*prativāpa*), one may liquefy metals until they resemble water.
I shall now describe the liquefaction of gems as well as the melting of the sky (*ākāśa*). [The substances are:
*triphalā*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), the three alkalis (*trikṣāra*), and the five salts (*paṭupañcaka*).
Balā and Atibalā, and the third, Mahābalā; Aśvagandhā, Cavī, Nārī, Bhūlatā, Mātṛvāhaka, Gopendramaṇḍalī, as well as Ṣaḍbindu and Dvimukhī.
Dhīra, sūraṇa-kanda, kañcukī, punarnavā, snuhī, arka, unmatta, halinī, pāṭhā, and uttaravāruṇī;
ayaskānta, gokṣura, mṛdu-dūrvā, and amlavetasa.
One should take ten *pala* each of *śilājatu*, *sauvīra*, *viṣagandha*, and *kaṭaṅkaṇa*, and have them all ground into a fine powder. Then,
one should prepare two *kumbha* measures of horse gram (*kulattha*) using wood from the *tiniśa* tree.
One should boil it over a mild heat until only one *kumbha* remains;
with that decoction, one should saturate the powder twenty-one times.
Having smeared the gems with that, one should blow upon them while they remain in the decoction.
In a single day and night,
those base metals such as mica and the like quickly melt like water; indeed, through non-discrimination, they become pure and resemble the seed-syllables of Hara.

They quickly unite with the essence; and those [metals] situated in the fire become inexhaustible by the mere touch of those liquefied [substances]. In an instant, the mercury (sūtaka) is bound. I shall describe the killing of metals; listen with a concentrated mind.
Cinnabar with the milk of *snuhī*, gold and silver likewise;
with that same [milk], honey and copper; sulfur with goat’s milk;
vermilion, sharp iron (*tīkṣṇa*), tin, and *palāśa* with breast milk.
O beloved, one should kill the *nāga* by making it into clear leaves with the milk of *śilārka*, using the *puṭapāka* method; it becomes ash that leaves no residue (*niruttha*).
There is no iron-elephant that the lion of sulfur does not conquer.

It would destroy [diseases] by its mere scent; or else, it is like a lion among bees. O Goddess worshipped by the gods, even metals that have been reduced to ash become liquid and remove all diseases; how much more so when they are combined with mercury?
Through the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*), they surely destroy wrinkles, gray hair, disease, and old age.

For the treatment of the body, diamond (*vajra*), honey-iron (*ākṣika*), sharp iron (*tīkṣṇa*), mica (*abhra*), lead (*nāga*), tin (*vaṅga*), and copper (*suvīra*) are recommended; one should employ these substances for medicinal purposes.
Furthermore, that iron which is *paribāla*, as well as that which originates from Malaya— O Goddess, these two types of iron provide exceptional protection for the body.
Having understood the coloring (*rāga*) of the great essences (*mahārasa*) and so forth, one should prepare the seed-mantras (*bīja*).
Therefore, tell me that, O Goddess of Gods; what else do you wish to hear?
[Bījasādhana] The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Lord of the Gods, tell me the number of the colors of the great metallic essences and the gems, as well as the method for preparing their seeds, O Master. Śrī Bhairava said:

In the great rasas, it is doubled; O Goddess of the Gods, when the defect of the mountain has been removed, they dye the mercury (sūtaka) with the redness of copper. Sasyaka, capala, rājāvarta, and mākṣika [are used for this].

Vimala and gairika are among these; each one should be doubled. Indeed, in the case of the attractive *bhrāmaka* and others, it is one, two, or three times that amount. And in the case of each type of mica (*abhra*), it is white, yellow, or reddish-white.
Eighteen thousand [are in] rāga; ten thousand, O Goddess, are in gandhaka and darada; two thousand are in śilā;
seven thousand are in rasa; and four thousand are in kaṅkuṣṭha.

They shine forth within the essence (*rasagarbha*), provided that there is indeed the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*). There are one hundred and twelve [units] of passion (*rāga*) established in lead (*nāga*);
however, one thousand minus one hundred—that is, nine hundred—[units] of passion are established in tin (*vaṅga*).
Five thousand colors are established within the copper; they are red, yellow, and white. Within gold, there are sixteen colors.
There are sixty thousand colors established within the sapphire (*śakranīla*).

O Goddess of the gods, in the Mahānīla [ruby], those red hues are present in double measure. But in the Māṇikya, O Mistress of the Suras, there are thirteen hundred thousand red hues. They know the pearl to be a gem produced from the water of the elephant.
Three thousand [piercings] on the elephant, six thousand on the lotus,
and nine hundred thousand on the ruby are established;
it pierces all metals, and that which cannot be pierced by anything else.

O Goddess of the gods, they know that diamond (*vajra*) of his to possess two hundred thousand units of color (*rāga*). O Beloved, sixteen thousand units of color are established in the *puṣparāga* (topaz), while those in the emerald (*marakata*) are said to be three-quarters of a hundred thousand.
He does not know the calculation of passion (*rāga*). However, when the mercury has been transmuted, it excessively destroys the metal; he should reveal that which is deficient.
O Pārvatī, the lord of men should perform this—he who indeed knows [it].
One should calculate the number of passions by means of a hundred koṭis, and likewise observe the tactile contact; for it is pierced by a hundred koṭis.
Beyond this, O Dear One, I shall explain the practice of the seed-syllables.
"O Īśvarī, the seed [of mercury] is first of two kinds according to the metal:
the gold-seed is [prepared] with yellow and reddish [substances], while the silver-seed should be prepared with white ones. Once it has been processed, dyed, and matured, it thus becomes threefold."
That [preparation] is twofold, being divided into pure and mixed. The preparation of the *rasas*, *uparasas*, and metals, as well as of the *bījas*, is distinct;
the pure is [prepared] individually, while the mixed arises from their combination, O Mistress of the Gods, according to what is available.
Sattva, having been revolved in the sky, purified with glass and borax,
and treated with sprinklings of the paste of tamarind fruit and *nirguṇḍī* leaves, when cooked and consolidated, O Goddess, it becomes fit for being ground with mercury.
By means of the groups of fats, alkalis, and acids; by three *puṭa* applications of realgar (*śilā*);
on the day of death, by means of the incense-smoke apparatus (*dhūpanāyantra*); by the application of incense-fragrance and ointment;
and according to the procedure for tin (*vaṅga*), or for killed orpiment (*tālaka*).
Or else, when mercury has been killed with realgar and cinnabar, or within the womb of mercury, the black leaf of gold and silver will melt.
But that which is called *saṃkara* is difficult to fuse, O Beloved; it is known as "soft-hard."
Then, O Goddess, once it has been thoroughly ground, the union of the couple quickly becomes a single essence within the womb, and the king of essences melts.
Hereafter I shall explain; listen to the union of the couple.
O beloved, the powder of *varṣābhū*, plantain root, *kākamācī*, *punarnavā*,
and human skull, combined with *guñjā* and *ṭaṅkaṇa*,
when thoroughly heated with milk and oil, causes gold and mica to merge.

By this very procedure, one should also combine tāra-bhra (silver ore). O Goddess of Gods, having melted vaṅga (tin), it should again be joined with mercury (sūtaka) and ground with the juice of plantain root (kadalīkanda) along with ṭaṅkaṇa (borax).

When heated in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), tin-mercury (*vaṅgābhra*) merges in an instant. (RA 8.27) The powder of a human skull, combined with breast milk, *vanaśigruka*, *guñjā*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, causes tin-mercury to merge in an instant. (RA 8.28)
Having powdered the mica (*abhraka*), it should be saturated with the juice of *kākamācī* and touched with the decoction of *kapittha*. Combined with mercury and *ṭaṅkaṇa*,
and placed between sheets of tin (*vaṅga*) leaf, the mica and tin, when heated, will merge.

Having stirred it with pungent oil, one should add the ashes of *apāmārga*, tin, mica, and yellow orpiment; for lead-mica, however, realgar is used. Gold-mica [is purified] by means of lead-sulfide (*nāgatāpya*), and silver-mica by means of tin and yellow orpiment.

With sulphur, one should combine copper-mercury; with sindhu and vermilion, steel-mercury; with orpiment, tin-mercury; and with realgar, lead-mercury shall unite. Lāṅgalī, yak-tail hair, cotton-seed, and horse-gram [are also used].
The creeper of the *bhūlatā* plant and *aśmadalanī*, along with human breast-milk and the *suragopaka* insect— when these are smeared inside a crucible and heated intensely with a fierce fire,
the pure *kānta* iron and mica instantly merge into one.
The flesh of the *latāchuchundarī* combined with poison and *ṭaṅkaṇa*,
when used as a coating for the crucible (*mūṣā*), effects the union [of metals] in all dual combinations.
[Also effective are] mica, *surasā*, horn, the fat of a frog, and poison.

Through the application of *guñjā* and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, there is a union with all sentient beings. (RA 8.35) By means of *ṭaṅkaṇa*, *ūrṇā*, *girija*, *tuvarī*, *karṇākhya*, *āmala*, and *karkaṭa*, when ground together with breast milk, all dualities are reconciled. (RA 8.36)

With *dhātakī*, *guggulu*, jaggery, *sarja*, barley-gruel, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, ground with breast milk, [one should apply] everything for the treatment of hemorrhoids; however, in the case of *rasāyana* for dual-origin [diseases],
one should take the essence of the plant (*khasattva*) as a fine powder combined with the aforementioned paste.

When placed in a blind crucible and blown with a blowpipe, the mixture unites in an instant. When the essence of *khasattva* is sown with *tāpya*, *rasaka*, *sasyaka*, and *darada*, it becomes firmly bound; when strongly blown, it then unites.
One should melt together all the mercury, secondary minerals, and metals;
they attain mutual union and flow like water. Thus are the seeds prepared; now hear further about how they are colored.

The thickening [of mercury] is by means of honey-powder; it is colored by copper-powder and processed with the essence of mica (*tāpyasattva*). This is the coloring of the king of essences (*rasarāja*).
It is repeatedly saturated with the juice of the reddish vine and cow's urine.
With realgar, sulphur, gold-ore,
and cinnabar— having been sown with and treated by these, and then killed by the red group of substances and oils— the coloring of the king of mercury [is achieved], especially with steel and copper.
Pure, stainless copper, when sown with cinnabar, becomes tripled once digested; it becomes a clear mercury with the luster of lac.
O Goddess, having added twice as much *rasaka* and well-heated the copper, [it becomes] purified.
And the powder of black mica (*kṛṣṇābhraka*), repeatedly processed with *puṭa* applications of the red group of substances;
or gold killed with *tāpya* [ore] and quenched three times; or *rasaka* in a crucible combined with *tāpya* and rock salt (*saindhava*).

Up to the point of resembling an *indragopa* insect, through double the amount of digestion (*jāraṇā*), all of it becomes a liquid mercury resembling gold; there is no doubt about this. Abhraka, gold, and copper [are processed] with *śilā* and *mākṣika*.
One should color [the seeds] with the primary red ochre and with mercury.
Thus, the seeds are colored; now hear about the ripened seeds.
One should add the great essences (*mahārasa*), the secondary essences (*anuparasa*), and the sharp metals (*tīkṣṇaloha*).
Equal parts of [mercury] and *akṣīka*, through the application of the addition of sulfur—
one should add this hundreds of times until it is not exhausted but has a remainder. Equal parts of the king of fluids (*rasarāja*) certainly melt within the womb.
This very [substance] is recommended for the process of *viṣṭi*, O Goddess of the Gods,

for the digestion (*jāraṇā*) and coloring (*rañjana*) of the king of mercury (*rasarāja*), and also for the process of *sāraṇā*. That same [substance], having been sprinkled hundreds of times with red-colored oils, [is thus prepared].
Among those, the piercer (*vedhakṛt*) is praised as being superior by a thousandfold. [The essence of] lead and tin is processed for use in gold and silver;
the essence of *khasattva* should be joined with copper, and it should be alloyed for the purpose of alchemy (*rasāyana*).
With oils, alkalis, and the five acids— these juices and minerals such as talaka— one should process tin and lead in copper in proportions of one, two, or three parts respectively.
That which has been drenched in red oil is known as *rasākṛṣṭi*.
Honey, sulphur, yellow orpiment, realgar, vaikrāntaka, the finest magnetite, sasyaka, vimalāñjana,
and processed rasaka— these should be ground into a powder and infused repeatedly into gold.
By means of repeated applications of *puṭapāka* with iron-foil (*lohaparpaṭikā*), *tāpya*, *kaṅkuṣṭha*, *vimalā*, *abhra*,
the essence of killed copper (*mṛtaśulva*), *śilā*, *sattva*, the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, and *hiṅgula*,
lead (*nāga*) attains the state of being lifeless (*nirjīvatā*).

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should process mercury, realgar, conch-shell, mica, the alkali of *ciñcā*, tin, killed lead, killed tin, copper, or killed iron— each individually— into the finest gold. (RA 8.60)

In *niruttha* it is like a serpent; in gold, it is like a hundredfold collection; in *nirvyūḍha*, its luster resembles *gorocanā*; in the sun, it resembles a star. *Tīkṣṇābhraka* is equal to the sun, and *mākṣika* is likewise twofold.

It is rolled and pulverized; it is killed by seven *puṭas*. When the gold has been increased a hundredfold, one should digest that seed in equal measure by means of a smear upon the leaves of *candrārka*; one should pierce [the gold] with a hundredth part of it.
Having added honey above and below, the copper becomes equal to gold;
thus, when processed tenfold, the seed becomes identical to its cause. Then, one should smelt mercury, mica, magnetite, and copper, increasing the proportions by one part each.

And that [lead] killed by *mākṣika* should be carried forth into the seed (*bīja*), O Dear One. Lead (*nāga*) multiplied thirty-two times in gold, and killed *tāpya* with thirty parts of *śilā* added, is declared to be the lead-seed (*nāgabīja*).

By adding *tāpya* and *tālaka*, one should extract the essence (*sattva*) of yellow *abhraka* into the seed; this acts as a penetrator (*vedhaka*) for that which has been processed with a woman. Lead (*nāga*) produces softness, and when extracted, it produces redness.

The sharp [iron] that has been sown [with mercury] attains yellowness; the blackness residing in gold is poison. This is declared to be the seed of gold (*hemabīja*); now hear the seed of silver (*tārabīja*).
Equal parts of sharp iron, mica, copper, *vimala*, and *rasaka*—

There are four parts of tin; everything is to be smelted and pulverized. It should be processed by means of a *puṭa* and struck [with a pestle]; then, having been refined, it should pierce silver, making the silver thirty-two times superior. One should carry the killed *tāpya* along with the tin.

From thirty times the amount of *tāla* powder, the seed of tin (*vaṅgabīja*) is declared. One should process crooked, pure, and sharp *khasattva*, as well as tin-cloud (*vaṅgābhra*) or the essence of *tāpya*, by means of the addition of *tāla* and honey.
One should perform the sprinkling with clusters of white flowers using substances mixed with oil.
(RA 8.72) The seed-syllables of *tāra* have been stated; now hear the coloring of the seeds.
(RA 8.73) [The ingredients are] sharp iron, copper, lead, and killed mercury.
One should dye the seeds with that [substance] until they resemble vermilion. Having placed the *nāga* in an earthen pan together with the petals of the *brahmabīja*,
and having applied fire beneath it, when it becomes the color of fire— (RA_8.75)
With *vāsaka*, *vibhīta*; with *śāka*, *kiṃśuka*, *śigru*, and the flower of *koraṇḍaka*; and with *bakula* and *arjuna*.
With *ahimāra* [one subdues] a female *nāga*; with a maiden, a daughter of the *nāgas*.
And with threefold stone [powder], and with boiled goat’s urine—
having soaked it while placed in a crucible,
and having repeatedly drenched it for exactly seven days, it is killed, O Goddess praised by the gods.
One should first envelop it with sulfur, and immediately thereafter with acidic substances;
this is to be employed for the coloring, the opening, and the transmutation of the petals, seeds, and the king of essences, especially for the stabilization of the paste.
In the juice of mañjiṣṭhā and kiṃśuka, having ground khadira, red sandalwood, karavīra, devadāru, sarala, the two types of haridrā,
and other red flowers with lac juice; (RA 8.80) [one should proceed].
O Goddess, one should cook the oil; with that, one should dye the seeds.
O Sovereign of the Gods, there should be double the amount of red flowers, four times as much decoction of the red and yellow groups [of herbs], and one part oil in milk.
[One should take] that which arises from the *jyotiṣmatī*, the *karañja*, and the *kaṭutumbī*,
combined with the juices of *pāṭalī*, *pippalī*, *kāma*, and *kākatuṇḍī*, [along with the flesh] of frogs,
pigs, rams, snakes, fish, tortoises, and leeches.
Combined with a single portion of fat and well-grounded in sixteen parts,
and cooked with the medicinal herbs for the union of pairs— namely, *bhūlatā*, *mala*, and *mākṣika*— and then filtered, this is called *sāraṇā-taila*.

Just as a seed is equal to its sap, O beloved, so all [the elements], having attained *garbhadruti*, are desired to be in equal proportions by virtue of their pervasiveness. That which is matured within the womb is excellent and balanced; it flows and dyes that [substance].
Thus have the seed-syllables been explained. Tell me that, O Goddess of Gods, regarding their digestion through the application of *viḍa* (fecal matter); what else do you wish to hear?
(RA_8.88) 9 [The Discourse on *Viḍa*]
The Śrī Devī said:
The maturation of the seeds has been declared, as well as their specific means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
You should explain those alchemists (*viḍas*) by whom they are digested so that they may bring forth [the fruit]. (RA 9.1)
Śrī Bhairava said:
Kāsīsa, saindhava, kāṅkṣī, sauvīra, vyoṣa, gandhaka,
sauvarcala, sarjikā, and that which is produced from the juice of mālatī.

This *viḍa* salt, sprinkled with the juice of the roots of the *śigru* tree, is a digester of all [substances]. O Goddess, conch powder that has been burnt and soaked a hundred times in the milk of the sun-plant (*ravikṣīra*), and then repeatedly subjected to *puṭa*-firing, is an excellent *viḍa* for digestion.
Or, sulphur ground into powder and saturated a hundred times with cow’s urine; likewise,
conch-shell powder burnt to ash and steeped a hundred times in water from the roots of the *śigru* tree, combined with poison and rock salt (*sindhūttha*), is called *vaḍavāmukha*.
O Goddess, one should saturate *ṭaṅkaṇa* a hundred times with the juices of *kiṃśuka*;
this is called *viḍa* or *vahnimukha*, which is dear for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of metals, O Beloved.
*Cūlikā* is *gandhapāṣāṇa* (sulphur), and the "mouth" (*mukha*) of *kānta* (magnetite), O Beloved.
Each one alone is sufficient for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of iron powder.
(RA 9.7) One should cook sulphur, *tālaka*, rock salt, *cūlī*, borax, and *bhūkhaga* with alkaline substances and urine; this is the *viḍa* called *Jvālāmukha*. (RA 9.8)
Twenty-one times processed with the juice of *devadālī* leaves,
the lye of *nicula* will digest all living beings.
[One should use] *vāstuka*, eggplant, banana, *devadālī*, and *punarnavā*.
Vāsā, palāśa, and nicula; tilaka, kāñcana, and mākṣika—(RA_9.10) all these cut into pieces from every limb, not too dried out, on a stone surface;
likewise with burnt stalks of sesame and the five parts of the radish. (RA_9.11)

One should wash it with the group of urines. Then, the water strained from that [mixture] should be cooked in an iron vessel using a *yantra* [apparatus], while one who knows the measure of fire attends to the *haṃsapāka* process.
When there is the emergence of many vapors and bubbles, [the cooking is complete].

Then, one should place the powder of green vitriol (*kāsīsa*), borax (*saurāṣṭrī*), the three salts, the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), sulfur, white [vitriol], asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and likewise the six salts,
inside a sealed iron crucible (*lohasampuṭa*).
After remaining underground for seven days, it becomes an excellent *viḍa* salt situated within grain.
It is cooked with the sour juice of *jambīra* and with the liquid from the roots of *śigru*.
Having been sprinkled with the essence of *cūlikā* and sulfur, two types of *viḍa* are produced in succession by the hundreds.

One should macerate *devadālī* and *śivā* seeds, along with *guñjā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), with the juices of *koṣātakī* leaves or with the alkalis derived from *nicula*. This *viḍa* salt is for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of gold.
Sulfur should be processed a hundred times with the alkaline juices of radish, fresh ginger, and *citrā*, strained through cow’s urine; this is the *viḍa* salt used for the digestion of gold.
[Also used are] yellow orpiment, mica, alkali, salt, conch-shell, and mother-of-pearl.
This *viḍa* salt, matured by the *haṃsapāka* process, is used for the digestion of gold. Having thus gathered the necessary materials, one should perform the work of mercury (*rasakarma*).
Tell me that, O Goddess of Gods; what else do you wish to hear?
10 [Purification of Mercury] The Śrīdevī said:
What is the characteristic of mercury, and what is the nature of its alchemical work?
"I do not know that, O Lord of Gods; you ought to explain it according to the truth.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"The origin of mercury has already been told; now hear its characteristics."
His thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of names cannot be recounted by me; listen as they are told in brief.
He is Rasa, Rasendra, Sūta, Pārada, and Miśraka.
One should know *rasa* to be perfected mercury (*siddharasa*). Taking refuge in a perfected field (*siddhakṣetra*), it destroys all diseases, as well as wrinkles and graying hair.
Now hear about the pure *rasendra*, which effects the transformation of the body and base metals.
In the body, in gold, in the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*), and in the processes of transmutation (*sāraṇā*);
(RA_10.6) the mercury (*sūtaka*) that is slightly yellow, has a rough body, and is possessed of defects;
(RA_10.7) that which is white on the outside and inside, and is largely enveloped by a coating (*kañcuka*).

One should know that, O Goddess, it is mercury; one should employ it in the rite of transmutation (*tārakarma*). Just as a vessel of milk is destroyed by contact with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), so too gold and the body are destroyed by mercury.
The wise know that when one sees mercury of a smoky color, it has the luster of a peacock's feather; specifically,
one should recognize such a mixture as being capable of performing the act of marriage.
Thus, O Goddess, the fivefold varieties of the distinctions of *rasa* have been described:

namely, sweating (*svedana*), rubbing (*mardana*), moving (*cāraṇa*), digesting (*jāraṇa*), liquefying (*drāvaṇa*), coloring (*rañjana*), extracting (*sāraṇa*), and transmuting (*krāmaṇa*) in their proper order.
Thus, for one who knows this according to reality, the *sūtaka* is perfected.
Intensity arises from sweating; purity results from rubbing;
one should produce strength through *cāraṇa*; and through *jāraṇā*, binding occurs.
Its unity arises from liquefying; its redness from red ointment (*raktakāñjana*);

its pervasiveness from spreading (*sāraṇa*); and likewise, its transference from transferring (*krāmaṇa*). Moving slowly, it takes the form of impurity (*mala*); moving swiftly, it becomes the *haṃsa*.
Malaga moves in the form of impurity; *sadhūma* becomes *dhūmaga*.
O Goddess, there is another course for the *jīva*; the *jīva* emerges like [an embryo] from an egg. As long as it sustains the *jīva*, by that [means] the *jīva* is known as *rasa*. (RA 10.14–15)
His course is fourfold; indeed, by one who is skillful, these four courses are perceived. The fifth course is unperceived.
(RA 10.16) By means of mantra, meditation, and so forth, his fifth course is exhausted. (RA 10.17)

Smoke, the *ciṭiciṭi* sound, the frog-leap, the motionless state, and the vibrating state— these are the five stages of the elixir (*rasa*) as it is being churned with the medicinal paste (*kalka*). Indeed, three modes of movement may arise.

The movement in water is the movement of impurity; thereafter, it becomes the movement of a swan. Then, having given pure gold, one should cook that [mercury] by means of a support, using a binding agent and the medicinal herbs of the group of binders, after adding the liquid.

When restrained, it does not move; likewise, O Śivā, it follows the path of smoke. When free from the movement of the *kaṇikā* and devoid of bubbles, this [fire] becomes restrained, like the fire on a hearth.
When, O auspicious lady, one causes [the mercury] to digest within a vessel of *kāñjika* without restraining the *sūta*, then its threefold course certainly arises;
for it has indeed been sweated by means of the swinging-bath (*dolāsveda*) for three days.

O Goddess, the king of essences (*rasarāja*) is not diminished by *vasu*, *bhaṇṭā*, and so forth. Having seen that the essence is undiminished, one should then apply [substances] such as space (*vyoma*),
followed by the process of sweating (*svedana*), and then the grinding (*mardana*) of what is being applied.
Food embraced by the *rasa* is called *piṣṭikā*;
when that [food] is quickly placed within the womb of the *rasa*, it is proclaimed as *jāraṇā*.
That indeed is designated as *jāraṇā*, and it is perceived in this very manner.

At the end of digestion, coloring should be performed using the group of red substances. Once it has been digested again and again, one should purify the well-colored [mercury] with equal gold by means of the application of the *sāraṇā* apparatus;
thus the processed mercury is bound.
It is indeed repeatedly processed; just as the mercury (*sūtaka*) becomes joined with *krāmaṇa*, one should employ it for the purpose of transmutation (*vedha*).
Āroṭa is mercury (*pārada*), which is Brahmā; when it is in a state of *mūrchita* (solidified), it is Janārdana.
But when bound, it takes on the form of Rudra; [thus] rasa [is perfected] through the power of karmayoga. (RA_10.30) Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the detailed exposition of karmayoga.
(RA_10.31) Mercury has three defects: poison, fire, and likewise impurity.

One should know that [the addition of] poison makes it poisonous; by [using it] in fire, a man becomes afflicted with leprosy; by [using it] with impurity, he suffers from abdominal disease; and he dies during the practice of *rasāyana*. Six *truṭis* make one *likṣā*, and six *likṣās* make one *yūka*.
Six *yūkās*, O lady of excellent vows, are said to be known as a *rajas*.
Six *rajas* are directly a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*), and that is proclaimed as a *siddhārtha*.
Six *siddhārthas*, O Queen of the Gods, are proclaimed to be one barley grain (*yava*).
Six *yava*s make one *guñjā*; six *guñjā*s make one *māṣaka*;
twelve *māṣas* make one *tola*; eight *tolas* make one *pala*.
O Goddess, thirty-two *palas* are proclaimed to be auspicious.
Two thousand *śubha*s are proclaimed to be one *bhāra*.
Two thousand *pala*s, or one thousand, or even one hundred; or twenty-eight *pala*s, or ten, or five. (RA 10.36–37)
The purification of the *sūtaka* (mercurial preparation) must be performed with exactly half a *palā* [of these ingredients]:
*mahābalā*, *nāgabalā*, *meghanādā*, *punarnavā*, and *meṣaśṛṅgī*. This should be combined with the essence (*sāra*) of those [plants] along with fresh *sāra*.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, one should cause the mercury (*pārada*) to sweat for three days. [The herbs used are:
*girikarṇī*, *mīnākṣī*, *sahadevī*, *punarnavā*, *uragā*, *triphalā*, *kāntā*, *laghuparṇī*, and *śatāvarī*.
In the case of *dhānyāmla* (sour gruel), one should throw everything— excluding the husks—
into this eleven-fold sour liquid after thoroughly churning it; it should be rubbed with sixteen parts of *āsurī*, salt, *vyoṣa*, *citraka*, fresh ginger, and radish.
O Goddess, one should sweat it in a swing for three days with a gentle fire. Aṅkola destroys poison; O Dear One, Āragvadha destroys [excessive] fire;
Citraka destroys impurity; and Kumārī destroys the seven sheaths.

Therefore, with these [ingredients] combined, the wise one should grind and cause it to fall. By means of the *vidyādhara* machine, O Goddess, he should then purify that mercury, free from defects, having filtered it while it rests upon a triple-layered cloth.

Because it possesses the fire-root of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), it should be combined with the juice of *gṛhakanyā*. One should grind it on a stone that does not emit steam, and then cause it to fall [into the crucible] again.
[One should further process it] with the essence of soot, jaggery, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), turmeric, and white mustard seeds.
One should grind it for three days with brick-dust and *kāñjika* sour gruel;
thereafter, the mercury becomes pure and shall manifest my power.
One should then grind it with *vāsaka* and *vibhītaka* and cause it to fall [into the crucible] once again.

The defects arising from impurities, such as those caused by *nāga* and *vaṅga*, go to destruction. Having removed the defects, one should grind [the mercury] with *kākamācī* seven times and cause it to fall [into the crucible] seven times; thus the mercury abandons the defect of the mountain.

O Goddess, one should avoid defects of the site; [the mercury] is intensified by the juice of *gokarṇa*. When steamed in the sap of cotton leaves mixed with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), the mercury is freed from its seven sheaths and, within seven days, becomes perfected.
Kākamācī, jayā, brāhmī; gāṅgerī, raktacitraka, maṇḍūkī, and mudgaparṇī; śṛṅgavera and rasāṅkuśa;
devadālī and śaṅkhapuṣpī; kākajaṅghā and śatāvarī.
Kumārī and Bhṛṅgarāja, Nirguṇḍī and Grīṣmasundara, Śūlinī and Śūrpaparṇī, Gojihvā and Kṣīrakañcuka—
[the substance] should be rubbed with the juices of these and precipitated; thus purified seven times, it becomes stainless.
Having made a paste with copper, one should cause it to fall [into the crucible] during upward sublimation (*ūrdhvapātana*), having discarded tin and lead; thus the mercury (*sūtaka*) becomes pure.
It should be rubbed with *triphalā*, *śigru*, black mustard, *paṭu*, and *citraka*.
It should be cooked placed within an upper vessel, with glowing stones beneath it.
By the obstruction of the "creation-lotus," the mercury (*rasa*) will be largely obtained when combined with *karkoṭī*,
*kañcukī*, *bimbī*, *sarpākṣī*, and the lotus.

One should place the mercury in a binding agent; thus purified, the mercury becomes radiant and stainless. It is dried with one-eighth part of *bhadrā*, along with small sour substances, salts, alkalis, earth-born [minerals], sky-born [salts], pungents, and *śigru*.
O Goddess, by means of sweating for three days with mustard seeds and carbonate of soda in sour gruel,
the mercury becomes ignited and becomes desirous of taking food (*grāsa*).
The seeds of *vyoma*, *sattva*, and so forth are used for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) and purification (*śodhana*) of mercury.
Therefore, tell me that, O Goddess of the Gods; what else do you wish to hear?
[Bālajāraṇa] The Illustrious Goddess said:
I have heard from you about the characteristics and purification of mercury, as well as its transmutation and digestion; now, O Bhairava, I wish to hear [more].
Śrī Bhairava said:

When the destruction of all sins has occurred, the digestion of the essence (*rasajāraṇā*) is attained; upon its attainment, that very consciousness which is the cause of liberation is indeed obtained. O Goddess, for the practitioner, this *jāraṇā* is the manifestor of liberation.
As long as the mercury (*sūta*) has not been matured, there is no liberation.
O Goddess, the crucible is the pedestal; the king of essences (*rasendra*) is said to be the *liṅga*.
Rubbing it is its prostration, and the swallowing of it is prescribed as its worship.
As many days as the mercury remains heated and maintained while situated in the fire,
for that many thousands of yugas it is honored in the world of Śiva. He who provides the sacrificial fire for the lord of mercury for even a single day [attains this same merit].
His sins melt away; even while acting, he is not defiled.

(RA 11.6) Alchemy (*jāraṇā*) is of two kinds: the alchemy of the raw (*bālajāraṇā*) and the alchemy of the bound (*baddhajāraṇā*). Among these, O Supreme Goddess, the alchemy of the raw shall first be explained. (RA 11.7)

First, one should digest the sky; thereafter, all the essences (*sarvasattva*); then, purified honey; and immediately after that, gold. Having caused [the mercury] situated within the womb to melt, it will then flow as an external liquefaction (*bāhyadruti*).
One should whiten with a white substance and dye red with a red one.
Having understood the processes of *sāraṇa* and *krāmaṇa*, one should then employ *vedha*. Oṃ, homage to the immortal metal, arisen from the essence of supreme nectar, hūṃ svāhā! (RA 11.9–11)

"For the benefit of all sentient beings, O Blessed One, I wish to perform the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*) with your permission. O Lord, please accept my offering. "Do so," Śiva replied; and it was accepted by Subuddhi.

Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain: the supreme digestion of *vyomaja* (sky-born), the digestion of *pattra-abhraja* (leaf-born and cloud-born), and the digestion of *sattva* (essence); these are its three types. Furthermore, they are classified as *nirmukha* (mouthless), *samukha* (with mouth), and *vāsanāmukha* (impregnated-mouth).
Each of these is threefold; I shall explain them in due order.

O Goddess, by means of contact with *vaikrānta* or *vajra*, or through the power of divine herbs, one who has mastered the mouth may consume [the substance], and in an instant, the mercury becomes like the sky.

In the work with gold, there is only gold; in silver, silver becomes the primary ingredient. A paste prepared from heated *khalva* stones [is used], along with very fine, minute quantities of mica (*abhraka*), and with *amlavetasa*, jambīra, bījapūra, sour earth, and mercury.
O Goddess, it moves having been crushed; this is *samukhajāraṇā* (face-to-face digestion).
One should digest the three alkalis, the five salts, *kākṣī*, *kāsīsa*, sulfur, and *mākṣika* combined with acid in a copper vessel.
Having caused this divine [substance] to be extracted from the pressing-stone, O Goddess worshipped by the gods,
the wise one should [use it] for the purpose of digesting (*jāraṇa*) seeds and especially diamonds. Into that [substance], lead or tin should be repeatedly circulated.
One should sprinkle it one hundred times, but not during the practice of *rasāyana*.
O Goddess, by this one should impregnate the entire process of *cāraṇa*; the *vyoma* [mercury] should be impregnated with alkalis and acids, and with the first *rajas*.

One should rub [the substance] with a drop of water from the three worlds (*sṛṣṭitraya*), or with the juice of *tumburu*, or it should be processed by being roasted (*puṭita*) with the juice of *yavaciñcā*. [The herbs are:
*śatāvarī*, *gadā*, *rambhā*, *meghanādā*, and *punarnavā*.
Śigruka and yavaciñcā are successively infused with their respective juices.
[One should take] the root of hilamocā, as well as the root of kauverī,
and likewise kadalī, musalī, śigru, tāmbūlī, vāṇa, and pīluka.
Alambuṣā, balā, kola, āsphoṭa, kharamañjarī, tumburu,
or tiktaśāka— by means of the juice of one of these,
combined with rājikā and vyoṣa, abhraka is steamed for three days.
Combined with green vitriol, alum, rock salt, and borax,
through the application of the aforementioned process of sublimation, the mercury moves in an instant;
it quickly becomes a pill that bestows all accomplishments.

O Goddess, having taken sour gruel (dhānyāmla) combined with the group of acidic substances, one should boil that abhraka; then one should rub it with the milk of the snuhī plant. [One should then place it] in a *kapota*-named *puṭa* using forest cow-dung.
With the sap of the plantain root, the juice of the radish tuber,
kākamācī, mīnākṣī, apāmārga, and likewise munī; as well as eraṇḍa, ginger, meghanādā, and punarnavā.
One should administer one *puṭa* for each [dose] using only liquids. One should cook it in a *dolāyantra* (swing-oven) combined with the milk of the *vajrī* plant;
then, having dried it in the shade, it should be combined with sour chickpea broth.
Navasāra, kāsīsa, vacā, and likewise nimba—
one should add each of these in a sixteenth part of the weight of the mica.
Having placed them in a copper vessel, one should grind them well, O lady of virtuous vows.

Then, O Goddess, one should cause it to be digested nine times in an iron vessel. Together with the mercury, O Mistress of the Gods, one should boil it with sour chickpea-water and sour gruel over a gentle fire; it will be produced in half a watch.
Having ground *vyoma* together with *sauvarcala* salt in the juices of *somavallī*,
one should administer it slowly in three *puṭa*s using *haṃsapādī*;
and one should administer it seven times using the juice of *somavallī* alone.
One should cause it to fall into an earthen vessel, combined with a liquid.
One should rub the root of the *siteṣupuṅkhā* plant with cow’s milk and smear it as a paste upon the mercury (*sūta*) and the "sky" (*gagana*), which rises above that.
One should heat it with the sun's heat; for a moment it swallows [the moisture] without opening its mouth, and a paste quickly arises. No deliberation is required here.
O Dear One, one should saturate the *gagana* with the juice of *tilaparṇī* itself.
From rubbing, a powder is produced; no deliberation is required here.
One should repeatedly soak mercury in the exudate of *muṇḍī*, and having saturated the mica (*abhraka*) with that, one should burn it in a crucible again and again.

With each of the roots of *citraka* and fresh ginger, it should be diligently soaked seven times. The powder of sulphur and mica should be processed with the juice of *nāgaśuṇḍī*, breast milk, *rajuṅga*, and sour gruel.
Likewise, it should be done with a sixteenth part; thus the mercury should be processed in a swinging vessel (*dolā*).
O Goddess, it may be performed sixty-four times, or thirty-two times, or sixteen times, or even eight times.
O Beloved, one should cause it to circulate [through the body] fourfold, twofold, or equally.
O Pārvatī, hear now about the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of the supreme essence of *bhraka* (mica):
the essence of *vyoma* (mica) combined with an equal portion of the essence of *tāpya* (copper).
O Goddess, he should indeed practice in this manner; thus the mercury becomes a liquefier of the womb (*garbhadrāvī*).

O Goddess, one should digest lead-cloud (*nāgābhra*), tin-cloud (*vaṅgābhra*), sharp iron-cloud (*tīkṣṇābhra*), copper-cloud (*bhāskarābhra*), silver-cloud (*tārābhra*), and gold-cloud (*hemābhra*) by means of the "essence-womb" (*rasagarbha*).
By means of the yoga of the previous consecration, it flows within the womb through friction.
The first [consecration] consists of sixty-four parts; the second, thirty-two parts;
the third, sixteen parts; and the fourth consists of eight parts alone.
The fifth [portion] is a fourth part; the sixth is proclaimed to be two parts. A morsel (*grāsa*) of mercury should be given to the *abhraka* ore that possesses *sattva*.
When the morsel consists of sixty-four parts, the mercury becomes a "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍadhārī*).
And in the second [stage], like a leech; in the union with the "swallowing" (*grāsa*), O Mistress of the Gods. By the third swallowing, one becomes like crow-dung;
by the fourth swallowing, one becomes like whey (*dadhi-maṇḍa*).
In the fifth stage of practice, during the consumption of food, it becomes like fresh butter;

in the sixth, however, it takes the form of a ball. These are the signs of its gradual digestion. When sprinkled with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), the red sky [of the heart] is saturated a hundred times over.

One should cause that [mercury] to circulate within a mortar, together with the *śulvavāsanā* (the processing of copper). Having rubbed gold and silver together, one should place mercury along with *kāsīsa* (iron sulfate) and *kāñjī* (sour gruel) into that mortar; by means of *sindhu* (salt), the mercury moves.
Having rubbed gold and lead together, one should cause mercury to be added there, along with lead, gold, and iron; once fully digested, it becomes liquefied.
By quickly adding the impurities of mica, this [mercury] moves by its very mouth alone.
Having rubbed together silver and tin, one should add mercury to it, along with lead, gold, and mica. When fully digested, it becomes liquefied;
the mica moves through the mouth [of the crucible]. This is recommended for the work of silver.

Whether with face-to-face (*samukha*) or face-away (*nirmukha*), one should diligently cause [the mercury] to move through the sky (*nabhas*). Having thus performed the threefold movement, one should digest the *garbhadhūti* in the mercury; one should cause the mass (*piṇḍa*) to sweat by means of the three stages of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Having smeared it with sharp sour substances, alkali, cow urine, and the milk of the *snuhī* plant,
and having bound it externally with a cloth, one should again present a morsel [of food] in alkali, fermented rice-gruel, and oil, and heat it over a gentle fire. (RA 11.61)
O Goddess of the Gods, by this sequence, the mercury— having been extracted from the apparatus and placed in an iron vessel— is matured over three days;
first washed with lukewarm *kāñjika* and filtered through a cloth.
With the hand, [one should place it] in a vessel while it is comfortably warm; one should knead it until the remainder is dissolved. (RA 11.63) Squeezed through a fourfold cloth, it becomes pure.
(RA 11.64) When the mass has been strained out by the process of filtering, it emerges from the pressing.

He should be the wielder of the staff, and likewise the essence that has digested its meal. When digestion is incomplete, one should cause the paste to cook, and likewise sweat it and rub it using the application of *vetasāmla*. Once digested, however, one should administer the meal.
Mercury should be rubbed with sixteen parts each of brick, jaggery, burnt wool, *rājī*, rock salt, and soot, along with fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), and then subjected to heating (*sveda*).
This is for the purpose of purification, to be done repeatedly at every morsel (*grāsa*).
Like a withered cloud or a withered seed, he who is stainless takes up the passions (*rāga*).
By this sequence, one should move the four morsels (*grāsa*) on the swing;
thereafter, by means of the tortoise-machine (*kacchapayantra*), there is burning and binding in due order.

Above and below, by an eighth part; having added viḍa, one should cause it to digest. When the mercury has fully digested the mica, O Dear One, it becomes a hundred-fold penetrator. With double [the amount], it is a thousand-fold penetrator; with triple, it is a ten-thousand-fold penetrator.

When it has been digested fivefold, O Goddess, the mercury becomes a "walker on earth" (bhūcara). When it is digested sixfold, the mercury attains the lifespan of Viṣṇu and becomes a "piercer of ten million" (koṭivedhī).
All the defects of mercury, however, come to destruction when it has been processed with six times its weight of mica; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
O beloved, when the sky [mica] has been digested sixfold within the king of essences, [the result is achieved].
Then it swallows metals and abandons its own course. Smoke, the *ciṭiciṭi* sound, the frog-leap, trembling, and the absence of trembling— these are the five stages of the mercury (*rasa*).
Then Kapila emits smokeless sparks;

remaining in the fire, he is unshakable—this is the characteristic of one who has digested the ether (*vyoma*). A child is "evenly digested" (*samajīrṇa*); one established in youth possesses four times that [quality].

But when it is old and decayed, it possesses sixfold power; it performs its work individually. A young metal acts by means of leaf-coating, while one in its prime does so through the application of paste. An old metal pierces other metals only when it has been smelted or refined.

But the *rasa*, O Goddess, is the *kumāra* (youthful); established in youth, the *rasa*, O Goddess, is not capable of alchemy (*rasāyana*), yet it is sufficient for the preservation of the body. And that *rasa* which exists in the state of old age may permeate the body through [the medium of] iron.
In the absence of *abhraka*-sattva, one should cause *kānta*-sattva to be given.
And in the absence of *kānta* as well, one should cause steel (*tīkṣṇaloha*) to be given. By this sequential application, one should digest all the *sattvas*.
Even a single [unit] combined with gold becomes golden-hued in an instant;
beyond that, there is nothing superior among the primary or secondary rasas.
By means of the previously mentioned application of the yantra, the sulphur is multiplied by sixteen times.

Alternatively, one should digest [the mercury] twelvefold or even sixfold. Having taken the essence (*sattva*) of honey-gold (*mākṣika*), one should digest it with a quarter-part [of the essence]; thereafter, one should cause all essences to melt within the womb of the mercury (*sūta*).
There is friendship between gold and fire; likewise, there is enmity between gold-mercury and fire-mercury. Friendship exists between their respective friends:
Agnika and Yavaciñcā, and Vasuhaṭṭa and Rāgiṇī.
Cooked by means of swinging and sweating, that is the supreme digestion of gold (*hemajāraṇa*).

Ashes of *palāśa*, *apāmārga*, barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*), sour gruel (*kāñjika*), black salt (*sauvarcala*), green vitriol (*kāsīsa*), sea salt (*sāmudra*), and likewise rock salt (*saindhava*)— (RA_11.87).
One should take equal parts of āsurī, ṭaṅkaṇa, navasāra, karpūra, and mākṣīka.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should apply a coating to the crucible using the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*.

Then, having added the powder of *viḍa* salt, one should digest the gold, O dear one. Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the process of digestion known as *bhūcara*. One should mix black, yellow, and red *abhra* with copper and steel.
When there is sharp powder in the crucible, O beloved, one should mix it in sequence:
twenty-two times [the amount] of gandhanāga, and half of that again; this should be added together with the gold, sixteen parts for every single part of mercury.
When the *gandhanāga* has been digested, then the mercury becomes bound;
when gold has been digested, one should then dye it with half as much dead iron. Copper killed by sulphur, *mākṣika*, cinnabar, and iron—

One should kill the pure [mercury] by means of a *puṭa* [firing]; one should add six times as much gold. When the seed of gold (*hemabīja*) has been digested during the *sūtaka* process, one should know it to be fourfold and fixed in its color; the mercury then becomes the luster of gold.
Situated within the *sāraṇā* apparatus, one should cause it to flow together with that very [substance];
having performed the *sāraṇā* for three parts, one should then cause it to digest (*jārayet*) right there. Thus, it is both digested and flowed; then again, it is digested and flowed.
Through the application of the sevenfold chain, the mercury becomes a "piercer of the peak" (*koṭivedhī*).
The digestion (*jāraṇā*) on earth has been explained; now hear about the digestion in the sky (*khecarī*).
One should cause gems, of which diamonds are foremost, to be rendered as the residue of the mercury.
The seeds of *kaṭutumba*—one should cause half of that to be given.
This is called "the great digestion" (*mahājāraṇa*). The wise man should prepare a paste and place it within the mouth of a *vajramūṣā* crucible; therein he should place the mercury.
Likewise, having combined *kataka* and gold, one should diligently grind them with ruby (*padmarāga*). One should then cause the "swallowing" (*grāsa*) of the mercury to take place,
up to eleven times the amount of the ruby in the flux (*sūtaka*).
But when the passion has been digested, O Goddess of Gods, the mercury takes the form of a *liṅga*.
It must be protected with great effort by the eight guardians of the world (*lokapāla*).
One should cause the sixth part of the lord of the mercury (*sūtaka*) to be given to all of them.
It should be consumed with effort, having bowed to the Guru and the Deity, and having paid homage to all the Siddhas and especially to the deities.
Thereafter, fainting and a burning sensation in the limbs arise; of this there is no doubt.
One should see oneself arisen, possessing divine splendor and great power. Amidst the resounding blasts of conchs and trumpets, together with *siddhas* and *vidyādharas*,
one may wander through the worlds at will, assuming any form desired and traveling in a celestial chariot.
And where the gods dissolve, there the Siddha likewise dissolves. (RA 11.107) Furthermore, I shall explain another [method], the supreme yoga of digestion (jāraṇā).
Then, the mercury (sūta), well-rubbed and cooked, is freed from all defects. (RA 11.108)

With the essence of *śākapallava* and the juice of *viṣṇukrāntā*, mercury is processed. With water from *palāśa* flowers, an equal amount of sulphur and an equal amount of the essence of black mica (*kṛṣṇābhrasattva*) are treated; thus the *rasaka* becomes eightfold in quality.
And likewise, one should digest sharp copper-venom with the tortoise-yantra;
afterwards, one should digest gold by means of a *viḍa* preparation, O Pārvatī. Then one should know it to be perfected; one should apply two parts of copper.
By the measure of the number of operations, the naga becomes gold. Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme process of digestion (*jāraṇā*):
having repeatedly saturated the seed-powders with oil...
One should slowly rub that [substance] with a finger using a sixteenth part [of the additive];
then, from the mixture of ginger and other ingredients, one should add [the additive] in sixteen parts.
Having applied it to birch bark, it should then be placed in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus).
Within a day and night, O beloved, Sūtaka devours that seed;
having extracted that mercury, O Goddess, one should then grind it in a mortar.
Then, having placed it in a yantra, [one should heat it] with a steady fire for a day and night.
Heated [mercury] extracted from the apparatus should be rubbed in a heated mortar. Having rubbed it and placed a lump of mica (*abhraka*) therein, one should apply a *puṭa* (roasting);
then it quickly falls into the interior, and one may easily digest it.
Then, having placed [the mercury] in a dolāyantra together with a moist mass,
on the third day the mercury digests— that is, it consumes [the substance].
Thereafter, until it is completely digested, the skillful [alchemist] should keep it in the dolāyantra.
Afterwards, by means of the tortoise-press (*kacchapayantra*). Once it is well-digested, O Pārvatī, one should digest that [substance] with a twelfth part of the dose by means of the tortoise-press.
As before, there is the application of ginger and the liquefaction within the womb (*garbhadrāvaṇa*).

Thereafter, O Goddess, having placed that [substance] inside, the wise one should apply the *puṭa* (encasement). Then, with an eighth part, he should take the morsel (*grāsa*) and the melting of the embryo (*garbhadrāva*) as before,
having cast that mercury (*sūtaka*) into the interior of the *kanda* of the *sūraṇa*.
One should indeed calcine it until the bulb is no longer burnt.
A dose consisting of a quarter-part of the crucible is prescribed for the mercury;
as before, one should add the *viḍa* salt and likewise effect the liquefaction of the embryo (*garbhadrāvaṇa*).

When [the mercury] has thus been digested through the fourfold process, the *sūtaka* becomes powerful; then, by means of a probe (*śalākā*), the mercury situated in the fire devours the morsels (*grāsa*). Then, the gems are to be digested according to the sequence that will be described.
Having added mica (*abhraka*), magnetite (*bhrāmaka*), and likewise conch-shell navel (*śaṅkhanābhi*),
along with primary and secondary minerals (*rasa* and *anuparasa*) combined with the great digestive agent (*mahājāraṇa*);
[and] *vajrakanda*, *vajralatā*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, and *amṛtā*.
One should cook the seeds of *kaṭutumba* with dead metals [in equal proportions].
All [the ingredients] should be in equal parts; the wise one should grind that [mixture] with peacock blood until the medicinal preparation becomes firm.

The crucible should be made in the shape of a *vallā* (a type of vessel); it should be provided with covers, and one should place the mercury (*sūta*) in its middle. One should blow [upon it] with downward air (*adhovāta*).
At the very beginning, one should apply there a diamond (*vajra*) smeared with medicinal herbs.

What doubt can there be in this? Just as when a crucible has been burnt by a fierce fire with a thunderbolt (*vajra*), one should grind it in a furnace fire until it has acquired eleven times its original quality; then one should again digest the *vajra*.
And with well-burnt conch-shell navel, soaked in the juice of *mātuluṅga*, pearls should then be added; when the mercury is thus digested by the diamond,
through this sequential application, it becomes eleven times [its original potency].
And simply peacock bile, mixed with indigo resin.
Blue lotuses smeared [with these] and cast into the juice during the process, according to the ritual procedure, produce great dyes; one should discard those that yield inferior colors.

One should smear [the vessel] with red substances, peacock bile, and excellent gems endowed with great jewels; by that, it will flow from within the mercury. Also, turmeric and kuṣṭha, impregnated with *brahmaniryāsa*.
This is the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of topaz; one should cause it to be administered together with that very [substance].

When many gems have been digested and when the *bhṛṅgarāga* [minerals] have been processed, O Goddess of good vows, the Lord of Mercury (*rasendra*) is seen to possess a blue, yellow, and reddish luster.
Pure gold leaves should be smeared with [the powder] by a hundredth part and killed by means of a *puṭa* [firing]; it becomes like an *indragopa* insect.
By its mere touch, it pierces everything; this, O Dear One, is dead gold.

One-third of the *sūtaka* [mercury] should be processed together with that very [substance]. When it is situated within the crucible (*mūṣā*), one should again digest it with that same [substance]. O Goddess, it will become a penetrator by fumes (*dhūmavedhī*). Then, having been processed and digested once more, [it attains its full power].

By this sequential method, if the threefold chain is worn out, it will pierce the mountain, the underworld, and the surface of the earth; there is no doubt in this. The light on the side will be visible, but that which is above will not be seen at all.
One should know that it moves upon the earth; this is the lord of mercury (*rasendra*), of this there is no doubt.
By means of it, O Goddess, one whose movement is unceasing may travel a hundred *yojanas*, possessing divine splendor, a great body, divine vision, and great strength.
Freed from all diseases, he shall live as long as the moon and stars endure; moreover,
his urine and feces dissolve all metals when combined with well-digested *vajra* and gold.
Stationed in the fire, it digests the metals; the mercury (*sūtaka*) undergoes binding. One should cause [the metal] to flow by means of that seed; one may pierce even a thousand [times].
Once it has been caused to flow, one should subsequently digest it; it is to be smeared and cast [into the crucible] thousands of times.
