O Goddess, this ordinary mercury becomes the maker of the body of Viṣṇu.
But he who is bound while deprived of food becomes a bringer of divine accomplishments.
The *mūlabandha* is the best; the binding of the mercury (*rasabandhana*) is middling;
the binding by cooking (*pākabandha*) is the lowest—thus is the threefold binding.

The root-binding (*mūlabandhana*) is that binding which is called the binding of latent impressions (*vāsanābandha*). (8.1) There may be some binding by means of the root from among the sixty-four roots.
(RA_13.8.2) The root-limb of animals, *asuras*, and so forth, is considered the limb of the deity. (RA_13.9.1)
And the stone is honored by both the perfected ones (*siddhas*) and human beings.
(RA 13.9.2) The binding is threefold, consisting of the *piṇḍikā*, *druti*, and *saṃkoca*.
(RA 13.10.1) And the pure binding previously mentioned is accomplished by means of divine medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*). (10.2)

The mercury is bound by means of *kṣaṇabandha* fluxes; this is declared to be *kṣaṇabandha*. (11) Abhra and *harabīja*, along with gold in the sixteenth part [of the weight], should be smelted in an open crucible and purified with glass and *ṭaṅkaṇa*. (RA 13.12.2)
When the mercury is blown [into the crucible] while rotating clockwise and melted with the seed-syllable of Hara,
O lady of excellent hips, it abandons the crucible and remains fixed like a bound substance.
With a dose of even half of a half-raktikā, it pierces even mountains.
O Goddess of the gods, by consuming it, a man becomes equal to Rudra;
he sports through the seven worlds with prowess equal to Śiva.
(RA_13.14.2–3) Regarding the "fusion of fluxes" (*drutimelana*), O Goddess, listen to the supreme [instruction on] the divine elixirs (*divyauṣadhi*) for the fusion of fluxes. (15)

Vajrakanda and lāṅgalī, combined with uccāṭana, cause the mica to dissolve quickly; otherwise, there is no transmutation. [The process of] the union of *druti* and *rasa* [is achieved] with black agallochum, conch-shell navel, garlic, white asafoetida, and *rāmaṭha*.

When combined with the menstrual blood of a woman (*nārī*), *kusuma*, *pālāśa*, seed-oil (*bījataila*), and heated together, all the molten metals (*drutayaḥ*) unite when boiled with these juices. This is the "union of all pairs" (*sarvadvandvamelāpana*). Furthermore, honey, poison (*viṣa*), *guñjā*, borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), and likewise the menstrual blood of a woman [are used].
Anointed with breast milk, it causes all dualities to merge.

(RA 13.18.2) With *jīva*, *ahi*, *vyoma*, and *pāṣāṇa*, and well-impregnated with *kroṣṭujihvā*, it is the transmuter (*krāmaṇa*) of all metals and the unifier of liquefied substances (*druti*). (RA 13.19.2)
One should introduce the saliva of a horse that pierces a *koṭi*, garlic, ginger, nimba leaves, borax,
mercury, mica, and diamond.
One should then combine these three— mica, gold-mercury, and quicksilver— in one place.

Having applied a coating to the crucible by means of *krāmaṇa*, the wise one should [place it] on the ground and heat it with a fire of husks and chaff; through this sweating process, [the substance] melts in an instant.
This [mercury], having undergone a hundredfold penetration (*śatavedhī*), acts upon copper, silver, and brass.
Into its center, one should again place the liquefied essence of mica and gold.
It should be subjected to sudation over a fire of husks and chaff until only the mercury remains.
That [mercury] shall possess a thousandfold penetrative power; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
In each successive stage of the *saṃkalikā* process, the piercing (*vedha*) increases tenfold.
A great elixir (*mahārasa*) bound by seven *saṃkalikās* pierces a distance of ten million *yojanas*.
When a wise person consumes it for the sake of the body, even in a dose of only one *guñjā*, [it grants immortality].
Combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*) and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), along with ghee and honey,
it should be taken after each previous dose has been digested, until the dose reaches eight *raktikās*.
As for the mercury that has been killed by a combination of [substances] numbering from one hundred up to ten million:

By that measure, one may live as long as mercury [endures] in the *vajravallī* plant. (RA_13.26.2) Through the liquefaction (*druti*) of gold, mica, and copper, combined with mercury, one attains the state of Viṣṇu.
(27.1) One should pierce [the body] by means of the aforementioned yoga and consume [the elixir] through every application. (RA_13.27.2)

One attains the station of Viṣṇu, possessing prowess equal to that of Viṣṇu. (RA 13.27.3) Regarding the immobilization (*stambhana*) of various metals: liquid mercury (*pārada*), combined with iron, mica, and gold, will certainly achieve immobilization when subjected to the *prativāpa* (re-precipitation) of tin in a hundredth part. (RA 13.28.2)
Likewise, when sharp iron (*tīkṣṇa*) and gold are combined with mercury (*pārada*),
there shall be a stabilization (*stambhana*) by means of a counter-application (*prativāpa*) of lead (*nāga*) at one hundredth part.
Similarly, when bell-metal (*ghoṣa*), silver (*tāra*), and mercury are combined— (RA 13.30.1)
By the addition of tin as a counter-poison (*prativāpa*), immobilization (*stambhana*) occurs in a hundredfold proportion.

(30.2) Thus indeed are the methods for liquefaction (*druti-yoga*) to be understood according to the prescribed rule. (RA 13.31.1) By this method of liquefaction, mercury (*rasa*) becomes the maker of bodies and metals. (RA 13.31.2)
14. Śrī Bhairava said:
O Sovereign of the Gods, I shall further explain another [mudrā], the Vajrabandha. (RA_14.1.2)
For the binding and digestion of mercury, a woman should consume the menstrual blood of another woman along with sulphur for twenty-one days;
that blood is beneficial for the binding and digestion of the king of mercury.
One part of diamond ash and three parts of purified mercury [should be used]. (RA_14.2.2) (3.1)
One should grind the *dvipadī* plant with dust until it reaches the state of a paste (*kalka*). Then, one should apply a coating of gold leaf using a quarter-part of that paste.
Furthermore, one should take the juice of *vyomavallī*, *kānta* iron, and finely powdered *ṭaṅkaṇa*.

Having placed the mica in a mortar with one-eighth part [of the other ingredients], one should grind it until it becomes a *naṣṭapiṣṭa* paste. Then, having encapsulated that quartet, one should fire it in a closed crucible (*andhamūṣā*). Once it has been blown in the closed crucible and combined with the *krāmaṇa* agent, [the process is complete].
O Goddess, the great mercury known as *śatavedhī* arises as *khoṭa*.
Having repeatedly added *sauvīra*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and glass (*kāca*), one should purify it.
When [the mercury] is not digested and is mixed with gold, *samāvarta* arises.
Then, one should proceed by increasing the number of links in a sequential order.
A single link made with mercury of one-fold potency is called the first link;
however, with mercury of three-fold potency, it becomes the second link.
With a mercury sixteen times [the weight of the base metal], the third amalgamation (*saṃkalī*) occurs;
with a mercury ten times [the weight], the fourth amalgamation occurs;
and with a mercury fifteen times [the weight], O Mistress, the fifth amalgamation occurs.
O Īśī, the sixth *saṃkalikā* is considered to be twenty-one-fold;
O Īśī, the seventh *saṃkalī* is remembered as being twenty-eight-fold;
the eighth *saṃkalikā* shall be connected with thirty-six folds.
The ninth *saṃkalī* is considered to consist of forty-five qualities;
the tenth *saṃkalī* is traditionally held to consist of fifty-five qualities.
Thus, through this gradual increase, there is the tenfold binding of the *saṃkalīs*.
Having pierced [the target] in the first [instance], one becomes a piercer of ten; in the second, a piercer of a hundred;
in the third, a piercer of a thousand; and in the fourth, a piercer of ten thousand.
In the fifth, one would be a piercer of a hundred thousand, and in the sixth, a piercer of a million.
In the seventh [stage], there is the piercing of the *koṭi*; likewise, in the eighth, ten *koṭis*.
In the ninth, there is the vision of smoke; in the tenth, the piercing by sound.
Bound by each successive stage, the piercing becomes tenfold.
Bound by ten links, piercing sound, and a great elixir—just as it acts upon metal, so does it act upon the body; of this there is no doubt.
One should pierce the elements and the physical body with that same measure.
One should have a divine pill made, the size of a jujube seed;
having worshipped Mahākālī, the wise person should wear it constantly.
I shall proclaim its mantra, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
The *praṇava* is the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī, and after that, the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī.

(RA 14.21) Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ Kālikā! O Kālī, O Mahākālī, O consumer of flesh and blood! (22.1) Hrīṃ hrīṃ huṃ! O Goddess with red and black faces, grant me the accomplishment of the elixir (*rasasiddhi*). (22.2)
*Śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ ramā śaktiś ca*; this mantra known as Tārā bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
(23) Having then worshipped the Goddess, and especially the *Siddhacakra*, one should cast that pill of divine form into the middle of the mouth. (RA_14.24.1–2)

O beloved, the pill bound with mercury through a hundredfold penetration (*śatavedha*), when kept in the mouth for one month, enables one to live for the duration of a *yuga*. Likewise, the auspicious pill bound through a thousandfold penetration (*sahasravedha*)— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; this translation reflects the portion available.*

If it remains in the mouth for two months, one may live as long as the moon, sun, and stars. O fair-faced one, if a pill is prepared through ten thousand piercings, then one's lifespan shall be equal to that of Śakra within three months.
The pill of divine form that is prepared by piercing one hundred thousand [times],
when kept in the mouth for four months, bestows the lifespan of Brahmā.
The pill of divine form that is prepared by piercing one million [times]...

If it remains in the mouth for five months, one shall obtain a lifespan equal to that of Viṣṇu. A pill of divine form, prepared by the "piercing of ten million" (*koṭivedha*), if kept in the mouth for six months, will indeed lead one directly to the state of Rudra himself.
The pill, possessing a divine form, is divided into one hundred crores [of types];
by keeping it in the mouth for seven months, one shall attain the state of Īśvara.
The pill, which has the form of Śiva, is bound [to the tongue] during the observation of smoke.

If it remains in the mouth for eight months, one shall obtain the fruit of Īśāna. That pill, which is the very form of Śiva and is bound by the piercing of sound, if kept in the mouth for nine months, that man shall become all-pervading.

Whether he be the Self-Existent One or Maheśvara, bound by nine chains, he is the creator, the destroyer, and the enjoyer himself; he bestows curses and favors. He is omniscient, the maker of all, subtle in form, and stainless.
By his own will he creates the world, and by his will he may withdraw it.
Having become one who moves at his own pleasure, that man becomes the universal form (viśvarūpa).
He is worshipped by all the gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Furthermore, I shall describe another *vajrabandha* which is very difficult to obtain.
One should cause a *vajrabandha* of equal parts to be prepared by consuming gold with pure mercury. One should grind dead-vajra (*mṛtavajra*) in the amount of one *pala* with the juices of *dvipadī*.

As previously stated, the remainder [of the procedure] involves grinding the previously prepared substance with *haṃsapādī*, impregnating it, and sealing it with jewels; as before, this will become fruitful.
One who has mastered this becomes bound by the vajra, a perfected one invincible even to gods and dānavas.
The leader of the twenty-four Siddhas, the bestower of all accomplishments:
one should grind mercury, equal in weight to diamond powder, with *haṃsapādī*;
having enclosed it in a crucible, one should kill it, and then add an equal amount of mercury again.
The purified *khoṭa* becomes quickly heated by means of glass and *ṭaṅkaṇa*;
O Beloved, that mercury arises with a brilliance like the rising sun.
One should then combine Vajrasattva, space, mercury, and gold.
One attains immortality by keeping [the mercury] in the mouth, O Lord of the Gods.
Having first digested the mercury, one should then digest it with that very same substance.
There is no doubt that what pierces ten million [atoms] when held in the mouth leads to the state of a sky-walker (*khecara*).
One should pierce the metal and the body with that same measure;
one should cause a divine pill to be made from gold by means of the *vajrasiddhi*.
By this sequential method, one should reduce [the metal] to its essence as much as possible.
O Goddess, that ash-mercury (*bhasmasūtaka*) is the destroyer of all diseases.
Having first refined it with gold, one should smear the "moon and sun" [the base metal] with a pill that transmutes the body of iron;
then, by adding a thirty-second part, it becomes half-gold, exceeding the measure.
The wise one should fashion a pill the size of a jujube seed;
just as it acts upon iron, so does it act upon the body, and never otherwise.
Gold, bound by mercury and joined with vajra, kāntaloha, and copper, [is thus prepared].
One should dye that finely powdered *khoṭa* seven times with menstrual blood,
adding five *guñjā* seeds.
Then, having placed it upon birch bark and tied it in a cloth bundle, one should bind it.
One should cause it to sweat, O Goddess of the God of Gods, until it becomes a *golaka*.
*Lāṅgalī*, *jīvaka*, and *mustā* combined with *indravāruṇī*—
one should place these into the mass and envelop the *vajragola* within them.
Having carefully placed [the substance] inside a crucible and sealed it,
one should set the crucible on the ground and apply a *puṭa* (heat-treatment) to its top.
By this very application, the great mercury attains *bandha* (solidification).
O beloved, if one holds a *golaka* in the mouth for one year,
one shall live for thousands of *kalpas*, like a serpent of great strength.
After twelve years, one truly becomes the very form of Rudra.

From the sweat of that body, eight metals and gold [are produced]. (55.2) Likewise, vajra-ash combined with mercury and gold—whosoever places this in his mouth becomes free of grey hair within a year. (56.1–56.2)
Regarding the *khoṭa* [residue] from *abhraka* and so forth—[it bestows] longevity: "The essence of black *abhraka*, silver, copper, and gold;
(57.1) one should prepare equal parts of *mākṣika*, *kāntaloha*, and *tīkṣṇaloha*.
When heated in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), it instantly becomes a *khoṭa*. (RA 14.57.2–58.1)
That pill should be made into a fine powder and formed into a ball with quicksilver;
one part of dead-vajra and four parts of the ball should be ground in a heated mortar until the mercury is reduced to ashes.
One should destroy [the substance] in the *bhūdhara* yantra according to the sequence of the seven *saṃkalikās*.
One should then cause that ash, in a quantity equal to a *guñjā* seed, to be licked with honey and clarified butter.
By practicing this for one year, a man shall indeed attain a lifespan of ten thousand years.
Free from wrinkles and grey hair, he possesses great strength and prowess.
One *pala* of that ash and one *pala* of sulphur,
placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heated, instantly become a solid bolus (*khoṭa*).
He shall live for thousands of kalpas, possessing great strength like the bodiless god of love.
By means of his urine and feces, the eight metals and gold [are transformed]. Afterwards, one should color that *khoṭa* with tin, mica, and *kapāli*.

One should dye it seven times, and it will become like saffron. Having processed it together with gold and subjected it to three cycles of *sāraṇā*, one should use that very substance, even in a thousandth part, to transmute all metals.
The essence of black mica, along with silver, copper, gold, iron, bound mercury, and *mākṣika* [pyrite],
when combined and heated in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), instantly becomes a solid pellet (*khoṭa*).
Having processed it together with gold and refined it through three cycles of *sāraṇā*,
one should apply a transmutation (*vedha*) using a hundredth part of that very [refined substance].
Thereby, divine gold is produced, fit for adorning the ornaments of the gods.
One part of bound mercury, one part of lead, one part of gold, and one part each of mica and antimony—
having combined these, they should be melted; once the mercury has been digested, one should digest [the mixture] further.
One should cause the transmutation (*vedha*) by means of that very [substance] at a hundredth part.
One part of bound mercury (*baddhasūta*) and one part of crooked iron (*kuṭila*),
placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and blown with a bellows, instantly becomes a solid bolus (*khoṭa*).

One part of that *khoṭa* and one part of sulfur, placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heated until only tin remains; by this sequential method, having extinguished the tin six times over, [it becomes pure]. (RA 14.72.1–2)

By this sequential method, one should cause the nāga to flow sixfold; thereafter, one should color that mercury with a *kapālin* of sharp copper (*tīkṣṇa-śulva*). One should diligently color it until it resembles saffron.
Having processed it together with gold and refined it through three cycles of *sāraṇā*, one should pierce the copper with a hundredth part [of the essence]; divine gold is thereby produced.
Furthermore, I shall describe another supreme method for the refinement of liquids.
One should color pure gold with a mixture of *tīkṣṇa*, copper, and *kapālin*.
Taking one part of the processed seed (*pakvabīja*) and one part of molten mercury, one should grind them with a moderate amount of acid; in an instant, a pill (*golaka*) is formed.

One part of *mṛtavajra* and four parts of *golaka* should be ground in a heated mortar; the mercury (*sūtaka*) is reduced to ashes. One should kill it in the *bhūdhara* yantra through the sequence of seven *saṃkalikās*.
Then, one should again grind that ash with sour gruel (*madhyamāmla*).
One should diligently apply the *puṭa* [roasting] process three hundred and sixty times. That ash becomes divine, resembling the reddish hue of vermilion (*sindūra*).
With that very [substance], one should pierce silver with a thousandth part of gold;
take one part of "dead-vajra" (mṛtavajra) and sixteen parts of mercury (sūtaka). It should be rubbed in succession with the juice of *devadālī* and *śaṅkhapuṣpī*.
One should kill [the mercury] in the *bhūdhara* yantra; it becomes ashes at that very moment.
Even when being smelted with a thousand *phūtkāra* breaths, it does not move. Such ash-mercury (*bhasmasūta*) should be applied to both the body and to metal.

For the piercing of copper (*śulbavedha*) using this *bhasmasūta*: one *pala* of that ash and one *pala* of sulfur, placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heated, instantly become a solid mass (*khoṭa*).
One should subsequently color (*rañjayet*) that *khoṭa* by means of the application of the *Kāpālika* method.

One should cause the transmutation (*vedha*) by means of the application of the three *sāraṇās*. (RA_14.85.2) The fusion of ash-mercury and lead: one *pala* of ash-mercury and one *pala* of lead, when subjected to a *puṭa* [firing], becomes an ash resembling the reddish hue of vermilion (*sindūra*). (RA_14.86.2)
Then, one should again grind that ash with cow-bile;
having placed it in a copper vessel, one should rub it with an iron hammer.
It should then be cooked over a gentle fire until its fusion with lead occurs.
With this product: one part of the ash of *śulba* (copper) and one part of a gold globule,
having combined and thoroughly rubbed these together with a *krāmaṇa* agent,
even silver (*tārāriṣṭa*) becomes gold by that very [mixture] in the proportion of one-thousandth part.
By this sequential process, tin ash is produced.
With a thousandth part of that very [ash], one should perform the transmutation of copper (*śulva-vedha*).
That copper becomes silver, resembling a conch shell, a *kunda* flower, or the moon.

Mercury killed by the *śulbavedha* process, the essence of white mica (*śvetābhra*), as well as magnetite, non-magnetite, and iron; tin, silver, white *vaikrānta*, and *kadambaka*—when these are placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heated until they form a solid mass (*khoṭa*) resembling jasmine or the moon. (92.1–92.2)

That pill, having been made into a fine powder, should be formed into a ball with quicksilver. One part of dead-vajra and four parts of the ball should be ground in a heated mortar; thus the mercury is reduced to ashes.
One should kill [the mercury] in the *bhūdhara* apparatus by means of the sequence of seven *saṃkalikās*;
thereafter, ashes arise that resemble a conch shell, the *kunda* flower, or the moon.
One *pala* of those ashes and one *pala* of sulfur—
When it has entered the blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and is blown [with a bellows], it becomes a *khoṭa* instantly.
Having processed it with silver (*tāra*) and subjected it to three rounds of *sāraṇā*,
one should cause it to penetrate (*vedha*) copper (*śulva*) by means of that very [substance] in a thousandth part.

One part of mercury reduced to ash with *vaṅga* (tin) [is combined with] eight *pala* of *tīkṣṇa* (steel) mercury and eight *pala* of liquefied mercury. One should grind this in a heated mortar (*taptakhalla*) with the juice of *kuṣṭha* bark.
At that very moment, a solid mass (*piṇḍa*) is produced—a spherical pellet together with the *tīkṣṇa*.
One should rub it with a heated mortar, and it becomes ash in that very instant.
One should kill [the mercury] in the *bhūdhara* machine through the process of seven *saṃkalikās*.
With that [ash] itself, one should effect the transmutation (*vedha*) of tin by means of a sixteenth part.

One *pala* of that ash and one *pala* of sulfur, placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heated, instantly become a solid mass (*khoṭa*). One part of that *khoṭa* and an equal amount of finely powdered *tīkṣṇa* [iron]—
Two parts of the liquefied mercury should be ground together with everything in one place. Having ground it in a heated mortar, a ball is formed in an instant.
One should then kill [the mercury] in the *bhūdhara* machine by means of the sequence of seven *saṃkalikās*.
All that is reduced to ash, resembling a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon. One should cause that ash to form a pill (*khoṭa*) combined with *tīkṣṇa* [iron] through this sequential yoga,
by means of the process of the seven layers (*saṃkalikā*).
Thereafter, one should digest that ash, having processed it through three cycles of *sāraṇā*.

With just a hundred-thousandth part (*lakṣāṃśa*) of that very [ash], one should effect the transmutation (*vedha*) of tin. One should smear one *pala* of pure tin with one *pala* of purified mercurial ash.
One should rub [the ingredients] in an iron vessel; thus, tin is killed in an instant.
Two palas of killed tin, two palas of copper-pierced (śulbavedha) killed tin, and two palas of silver powder—(107.2)—to these one should add two palas of sulfur and one pala of borax. (108.1)
When heated in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), it instantly becomes a solid mass (*khoṭa*).
(108.2) One *pala* of powdered *khoṭa* and one *pala* of molten mercury should be rubbed with the acidic juice of *mātuluṅga*; it becomes a pill (*golaka*) in an instant. (RA_14.109.1–2)
With that very same sixteenth part, one should cause the transmutation (*vedha*) by means of mercury (*śulva*).
One should place lead (*nāga*) in the place of tin (*vaṅga*), and gold in the place of silver (*tāra*).
Through the sequential application of the previously described transmutation of silver and lead, one should cause the mercury to form a solid pellet (*khoṭa*).
That cinnabar should be reduced to a fine powder and made into a ball with quicksilver;
with that very [substance] in a sixteenth part [of its weight], one should transmute silver ore.
One *pala* of dead tin and one *pala* of quicksilver—(RA_14.113.1)
One *pala* of *sattva-cūrṇa*—these three should be mixed together.

One should rub them with the acidic juice of *mātuluṅga*; in an instant, it becomes a ball (*golaka*). This is the stabilization of tin (*vaṅga-stambhana*). One part of "dead vajra" (*mṛta-vajra*) and four parts of the ball [are used]. (115.1)
One should grind it together with the juice of the medicinal herbs in a mortar;
then, one should cause it to die in the *bhūdhara* apparatus by means of seven *puṭa* applications. By the power of the *vajra* itself, all of that becomes ash.
O Goddess, one should cause sea salt and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) to be placed into the midst of the ashes;
then, having combined them and ground them together for three days in *vajrī* milk,
one should apply the *puṭa* treatment in an earthen vessel (*bhūdhara*) containing the skull of Viśvāmitra.
All that becomes ash, resembling a conch shell, the *kunda* flower, or the moon.
By that very [substance], when it is the size of a barley grain, one instantly immobilizes tin (*vaṅga*).
Tin, silver, and likewise the essence (*sattva*), when combined with an equal amount of mercury, form a globule (*golaka*).
By this sequential method, one should kill each [element] individually;
all that becomes ash through the power of the vajra alone.
One *pala* of *siddharasa* (or *bhasmasūta*) and two *palas* of tin ash...
Two *pala*s of dead mercury, two *pala*s of the ashes of living beings,
one *pala* of conch powder, five *pala*s of sea salt,
and eight *pala*s of *ṭaṅkaṇa*— one should grind all these together in a single place.
Having ground it with *vajrī* milk, one should apply fourteen *puṭas*.
This is the perfected elixir (*siddharasa*) itself, difficult to obtain even by the gods.
Afterwards, one should melt tin in an earthen vessel.
The perfected ash should be stirred with an iron rod;
one should blow [the fire] with effort until it reaches a state of hardness.
When placed in a blind crucible and blown, it becomes beautiful silver.
The production of excellent silver through the addition of tin: "Sometimes, when the silver has been smelted, one should again add tin.
When tested by heating on a leaf, by scratching, and by cutting, that silver becomes eternal.
That [silver] is solidified into a globule, endowed with a sixteenth part [of the alloy]. (126.1–127.1)
One part of *mṛtavajra* should be ground together in one place.
One should then grind it with the juice of *devadālī* and *śaṅkhapuṣpī*.
One should kill [the mercury] in a *bhūdhara* yantra by means of seven *puṭa* applications.

Then, one should subsequently cook that ash in a *dīpayaṃtra*. (RA_14.129) This is the method for the immobilization of tin (*vaṅgastambhana*). One *pala* of mercury-ash and two *palas* of white mica;
(130.1) one *pala* of conch-shell powder and one *pala* of borax. (RA_14.130.2)
Then, having combined all of that, one should grind it with *vajrī* milk.
Afterwards, one should apply fourteen *puṭas* using wild stones (*āraṇyopalaka*).
This mercury, even in a dose the size of a barley grain, solidifies tin (*vaṅga*) in an instant.

One *pala* of black mica (*abhraka*) and one *pala* of mercury killed by the "serpent-piercing" (*nāgavedha*) method, along with one *pala* of sulfur—having combined these, one should then grind them. While being ground with great effort, it becomes a pill (*golaka*) in an instant. (RA 14.132.2–133)

One part of *mṛtavajra* and four parts of *golaka* should be ground together for one *prahara*; the mercury (*sūtaka*) will then be reduced to ashes. One should apply a *puṭa* using wild cow dung within an earthen vessel (*bhūdhara*).
By this sequential method, prepare the seven-layered compound.
With that very same hundredth part, one should cause the piercing (*vedha*) of the *nāga* to be performed.
Afterwards, one should color that *khoṭa* with the *kapāla* of mercury, mica, and copper.
Thereafter, one should again color it with a *kapāli* of sharp copper (*tīkṣṇa-śulva*).
Thereafter, one should again color it with a *kapāli* of lead and mica (*nāgābhrāka*). Having amalgamated it together with gold, it should be processed through three *sāraṇā*s.
By means of that very same thousandth part, one should cause the transmutation (*vedha*) by means of mercury;
divine gold is produced, the supreme ornament for the gods.
Like the coloring of the moon and sun, diamond-ash (*vajrabhasma*), when encapsulated in the milk of *snuhī* for ten cycles of heating (*puṭa*), [achieves this].
One should grind mercury equal in quantity to that [substance] and roast it with the juices of *devadālī*.
Then one should roast iron (*tīkṣṇa*) equal in quantity to that with the juice of *triphalā*.
Finally, one should roast lead (*nāga*) equal in quantity to that with *ahi*, *mārā*, and *rāṭarūṣaka*.
Indeed, that which bestows a golden color, when joined with one-twentieth part [of it],
and this pure silver, when joined with sixty-fourth part [of it], should be colored. With one-eighth part of that very same substance, one should smear the leaves of the *nāga* plant.
One should kill the *nāga* [mercury], which resembles vermilion in its reddish hue, by means of *puṭa* [roasting].

One should kill gold equal in weight to that [mercury] by roasting it in the juice of the *kāñcanāra* tree. And one should kill copper equal in weight to that [gold] with the juice of the *gṛhakanyā* plant.
Afterwards, one should roast it with acid until it resembles vermilion. With that [substance], one should color mercury and then pierce [the base metal] with a hundredth part of it.
This may be done with mercury either containing seed (*sabīja*) or devoid of seed (*bījavarja*), together with diamond (*vajra*).
One should then grind that ash with the juice of gold-leaf (*svarṇapattra*). With that very [mixture], one should transmute copper (*śulva*); then one should join that copper with silver (*tāra*).
One should couple gold with diamond (*vajra*), and one should couple mercury (*rasa*) with gold.

One should saturate the body with the essence; indeed, that body becomes free from old age and death. (RA_14.148.2) The *melāpana* of all dualities consists of plantain root and *sauvīra* salt saturated with the juice of *kaṇṭakārī*;
it is the transmuter (*krāmaṇa*) of all metals and the unifier of all dualities. (RA_14.149.1–2)
Having combined the two-fold gold with the five-fold *pañcāṅga* and the seed of the *mārjārī*,
one should then grind them together and pierce the *vajra* with that very mixture.
Once placed in a *vajra*-crucible and heated by blowing, one should thus produce the two-fold gold.
Vajramelāpaka, *tejaspuṅkha*, powder of *kāntapāṣāṇa*, *bhūlatā*, *rāmaṭha*, honey, *guñjā*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, glass (*kāca*), the shell of a crab, and the milk of *snuhī*—
all these should be combined in equal parts and ground with breast milk. (RA 14.152.1–2)
When applied to the crucible at its edge, the union with the *vajra* is blissful.
In the *haṭha*-fire within the *vajra*-crucible, the firm *vajras* meet;
having become exceedingly subtle pigments, they indeed attain a state of oneness.
Blown with the addition of glass and borax, it attains purity;
through many crucibles, it becomes a mass of radiant luster.
For the amalgamation of diamond and gold: one part of dead diamond and sixteen parts of gold.
One should provide sixteen parts of powdered white glass;
having been heated while placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), one should effect a "vajra-binding" (*vajrabandha*).
By means of this sequential procedure, one should perform this heating seven times.
It unites at that very moment, like water with gold.
(157.3) Into the powder of the union of diamond and gold, one should add the "dead diamond" (*mṛtavajra*) of *Narakapāla*.
When blown [into the fire] while contained within a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), it unites with the gold at that very moment. (RA 14.158.2)
One should grind together mercury, gold, *bhṛṅgapakṣa*, human hair, antimony, and borax, along with the dung of a young calf, using breast milk. Then,
having applied this as a coating to the crucible, one should place the mercury and gold inside.

When heated in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), the *vajra* melts; it does not otherwise. (RA 14.160.2) For the union of *vajra* and gold, one should take the four ingredients—*kānta*, *vajra*, *guñjā*, and sulfur—and grind them with breast milk to form a coating for the crucible. (RA 14.161.2)
When blown in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), the diamond (*vajra*) unites at that very moment.
One should saturate the dead diamond with the milk of *uttaravāruṇī* for the purpose of binding the liquefied [metal].
Then, one should place the diamond in the middle of a gold paste right there.
One should wrap it with birch bark and then wrap it externally with cloth;
having placed it in the midst of grain, one should leave it there continuously for one fortnight.
Once it has been carefully extracted, one should perform the vajra-binding.
O Pārvatī, the liquefied *vajras* should be mixed with that very [substance].
That is to be known as the "liquefied bond" (*drutabandha*), which effects a penetration (*vedha*) of a hundred thousand times.
Likewise, having penetrated all the gems according to the prescribed rule, [one attains the same result].

It pierces through a hundred thousand [leaves] and bestows the perfection of the body. (RA 14.167.2) Gems, flux, mercury, and amalgamation; *musalī*, *citraka*, *vandhyākarkoṭī*, *kandapadminī*, (168.1) *kañcukī*, *nīlasindūrī*, *vāsā*, and likewise *nāgabalā*. (RA 14.168.2)
The juices of these [herbs] and likewise the liquefied forms of these gems should be placed in a bell-metal vessel; having held it in the sun, one should then apply fire beneath it.
Having prepared the juice of the medicinal herbs, one should clarify it again and again.
When heated for just one watch (yāma), the mercury indeed melts into a liquid state;
it is impossible to describe their transmutation even in hundreds of years.
Saindhava salt and nimba leaves wrapped in vākucī and nalā [are used].
The union with the juice of molten cloud (drutābhra) alone is considered supreme.
O Īśānī, the "vajra" is the pair; by means of the vajra, the killing of the mercury (*rasa*) is performed.
This is declared to be the "killing with seed" (*sabījamāraṇa*), as well as the binding of the *khoṭa*.
Therefore, tell me that, O Goddess of the Gods; what else do you wish to hear?
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord, command [me] regarding the binding of the king of mercury (*rasarāja*) by means of the primary essences (*mahārasa*), the secondary essences (*uparasa*), and the metals (*loha*).
Śrī Bhairava said: (2.1) "Command me regarding the entire binding of the king of mercury.
Śrī Bhairava said:

One part of *vaikrānta* [ore] should be pierced by [mercury]; one part of *vaikrānta* and eight parts of mercury, seven parts of gold, along with *dvipadī*, juice, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*—when ground into a paste, dried, and blown [in the furnace], it becomes a *khoṭa*, O Dear One. (2.2–3.1)

Having repeatedly added *sauvīra*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and glass (*kāca*), one should purify [the mercury]. Then, having processed the mercury with an equal amount of gold, it should be placed in a crucible (*mūṣā*). One should then cause that mercury to consume an equal portion [of the other substances] along with purified mercury.
One should cause vaikrānta to be heated according to the previous method in sixteen parts;
through the application of ten *saṃkalikās*, the piercing (*vedha*) is ten times greater.
Through the application of seven *saṃkalikās*, the piercing is ten times greater.
Vaikrānta is to be known as being like a diamond; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Furthermore, I shall describe another practice that is difficult to find on earth. O Goddess, the essence of vaikrānta combined with mercury is used for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of vaikrānta.
Once it has been melted together with an equal amount of gold, one should place it in a stone vessel.
After it has remained buried in the ground for one month, one should carefully extract it.
O Goddess, this divine mercury will then serve as the material for the body.

Whatever *vaikrāntaka* stones there may be, O Goddess, having been steamed and ground for seven days each with the juice of *triphalā*, the essence of *bhūmyāmalaka*, and the juice of *vasuhaṭṭa*, [they become effective]. (9.1–10.1)
When well-smelted in a sealed crucible, the *khoṭa* becomes inexhaustible.
One should combine *kānta* iron, silver, gold, and mercury;
then add copper as a third part, together with antimony (*srotoñjana*).
When that is blown [in the furnace], it attains the state of *khoṭa* (solidified mass) and becomes a body-transforming metal (*dehaloha*).

[The process for] white *vaikrānta*: [its] juice withstands fire; [it is used for] piercing (*vedha*), which counters old age and other ailments. One should grind the powder of white *vaikrānta* with horse urine.
First, having taken [the powder] after it has been well-steamed, one should add one hundred *pala* [of mercury] for every single *pala* [of the powder].
The ash of silver (*tāra*) arises, having the appearance of pure crystal.
A wise person should mix that ash with mercury in equal proportions.
One should cause the silver to dissolve into the mercury and rub it with the urine of a horse.

One should seal it in an *andhamūṣā* crucible with a gentle fire in due order. The wise practitioner, having combined [the mercury] with a *krāmaṇa* agent, places it within the crucible; thus the mercury becomes capable of enduring the fire for one day and night, or even three nights.
By touching it, one will turn all metals into silver.
When consumed according to what is about to be described, it destroys old age and poverty.
The ritual for the red variety, which destroys old age and poverty, shall now be explained.

One should process its powder seven times with water from the *vyāghrī* root. One *pala* of that [powder], one *pala* of gold, and one *pala* of pure mercury shall all become pure ash; then, one should again add a hundred *palas* of gold.
That ash quickly arises, possessing a luster equal to pure gold.
One should then mix that ash with mercury and with gold;
O Goddess, it will become fire-resistant, and thereafter it becomes the supreme mercury.

The mercury becomes a "touch-penetrator" (*sparśavedhī*), and the great elixir (*mahārasa*) becomes a "ten-million-fold penetrator" (*koṭivedhī*). One should then mix the essence of red *vaikrānta* with gold;
having processed that [essence] to an equal amount, one should digest it with the mercury using an equal quantity.
One may pierce metals with a thousandth part [of it]; there is no doubt in this.
One part of black *vaikrānta* and one *pala* of pure mercury—these two should be ground together in a mortar until they become a powder. (RA_15.22.2)

Take one part of this powder and one thousand parts of gold; grind them together until they become a fine ash. Then, one should blow [the mixture] in a closed crucible (*andhamūṣā*) until it becomes a solid mass (*khoṭa*).
One should cause that pure mercury to consume an equal portion [of the powder];
O Pārvatī, it will transmute all metals by mere touch.
One should grind that powder together with mica and mercury.
One should grind it together until ash is produced;
then one should blow it in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) until it becomes a solid mass (*khoṭa*).
The wise one should then prepare a paste of that [ash] for consumption in equal parts.

It would transmute all metals into gold by mere touch. (RA 15.28.1) One should grind that powder and mica together with mercury. (28.2) One should subject it to sweating and digestion; thereafter, it will become fire-resistant. (RA 15.29.1)
That mercury, once processed, penetrates all metals.
(RA_15.29.2) Regarding yellow, red, and black: even though vaikrānta may be yellow in color, the procedure for the red and black varieties is also prescribed.
(30) As for yellow vaikrānta powder, it should be combined with gold powder. (RA_15.31.1)
Having mixed the great mercury with the powder of yellow mica, it is then subjected to sweating and grinding; after one month, the mercury becomes capable of withstanding fire.
It may be white, yellow, black, or likewise red in color.
Thus, O lady of excellent complexion, there are four kinds of minerals in vaikrānta.
Vaikrānta is situated in the place of the vajra; it is considered the supreme conjunction (*melana*).
And mercury (*pārada*), O beloved, which produces an iron-like body, is like iron.

Blue-colored vaikrānta, when combined with mercury, undergoes fixation (*mriyate*). O Goddess, if one should consume it together with honey and clarified butter in the form of a *maṇḍala*, one shall live as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
Whichever specific formulation is appropriate for each individual,
having prepared that medicine in the measure of one *guñjā* combined with the three types of honey,
one should consume wholesome milk, clarified butter, and *śāli* rice, while avoiding all other food. (RA 15.36.2–37)
A man should remain clothed in a dwelling situated in the middle of a couch in a secluded place.
The mantra *rasamṛtyuñjaya* should always be recited within his heart.
He should turn away from cattle and must not even look at women there.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes and devoted to mantra and meditation, a mortal who practices for one year will attain accomplishment; of this there is no doubt.
(RA 15.38.4–5) Regarding the binding of mercury (*rasabandhana*): one should grind mercury with *luṅgā* acid together with *vaikrānta*, sattva, and earth from a fissure. (38.6)
One should heat it with a lukewarm temperature and fill it with water.
Having mixed the *sattva* and the mercury (*sūta*), one should blow upon it; thus there shall be the binding of the mercury.
Having cast the bound mercury into the mouth, one beholds the cavities of the earth.

One *niṣka* of *vaikrānta* one should grind with horse urine for one day, O Goddess; having ground it thus, it becomes dead. Having performed this for four days, one should bring together an equal amount of mercury.
One whose mind is purified should perform the rubbing and sweating as previously described.
Each of the seven pairs [of substances] should be seven *pala* each, and the eighth should be eight *pala*.
One should grind them with the sour juice of *mātuluṅga* and administer sixty-four *puṭas*.
Resembling the dawn-sun, it pierces all metals.
The essence (*sattva*) of black mica (*kṛṣṇābhra*) becomes equal to gold;
having cast it into a diamond-crucible (*vajramūṣā*) and blown [the bellows], one should bring it to the state of a solid bolus (*khoṭa*).

Having cast the bound *rasa* into the mouth, one indeed attains freedom from old age and death. By mixing that very [substance] with ash until it becomes like black mica (*abhraka*), one should grind it for a day with the water of the root of *śalyāviśalyā*. (45.2)

The *puṭa* should remain in the center of the *bhramarāyantra* for seven days. That purified ash should be consumed in a dose of one *guñjā*, [increasing] by one up to five, with the middle amount being recommended once again. (RA 15.47.1–2)

O Goddess, as before, through binding, the great elixir (*mahārasa*) pierces the target at a distance of ten million units (*koṭivedhī*). Having pierced it, one takes *kānta* iron of red color, shining like lac juice;
when split, it resembles female blood. That powder, combined with mercury (*sūta*), [is used].
One should rub it with goat's blood; when blown [into a flame], it becomes a *khoṭa*, O Dear One.
That mercury (*sūta*) is a hundred-fold penetrator (*śatavedhī*) and shall be the remover of all diseases.
By wearing a pill in the mouth, one shall live for a thousand years.
Yellow-colored magnetite, when split, possesses a luster equal to gold;
O beautiful one, it pierces all metals by mere touch.
[The process of piercing] from the mercury-pellet (*rasakhoṭa*) up to gold: *lāṅgalī*, *karavīra*, *citraka*, and *girikarṇikā*. (51.1)
One should apply a coating of woman’s breast milk and *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax) to the crucible.
Take mercury twice the amount of the volatile substance (*capala*), and gold twice the amount of the mercury;
having made this into a fine paste (*naṣṭapiṣṭa*), one should heat it in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*).
Established therein, this mercury becomes an excellent *khoṭa*;
it penetrates lead by a hundredth part, and [the lead] becomes the color of a *guñjā* berry.
By that hundredth part of lead, copper becomes red in appearance.
With that hundredth part of copper, one pierces the silver to produce gold.
Furthermore, there are six parts of capala and seven parts of silver;
eight parts of gold and nine parts of mercury [are combined].
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, when these thirty parts are combined,
one should take *citraka*, *karavīra*, *lāṅgalī*, and likewise *gṛdhraviṭ*;
having ground them in the sour juice of *mātuluṅga*, one should apply it as a coating to the crucible.
Having blinded it, O Goddess, one should blow upon it; it becomes a beautiful *khoṭa*.
Pierced by a hundredth part of that *khoṭa*, lead (*nāga*) becomes ruddy.
When copper (*śulva*) is pierced by that lead, it becomes like a *guñjā* berry.

By means of that flux, silver becomes gold when pierced. O Goddess, [silver] that has the luster of gold but is volatile, when combined with one-quarter part [of the flux], and having added one-quarter part of gold, one should grind it for a moment with realgar.
Lāṅgalī, citraka, breast milk, karavīraka,
and vulture droppings— one should apply all of these as a coating to the crucible.
When [the substance] placed in its center is heated, it becomes a beautiful *khoṭa*.

One should pierce this as previously described; it becomes seedless gold. Having prepared the mercury with its seed (*sabīja*), one should cast a full *pala* of it into a well-heated iron vessel and cause it to settle upon the *capala*.
The mercury, red as lac, is bound like a great elephant by a [taming] elephant;
one *pala* of pure mercury and one *pala* of sulfur,
having combined these and then thoroughly rubbed them with the juice of *dhuttūra*, [one should proceed].
One should cultivate [the practice] by means of the wheel-yoga, and the mercury (*sūtaka*) is reduced to ashes.
When heated within a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), it becomes a beautiful *khoṭa* [pill].
It pierces mercury, gold, lead, and even the moon and sun [silver and copper].
One *pala* of pure mercury and one *karṣa* of sulfur should be rubbed in a smooth mortar moistened with the juice of *devadālī*;
by rubbing it with the hand and fingers, a paste of sulfur is produced.
One should grind [the substance] for one day with the fresh juice of *jambīra* (citron),
and thereafter grind it for three days with a decoction of the roots of *palāśa*. Then,
one should prepare auspicious pills combined with the five fluxing agents (*drāvaka*).
One should smear that pill with a paste of *palāśa* root;
it should be heated until the residue (*khoṭa*) becomes white through the application of glass and *taṅkaṇa*.
One should purify it with great effort until it attains complete purity.
O Goddess, one should then dye that *khoṭa* three times with *pannaga*.
Afterwards, one should dye it a hundred times with pure *abhraka-kapāli*.
This *khoṭa* pierces copper and silver by a thousandth part.
When mercury has been killed by sulphur through the process of *ghoṣavedha*, one should cause the dead metals to flow [into it].
(70.2) Having again refined the gold, consume it in equal parts.
When the copper and silver have been processed, the mercury penetrates the *ghoṣa* [alloy]. (RA_15.71.1–2)
Having made the mercury equal to gold, one should take half as much sulphur as the paste;
this, combined with the dust of *dvipadī* and mixed with *ṭaṅkaṇa*, should be rubbed together.
When that copper has been reduced to a fine powder (*naṣṭapiṣṭa*) and blown in the furnace, it then becomes a solid bolus (*khoṭa*).
Having repeatedly added *sauvīra*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and glass (*kāca*), one should purify it.
When it is not diminished, it mingles with the gold, and the *samāvarta* [reversion] occurs.
One should cause the consumption of equal parts of pure mercury (*sūta*) within the gold.
That mercury, when heated until it is reduced to ashes, becomes a solid residue (*khoṭa*). Then, one should grind that together with the dust of *dvipadī* and combined with borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*).
When pierced by a sixteenth part of silver and gold (*candrārka*), it becomes gold.
When that half of gold is combined, it attains equality with the *mātṛkā*.
Through the application of the *saṃkalikā* method, one should perform a piercing (*vedha*) ten times greater [in potency].
Just as in gold, so too in silver (*tāra*), one should apply the primordial seed-syllables (*ādibīja*).
One should pierce [the metal] with eightfold alloys, gold, and the piercing of the third *saṃkalā*, using a six-hundredth part;
with four times that same amount, one should pierce it with a thousandth part of gold. By this sequential method, if there are seven *saṃkalās*—
O beautiful one, it produces divine gold and the eight metals. (RA_15.79.2) Having powdered that again, one should roast it; it becomes ash.
(80.1) O Goddess, it removes all diseases when even a single *pala* of it is consumed. (RA_15.80.2)
With two palas, there is the lifespan of Brahmā; with three palas, it becomes that of Viṣṇu.
With four palas, one attains the state of Rudra; with five palas, one becomes Īśa.
When six palas have been consumed, O Goddess, one becomes the very body of Sadāśiva.
One should grind mercury, sulphur, and silver with the juice of *meṣavallī* for three days; then, one should mix [the resulting paste] with a quarter-part of tin (*tīkṣṇa*).
When heated in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), it instantly solidifies the tin.
O Goddess, powdered sulphur, impregnated with the juice of *markaṭī*, should be processed one hundred times; thus, even the ash of a living being is transmuted.
One should ignite it in an earthen vessel, combined with the mercury.
One should heat it with the heat of the sun combined with the juice of *markaṭī*;
mercury (*sūta*) swallows the sulfur (*gandhaka*), and in an instant it becomes a paste (*piṣṭikā*).
O Dear One, one should saturate the sulfur for the fragrant paste (*gandhapiṣṭikā*) with the juice of *tilaparṇī* alone.

O Goddess of gods, having dried it repeatedly in the shade for seven days, O beloved, one should place one *pala* of purified and fallen mercury (*sūta*) into the middle of a crucible (*mūṣā*), combined with the essence of *narendra*.
One should again digest processed sulfur in a *vālukāyantra*.
Sulfur should be added very gradually, again and again.
By this sequential method, a powder of sulfur (*gandhapiṣṭikā*) is produced.
Having combined the fragrant powder with the powder of sulphur and the juice of *kanaka*,
one should grind them together in a mortar according to the prescribed method,
O Goddess, and place that mixture in the sun to dry using the juice of *kanaka*.

One should perform the impregnation seven times with the menstrual blood of a woman, and likewise seven times [with other substances]. Then, one should place one *pala* of pure mercury in an earthen pan.
Next, one should add the impregnated sulfur combined with human bile.
Shaken by the heat of the sun, it becomes a paste in an instant.
O Bhairavī, one should take finely powdered sulphur and saturate it seven times with sour chickpea juice (*caṇakāmla*) and seven times with menstrual blood.
Into the midst of molten mercury, one should add camphor and sulphur in equal parts; having placed this in a cow-pen for seven days, it becomes a fragrant paste (*gandhapiṣṭikā*).
One should also take the seeds of *kaṭukośātakī* and the bulb of *caṇḍālī*.
Having ground it with breast milk, one should smear it with that paste.
One should place it in a *bhūdhara* (earth) crucible; it will be immobilized, of this there is no doubt.
Then, one should cause it to undergo a complete revolution within a gold crucible.
With that very eighth part, one should cause the piercing of the *nāga* to be performed;
that *nāga* becomes divine, resembling the deep red of vermilion (*sindūra*).
With that *nāga*, using an eighth part, one should cause the piercing of the copper (*śulva*) to be performed.

With that very sixteenth part, one should cause the piercing (*vedha*) of the silver; by that, the silver becomes gold—this is the doctrine of the *Siddhayogeśvarīmata*. [Regarding] the killing of lead: one *pala* of fragrant paste (*gandhapiṣṭi*) and eight *palas* of lead-paste.
One should smear the leaves of the *nāga* plant and then dry them in the shade.
Next, one should smear the *nāga* leaves with a paste of *āṭarūṣaka*. O Goddess, one should then apply three *puṭa* treatments using wild stones (*āraṇyopalaka*).

That divine *nāga* dies, resembling the crimson hue of vermilion. (RA 15.101) One *pala* of that *nāga*-ash and eight *palas* of copper powder should be ground for one *prahara* with the juice of *vāsaka*. (RA 15.102.1–2)
One should kill the copper in a *pātanāyantra*; it is killed in an instant.
With that very [substance] in a sixteenth part, one should perform the transmutation (*vedha*) of silver;
divine gold is produced, the most excellent ornament for the gods.
Whatever fragrant paste there may be, one should first kill the *nāga*;
having pierced the *nāga*, one should pierce the copper, and having pierced the copper, one should pierce the silver.
Divine gold is thus produced; this is declared to be the perfected yoga.
Sulphur combined with honey and rubbed with the seed-syllable of Hara (*haḥ*),
when buried in the earth for six months, becomes silver and gold.
An ointment made from that very same substance destroys the disease of leprosy.
Combined with clarified butter, it destroys diseases of the wounds;
by practicing this for one year, a man shall attain a lifespan of a thousand years.
[Method of Gradual Penetration: One *pala* of purified mercury (*mṛtarasa*) and one *pala* of *tālaka* (orpiment).
Then, having combined and thoroughly rubbed it with the juice of *unmattaka*, one should kill it using a *cakrayantra* machine; the mercury (*sūtaka*) is reduced to ashes.
When placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heated, it becomes an excellent *khoṭa*.
The mercury should successively transfix tin, silver, and copper.
(108.2) One *pala* of pure tin and one *pala* of mercury, along with two *palas* of *tālaka*, should be rubbed with the juice of *unmatta*. (109.1–2)
One should kill [the mercury] in a *pātanāyantra* by heating it, thereby bringing it to the state of a *khoṭa*.
Take one *pala* of *tālapiṣṭī* (ground *haritāla*) and one *pala* of *gandhaka* (sulfur), along with two *palas* of purified *sūta* (mercury). With these, for one day indeed— (RA_15.110.2)

Then, having combined and thoroughly ground [the ingredients] with the juice of *unmattaka*, one should kill [the mercury] in a *pātanāyantra* by means of heating, thereby bringing it to the state of a *khoṭa*.
[The composition of the] *piṣṭī* consists of lead (*nāga*), mercury (*sūta*), and realgar (*manaḥśilā*). One *pala* of pure lead and one *pala* of mercury— (112.1) [are to be used].
One should grind two *pala* of realgar (*kunaṭī*) with everything else together in one place.
One should kill [the mixture] in a *pātanāyantra* by means of heating and bring it to the state of a solid bolus (*khoṭa*).
[Regarding the preparation of] the *piṣṭī* of gold and sulfur: one *pala* of gold *piṣṭī* and one *pala* of sulfur. (113.1)
Then, having combined and thoroughly ground [the ingredients] with the juice of *dhuttūraka*,
one should kill [the mercury] in a *pātanāyantra* by means of heating, thereby bringing it to the state of a *khoṭa*.
[One should also employ] the essence of black *abhraka*, magnetite (*kānta*), steel (*tīkṣṇa*), and gold (*hāṭaka*).
Pure copper, silver, and *mākṣika* [pyrite] in equal parts, when heated in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), instantly become a *khoṭa*.
Regarding the further processing of this *khoṭa*: one *pala* of that *khoṭa* and one *pala* of mercury...
One should grind two *pala* of realgar and [the other ingredients] all together in one place.
One should kill it in a *pātanāyantra* by means of heating and thereby bring it to the state of a solid bolus (*khoṭa*).
Then, one *pala* of black mica (*abhraka*) and likewise one *pala* of mercury (*rasaka*).
O beloved, one *pala* of *sūtaka* (mercury), having been combined with everything else,
should be rubbed for two *praharas* with the juice of *unmattaka*.
Then it should be rubbed for one day together with *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax).
O Goddess, one should have a pill prepared and allow it to dry in the shade.
When heated and melted in a great fire, the mercury becomes a *khoṭa*.

To further process this *khoṭa*, one should purify it through the application of white glass (*śvetakāca*) and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*). This results in the *koṭivedhi-rasa* (mercury that pierces ten million [leaves]).
Having processed it together with gold and refined it through three cycles of *sāraṇā*,
one should cause the mercury to undergo *vedha* with that very [gold] in a thousandth part.
By this sequential application, the mercury becomes capable of *koṭivedha*.
Two seeds of *palāśa* and one *pala* of mercury,
having been ground together with the sour juice of *jambīra*, should be dried in the shade.
[Then take] *tumbī*, *meghanādā*, *kākajaṅghā*, and *cūlikā*.
One should place [the substance] into a crucible smeared with breast milk and blow it with charcoal from the *khadira* tree;
thus the *khoṭa* becomes inexhaustible.
Having ground *palāśa* oil with mercury until it becomes a mercurial paste, [one should proceed].
When blown in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), it instantly becomes a *khoṭa* [solidified mass].

(124.2) O Pārvatī, with mercury previously purified along with gold, one should perform piercing (*vedha*), as well as the solidification of the paste (*piṣṭīstambhana*). Having ground them together, one should form a ball (*golaka*) from that which has been liquefied. (RA_15.125.2)
The seeds of the *brahmavṛkṣa*, cotton seeds, and *vibhītaka*;
together with *yavaciñcā*, *vandhyā*, and black mustard—
having ground all these into a fine powder, one should smear a ball (*golaka*) with it.
O Goddess, by seven *puṭas* there shall be the solidification (*stambhana*) of the paste.

Then, having applied a large *puṭa*, one should process that [substance] within a crucible. That mercury (*sūta*), having been subjected to equal revolutions (*samāvarta*), should be joined with an equal amount of gold.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should pierce the moon and sun with a hundredth part [of the essence].
Again, by that very same yoga, one should effect the solidification of the *piṣṭī*.
Having then refined it with gold, one should pierce it a thousandfold.
In this manner, one should pierce a hundred thousand and ten million [times] through the sequential application;
having placed the *golaka* upon the mouth above the seven joints,
by means of a single year, one becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair.
One should grind together *cāṇḍālī*, *rākṣasī*, the mercury produced from *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, *bīja*, *sūta*, and *vaikrānta* for three *praharas*.
Having purified the *golaka*, one should place it in a *mūka-mūṣā* crucible and subject it to heating (*puṭa*).
But the *khoṭa* is produced, O Goddess, when it has been well-smelted by the fire of *khadira* wood.
(RA 15.132.2) The *khoṭa* [is prepared] from various substances with the juice of the flowers of the *cāṇḍālī* and *rākṣasī* plants, honey, clarified butter, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
(133.1) One should also employ a single *mahārasa* from among the eight, as well as mica (*abhra*). (RA 15.133.2)
One should grind together lead, tin, and mercury in equal parts, along with gold or silver,
or else mica and *drutisattva*, for two *praharas*. Then, having dried the resulting mass in the shade, one should place it as a ball inside a *mūkamūṣā* crucible and heat it.
Having given a small packet, O Goddess, it becomes an excellent *khoṭa*.
(RA 15.135.2) *Rambhā*, *vīrā*, the milk of *snuhī*, *kañcukī*, *yavaciñcikā*, *vārāhī*, *gorambhā*, *mīnākṣī*, and *kākamācikā*. (RA 15.136.2)
For the mercury processed with these, rebirth no longer exists.
Through the sequential application as before, the pill (*khoṭa*) becomes beautiful.
Viṣṇukrāntā, Cakrāṅkā, Balā, and likewise Tulasī—(138.1)
O beautiful one, with mahāsomā, ahivallī, and sūryāvarta, the mercury, when rubbed with these, shall attain the state of a *khoṭa* as before.
By means of that, O beautiful one, it swallows the morsel with its mouth; that is *jāraṇā*.
O woman of excellent complexion, [the mercury] should be rubbed with garlic, black mustard, and roots;
it should be cooked in a pouch made of divine herbs—this is the characteristic of *rasakhoṭa*.
This secret has been told to you; it is to be understood by those who practice alchemy (*rasavādin*).
By my grace, O Goddess of gods, he shall attain success without a doubt.
[Take] the milky sap of *snuhī* mixed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), the seeds of gold (*kanaka*),
*kañcukī*, *lāṅgalī*, *indravāruṇī*, and *viṣamuṣṭikā*.
One should grind mercury with water from the roots of the *palāśa* tree.
A wise man should form a paste (*piṣṭikā*) using equal parts of gold and mercury.
For the sake of forming the paste, one should grind the great minerals (*mahārasa*) with the juices of medicinal herbs.
Having rubbed it for three *yāmas*, the wise one should form it into a ball (*golaka*).
Having bound it with a paste (*piṣṭikā*), he should cook it in scented oil.
He should place the ball inside a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and cause it to dry in the shade.
Then, having placed it in a small crucible, one should heat it in a fire of *khadira* wood.
A *khoṭa* (solidified mass) is produced in the gold; one should then refine it together with the gold.
When it is not diminished, it mingles with the gold, and a *samāvarta* (re-merging) occurs.
Merely by consuming the *sūta* (mercury), a man shall obtain a divine body.
The processed and colored mercury shall penetrate all metals.
One should rub the mercury with the juices of medicinal herbs after it has been consumed in equal proportions during the process of *vedha*.
Having rendered that [substance] into a pulverized paste, one should heat it according to the previous method.
A divine *khoṭa* is then produced; with a sixteenth part of it, one should perform the piercing (*vedhana*).
Bound by means of the *saṃkalikā* yoga, it pierces ten times more than before.
O beautiful goddess, one should grind together rasapiṣṭikā, mṛgadūrvā, candravallī, ripe ciñcā fruit, as well as kokilā, karavīra, the seed of unmattaka, and the fruit of kākāṇḍī. (148.1–3)
The wise one should cause an equal amount of mercury to be combined with gold and made into a paste (*piṣṭikā*). Alternatively, having purified the mercury together with an equal amount [of gold],
one should grind the great essence (*mahārasa*) with the juices of medicinal herbs for the purpose of making a paste.
Having rubbed it for three watches, one should then form it into a ball (*golaka*).
Then, having placed the ball inside a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), one should cause it to dry in the shade.
Then, having applied a light seal (*laghupuṭa*), when blown [with fire], O Dear One, it becomes a *khoṭa*.
The processing of the *sūtaka* (mercurial essence) with the juices of *mṛga*, *dūrvā*,
and *tamāla* is neutralized by the roots of the three [plants], *lāṅgalī*, and *rāmaṭha*.
A wise person should then cause a paste to be made by combining it with an equal amount of gold.
Then, one should cause the powder of *tāraka* to be processed with equal mercury (*sūta*).
By the sequence of procedures as before, a beautiful *khoṭa* is produced.
Placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) on the ground, one should subject it to heat by means of a fire of cow-dung (*kariṣāgni*).
Then, a powder-binding (*cūrṇabandha*) may last for one day and night or for three nights;

that powder-binding effects a transmutation (*vedha*) ten times greater [than the previous]. (156.1–2) A mercury-pellet (*rasakhoṭa*) consisting of *śūlinī* juice, mercury, and combined with antimony (*srotoñjana*), [is likewise effective]. (157.1)

As before, through the application of the paste, an excellent *khoṭa* is produced. (157.2) One should blow upon the mercury—which consists of *srotoñjana*, *satagara*, and the three pastes—when it has been cast into the fire; thus the *sūtaka* performs all operations. (158.1–2)
One should pierce gold-colored mica, star-like mica, copper-colored mica, and black mica (abhratīkṣṇaka),
as well as tin-colored mica and lead-colored mica, using an equal amount of mercury (sūta).
This should be rubbed with whatever medicinal herbs are available and combined with a great mineral essence (mahārasa).
With gold, silver, tin, iron, copper, and lead—
using these either individually or all together— one should prepare a paste in equal proportions and,
according to the previously described method, reduce it to a state of death within a *garbhayantra* using a fire of chaff.

Having given equal portions of *sūtaka* again and again, repeatedly, various types of *khoṭas* arise; this is the great essence (*mahārasa*) bound by the *kānta*. Through the application of the *saṃkalikā-yoga*, the piercing (*vedha*) becomes ten times greater.

Khoṭa, poṭa, as well as bhasma, dhūli, and kalka as the fifth—these, when combined with nigala and gola, result in the attainment of all types of bonds. (164.1–2) For the nigala bond: lye derived from *śigru* and *sarja*, *brahmabīja*, and *guggulu*. (165.1)
Having added double the amount of rock salt (*saindhava*) and having ground it thoroughly, O beautiful one, the wise practitioner should enclose the paste within a dough-wrapping. Then,
having fashioned a very firm and auspicious crucible (*mūṣā*) the size of a *bilva* fruit, [he should place the mixture inside].
Having placed salt above and below, one should pour the mercury into the middle of the crucible.
A coating for the crucible should be applied using the powder of burnt conch-shell and other such materials.
Then, its mouth should be firmly sealed once again with salt-clay.
One should apply a coating of lime and have it dried in the shade.
This method of binding with shackles has been described; it is not taught even for one's own son.
One should, however, apply mild fomentation on the ground using a fire of a handful of husks.
Having carefully applied a crucible for the duration of a day and night,
O Great Goddess, the crucible thus brings the mercury to the state of a solid bolus (*khoṭa*).
When well-heated with charcoal from the *khadira* tree, the lord of mercury attains the state of a solid bolus.
Having added *sauvīra*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and glass, one should purify the *khoṭa*;
when it does not diminish, it merges into gold, and a *samāvarta* is produced.
One should cause that [mercury] to consume equal portions together with purified mercury.
One should heat the lord of essences (*rasendra*) according to the previous method and bring it to the state of a solid bolus (*khoṭa*).
Through the application of *saṃkalikā*, the piercing (*vedha*) shall be ten times greater.
[Take] the exudate of *palāśa* seeds, *kokila*, *unmatta*, and *vāruṇī*.
One should grind [the substance] together with the juice of *śūlinī* and combined with *saindhava* salt.
Having made a wrapping for the paste, one should bind it with a *nigala*.
O Goddess, according to the command of Śiva, the *mūṣā* crucible is smeared with the *nigala*.
For the transformation of the *rasa*, one should remain with a great fire.
(RA_15.177.2) With a leaf of *nigala* and *abhraka*, with *vajra*, *arkakṣīra*, and *sindhu*, with *tāpya*, iron dross (*lohakiṭṭa*), and with sand and clay; (RA_15.178.2)
But when bound by these fetters, the great mercury from Pāradī does not overstep its bounds, just as the great ocean does not overstep the shoreline.
Among the various types of fetters, *tailā*, *arkakṣīrā*, *vārāhī*, and *lāṅgalī* are the supreme fetters.
Crows' droppings, *brahmabīja*, *lāṅgalī*, and *nigala* are excellent;
*vākucī*, *brahmabīja*, and the bones of a crab, O beautiful one; as well as sea salt and rock salt—these are the supreme *nigala*.
One should grind the milk produced from *snuhī* and *arka*, the seeds of *brahma*, *kokilā*, and the seeds of *karakā*, with an eighth part of iron (*loha*).
Another binding (*nigala*) consists of the roots of *gojihvā*; another is [made from] female blood (*strīrajas*).
Vākucī, seeds of the Brahma-tree, the milks of *snuhi* and *arka*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *jvālinī*, and crow-dung are praised as the best for breaking open locks.
Salt, borax, alkali, realgar, orpiment, and sulfur [are also used].

Likewise, one should grind equal parts of *amlavetasa*, *tāpya*, and *hiṅgula* together with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*; this is the supreme fetter (*nigala*). One should then wrap the paste with one of these very fetters.
Having first prepared a *khoṭa* as before within an iron crucible, one should then perform the transmutation (*vedha*).
(185.2) I shall now describe the second method, the "Ball" (*golaka*), which is the supreme stabilization of the paste (*piṣṭikā-stambha*).
(186) [The ingredients are: the urine of a two-footed animal, rock salt (*saindhava*), mica (*abhra*), and *guggulu*. (RA_15.187.1)

Having wrapped the paste in clay, one should again apply it eight times; then, on the ground, one should apply mild heat using a fire of chaff for one day and night or three nights, and as before, bring it to the state of a *khoṭa*.
Vākucī, seeds of Brahma, clear sky-stone (*gagana*), and *maṇi*;
sauvarcala, *saindhava*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and likewise *guggulu*;
and urine with the dust of *dvipadī*—one should grind these together until they are very fine.
Having enveloped the paste with a dough-mass as before, one should bring it to the state of a pill (*khoṭa*).
(190.2) The seed of poison (*viṣabīja*), the seed of *brahma* (*brahmabīja*), and the seeds of gold; (191.1) the roots of *yavaciñcā*, *lāṅgalī*, and *indravāruṇī*. (RA_15.191.2)
The latex of *kokilā*, *arka*, and *snuhī*, along with rock salt (*saindhava*), mica (*abhraka*), and *guggulu*—
having enveloped a paste made from these ingredients as before, one should bring it to the state of a solid bolus (*khoṭa*).
*Lāṅgalī*, seeds of the *brahma* plant, crow dung, and *guggulu*.
The roots of śvetāśvamāra and the root of kanakavāruṇī—
[with these] a wise person should grind [the substance] together with oil and rock salt.
Having enveloped the paste in a dough-mass (*piṣṭī*), one should bring it to the state of a pill (*khoṭa*) as previously described.
Vākucī, seeds of Brahma, the two types of cumin, guggulu, rock salt, mica, crab-shell, borax, and the juice of jvālinī—
having wrapped the paste in a cloth and then again with clay eight times over; (195.1–196.1)

One should apply gentle heat to the mercury on the ground using a fire of husks and grain-chaff for one day and night or for three nights; thus the king of essences (*rasendra*) is brought to the state of a solid bolus (*khoṭa*). Through the application of ten *saṃkalikās*, the great essence becomes capable of "piercing by sound" (*śabdavedhin*).
Taking two parts of *śaṅkara* and three parts of mercury,
one should form a paste with that in a heated mortar using *kāñjika*.
Having prepared a *khoṭa* (pill) provided with a seal as before, one should then perform the transmutation (*vedha*).

Through the application of ten layers, the great mercury becomes a piercer of sound (*śabdavedhī*). (RA 15.199.2) The preparation of *bubhukṣitarasa*: the king of mercury (*sūtakarājendra*) bound with *śilā*, sulphur, and *mākṣika*, combined with the powder of *kāntapāṣāṇa* and *bhūlatā*. (RA 15.200.1–2)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, this mercury, when blown upon and placed within the crucible,
consumes other mercuries, minor metallic ores, metals, gems, and jewels— just as the submarine fire (vaḍavānala) devours everything within the womb of the manifest crucible.
Honey, cinnabar, sulphur, realgar, lapis lazuli,
coral, kaṅkuṣṭha,
and blue vitriol— these should be processed with yellow and red groups of substances mixed with kaṅguṇī oil.
One should place the solidified mass, cooked in a pot, quickly into a nalika tube. Having placed sand in the pot, one should heat it for even three nights.
That [substance], having been steamed with sour gruel (*āranāla*) and suspended in a swing (*dolā*), [is prepared].
Thus gratified, the charioteer becomes a provider of both body and wealth.
This supreme *udghāṭa* is declared to be beneficial for all ritual actions;
it is the highest [remedy], and one who has received it does not become a *chattrī*, a *pataṅgī*, a *durdrāvī*, or a *durmelī*.
O lady of excellent complexion, she effects a change in color and causes [the metal] to burst open.
Having thus quickly effected the binding, she performs the digestion by vajra (*vajrajāraṇa*).
Tell me that, O Goddess of Gods; what else do you wish to hear?
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Lord, how is the liquefaction of the bound king of essences (*rasarāja*) achieved?
"And furthermore, O Lord, command how the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of *vajra* and the other substances is performed.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"One should dissolve that *khoṭa* of mercury and reduce it to a fine powder, then saturate it with the menses of a woman."
One should grind together punarnavā, mīnākṣī, rambhākanda, the menstrual blood of a woman, maṇimantha, and śilādhātu. This paste should be spread over [the mercury] and combined with āroṭa-rasa.
Then, having bound that mercury into a pouch made of birch bark,
one should subject it to sweating for three days in a *dolāyantra*, O Goddess of the Gods.
By this sequential application, the dead mercury becomes liquefied.

For the liquefaction and digestion of mercury: "Fresh ginger, radish, dry ginger, garlic, asafoetida, honey, (6.1) the three alkalis, the five salts, potassium carbonate, iron sulfate, and sulfur—combined with the group of acidic substances, O Dear One, one should fashion a ball. (RA_16.6.2–3)
The medicinal paste situated in its center, however, melts through heating in a swing;
of this there is no doubt. Once melted, it quickly digests the mercury.
O Goddess, it causes the bound great-essence (mahārasa) to melt by means of the application of the "feet."
Then, having liquefied it, one should give [the ingredients] at the stage of the liquid state, and it should flow once more.
Having thus made the bound [substance] liquid in equal, double, triple, or greater proportions,
the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*) must be performed upon that liquid by those who know the ritual.

The mercury, having been processed with *sūtajāraṇa*, *kukkuṭīkanda*, *mārjārī*, *uccaṭā*, and *īśvarī*, and combined with *kṣīrakañcukā*, is then subjected to sweating (*svedita*). Once liquefied, it is processed for three days using *kukkuṭī* and other substances within a swinging apparatus (*dolā*) or similar device. (RA 16.10.2–16.11.1)
That mercury, having been liquefied by means of ginger and other such substances, should then undergo the process of sweating.

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, just as one should digest liquefied mercury with a *vajra* [diamond], so too should one know the Lord, the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, to be its master. (11.2; RA_16.12.1–2)
Having prepared a *khoṭa* from whatever mercury has been raised from the dead,
one should burnish the gold sixfold and perform three *sāraṇā* purifications.
Then, with that very [mercury] at a part of one ten-millionth (*koṭyaṃśa*), one should effect the transmutation (*vedha*) of copper.

Divine gold is produced, serving as an ornament for the jewelry of the gods. Furthermore, one should digest diamonds and gems within that mercury; it is digested in an instant by means of a forced fire inside an open crucible.
The liquefaction of gems [is achieved] by *uccaṭā*, *mīnanayanā*, *sarpākṣī*, and *raktacitraka*;
by these, blue sapphire, ruby, and pearl quickly melt.
The digestion of mercury (*sūta*) [is achieved] by *viṣṇukrāntā*, *cakrāṅkā*, *kumārī*, and *yavaciñcikā*.
Having added the liquid of medicinal herbs—diamonds, rubies, rājāvarta, and *sasyaka*—one should pour it into the heated mercury.
Afterwards, the gems should be added; they melt just like water.
O Goddess, one should cause it to sweat in a swing and digest it by means of a *viḍa* mixture;
furthermore, within the interior of an open crucible, one should cause it to digest in an instant through a fierce fire.
For the digestion of the *khoṭa*, it should be subjected to a hundred-fold application of a *puṭa* using conch-shell and the milk of the *arka* plant.

One should impregnate that seed with alkali and with the group of sour substances. Sulfur combined with *viḍa* salt, asafoetida, *rājāvarta*, and coral, along with realgar, is beneficial for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of the pills (*khoṭa*).
The digestion (*jāraṇa*) of bound gold occurs through the application of crucible coatings (*mūṣālepa*) and other such combinations for the digestion of bound gold.
O Goddess, that digestion arises from the casting [of the substance] by means of the application of *viḍa*.
Subsequently, gold should be added along with a liquid possessing thirty-six parts.
From that, indeed, the circle of rays of the king of elixirs arises,
filled by a mass of splendor pervading horizontally, upwards, and downwards. In this way,
the elixir becomes pure, like a wish-fulfilling gem itself.
He is worshipped by the gods and the Siddhas like a second Śaṅkara;
he is the benefactor of the worlds and the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And he should digest the great blue gem according to the sequence of the number of principles.
When that mercury, moving through the sky, revolves clockwise, O Pārvatī, it pierces all metals in quantities measured by the bhāra.
Listen now to the description of the *kāpāli-rañjana* for mercury that has been thus digested; this is the *kāpāli-rañjana*.
One *pala* of copper leaf and half a *pala* of sulfur, one *karṣa* of borax,
and one *karṣa* of mercury-ink (*rasakajjalī*),
as well as one *karṣa* of *mākṣika*, should all be combined together in one place.
When placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and blown [with a bellows], it instantly becomes a *khoṭa*.
**Further Processing: Transformation into Gold (*kāpālikayoga*):** One should grind that *khoṭa* into a fine powder and rub it with sour chickpea juice (*caṇakāmla*).
One should then apply fourteen *puṭa* (roastings) using only forest cow-dung.
It arises resembling an *indragopaka* insect; there is no doubt about this.
That powder, when combined with honey, will dye pure silver. By dyeing it three times, beautiful gold is produced.
