This Kāpālika yoga shall color all metals; it shall color bound mercury and shall also color the diamond-binding (*vajrabandha*). Regarding the methods of coloring: one *pala* of *ārā*-powder or one *pala* of dead lead.
Either one pala of tin and mica-foils, or one pala of the powder of *tīkṣṇa* (steel);
or three parts of copper with one part each of lead and tin;
or three parts of copper with one part of red ochre; or else, *tīkṣṇa* and honey [in equal parts].

Alternatively, there are two parts of *tīkṣṇa*, three of *ghoṣa*, nine of *nāga*, nine parts of copper (*tāmra*), and four parts of *āra*. Or else, O Goddess of the gods, there may be two *pala* of *mākṣika*.
One part of peacock-neck [mineral] and tuttha, and likewise one pala of dead naga;
or else, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one part each of vanga and naga;
two parts of tikshna, three of copper, and four of gold and tāpya.

Alternatively, O Goddess, one may use pure vaikrānta, vaṅga, nāga, rītikā, along with śulva, or else gold, pure [mercury], and bhujaṃgama; any one of these, O Goddess, provided it is prepared according to the previous ritual procedure.
When placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and blown with a bellows, it becomes a *khoṭa* instantly.
One should perform the *puṭa* according to the previous method and dye it according to the previous method.
Likewise, lead, copper, and steel [are treated] by the supreme *kāpālika* process.
With that very [substance], one should repeatedly color silver seven times over.
With that very [substance], one should repeatedly color gold seven times over.
This is the best ripened seed; one should employ it in all ritual actions.
Silver is colored by *tārarañjana*, *vaṅga*, *tīkṣṇa*, *kapālī*, and copper; it shall color all metals until they resemble saffron. Pure silver is colored by *vaikrānta*, *nāga*, and *kāpālī*.
One should dye it with gold, and it will become like saffron.
When the gold-dyeing process is infused with red oil, it destroys the transference of iron.
One should dye pure silver with the powder of brass and earthenware shards.
And with the *vimala* nāga, the supreme sovereign Kāpālī shall color all metals, especially silver and gold;
by coloring them three times, beautiful gold is produced.
One should dye the gold with that very [substance] seven times over and over again. When the gold-dyeing [mixture] is sprinkled with salt water, it destroys the transference of base metals.
Likewise, tin, lead, magnetite, copper, iron, and pyrite [are treated in this way].
Ravināgakapālī shall dye pure silver;
it should dye it three times, whereby the *tārāriṣṭa* is produced.
With that very [substance], O Pārvatī, one should dye gold seven times.
When drenched with the group of red substances, it destroys the transmutation of iron;
likewise, tin, lead, and copper, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, [are treated] with jaggery, blue glass, *tuttha*, sour gruel, and salt. (52.1–53.1)
One should destroy [the defects] occurring at the time of transference by grinding together poison, bile, and sour substances.
(RA 16.53.2) One should grind red ochre, sulfur, and mercury with sesame oil; having applied this to silver leaves, one should place them inside a crucible of copper. (RA 16.54.2)
Above and below, within a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), the golden leaf shall become bright.
(RA 16.55) One part of yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), one part of red ochre (*gairika*), one part of the paste of *mākṣika* [honey-ore], and four parts of the globule (*golaka*). (RA 16.56.1–2)
Gold placed in a blind crucible and blown with the bellows is colored in an instant.
By this sequential method, one should color it four times.
This is the excellent "ripened seed," possessing a luster like that of the rising sun.
By that, an excellence of two colors arises by means of a sixteenth part.
And when poured into red oil, it destroys the transference of iron.
As for *rasaka*, however, *kāpālī* [is used] with mercury and copper in a hundredth part.
When heated in an *andhamūṣā* crucible, it becomes beautiful gold.

(RA 16.59.3) Regarding the preparation of the *khoṭa*: one *pala* of pure lead (*nāga*) and one *karṣa* of melted mercury (*sūtaka*) should be refined in a *sāraṇāyantra* [refining apparatus]; thus the mercury becomes a *khoṭa*. (RA 16.60.2)
One *pala* of *khoṭa* and likewise one *pala* of honey,
having combined and thoroughly ground them with the juice of gold,
one should cook it in an earthen vessel; it will become like the color of saffron.

One should first prepare a *khoṭa* combined with the previous paste; this powder, through the *kāpālika* yoga, should be rubbed with acid. One should then perform the *puṭa* according to the previous method and dye it according to the previous method.
Having bound mercury with any [substance] by means of gold, sulphur, realgar, and mercury,
and having wrapped it in sequence and heated it one hundred times, it will pierce [the metal]. First, however, [one should treat] the bound mercury, tin, silver, and realgar.
One should wrap it in sequence and heat it; it will undoubtedly achieve a hundredfold penetration (*śatavedhī*).
By means of this, one makes silver (*tāra*) into gold with gold.
Mortar that has been killed [by processing] destroys tin (*vaṅga*) with an equal amount, and by that same [mortar], one should destroy twice as much silver.
Silver turns into sixty-four suns [of gold], and likewise gold through the application of mercury and gold.

(67.2) One *pala* of processed mercury (*mṛtarasa*) mixed with five *nāgas* and combined with one *pala* of gold should be blown in the furnace until only the mercury remains. (68.1) If this process is repeated exactly one hundred times in this same sequence, the king of elixirs (*rasarāja*) gradually becomes capable of piercing ten million (*koṭivedhin*). (68.2)
One *pala* of dead lead (*mṛtasūta*), two *palas* of vermilion (*darada*),
four *palas* of sulfur (*gandhaka*), three *palas* of *kaṅkuṣṭha*,
and five *palas* of realgar (*śilā*) should be ground together with cow bile.
One should smear the palāśa leaves with that paste;
by means of the *puṭa* application, one should kill [the mercury], and this nāga dies in an instant.
Afterwards, one should prepare pills numbering three hundred and sixty.
Then one should rub each individual pill with cow-bile.
By this sequential process, one should administer a hundred *puṭas*;
thus, O Goddess, this mercury (*nāga*) arises resembling the crimson red of vermilion.
With that very same hundredth part, O Goddess, one should cause the piercing (*vedha*) of silver to be performed;
that silver becomes the supreme ornament for the gods.
One *pala* of dead lead and an equal amount of gold-leaf—
One should kill it by means of the *puṭa* process; gold dies at that very moment.
That ash, combined with an equal part of lead, should be applied to a leaf of gold of the same weight;
one should kill it by means of the *puṭa* process; gold dies at that very moment.
By this sequential method, one should perform [the process] three times;
by that very thousandth part, one should cause the piercing (*vedha*) of the *tāra* [silver].
Through this easily accomplished practice, that *tāra* shall become gold.
O Goddess of the Gods, I shall now describe *kalkavedha*, which is easy to accomplish.
Palāśa, nimba, bilva, akṣa, kārpāsa, kaṭutumbinī, kaṅguṇī, and mustard oil— each one of these is a destroyer of mercury.
Equal amounts of mercury, silver, or even copper should be combined with the metal.
Among the eight great minerals (*mahārasa*), there are likewise four secondary minerals (*uparasa*).
One should grind them in a mortar with sour fruits and *kāñjika* vinegar over a medium charcoal fire.
Alternatively, on a red-hot iron plate with a soft fire using an iron hammer,
the wise practitioner, having added oil to the previously mentioned sand-yantra,
should grind it diligently day and night for one fortnight.
That paste becomes supreme, bestowing virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation;
it pierces even the eight metals, which are difficult even for the gods to master.
There is no doubt that with a single *pala* of it, one destroys all diseases.
One should consume it combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*) and the three fruits (*triphalā*), along with honey and clarified butter.
O Goddess of the Gods, one *guñjā* bound with gold, two with silver,
or three *guñjās* with copper, taken for a year, will make one free from old age and immortal.
Those with moon-like faces, adorned with all ornaments, attend upon him.

Having administered the seeds of *triphalā* with honey and clarified butter as a nasal drop (*nasya*) during the nights, one should consume the elixir in the morning; thus, no indigestion shall ever arise.
The wise one should consume sulphur as a drink, as an ointment, or as *kaṅkuṣṭha*. One should consume one *pala* of mercury, which is honored by gods and demons;
it takes on the appearance of molten gold and possesses a radiance like that of the rising sun.
One should pierce all metals; there is no doubt regarding cutting or burning.
When bound with the bonds of the *saṃkalā*, the pill becomes a *khecarī*.
[The plants are] *mahālatā*, *kākajaṅghā*, *bṛhatī*, *śarapuṅkhā*, and *ajaśṛṅgikā*.
Śivā, Śakralatā, and Kanyā—these seven are indeed the great creepers (*mahālatā*).
This most secret of secrets has been declared, combined with the affection of Vātāri.
O beloved, [this] mercury (*sūta*) is equal when applied to equal amounts of gold, silver, or copper.
One should add one part of each of the eight great minerals (mahārasa) as well as the secondary minerals (tūparasa);
then one should grind them on a stone mortar until they become insentient (niścetana).
One should then steam them with fermented rice-gruel (āranāla) and grind them again as was done for the previous paste.

And one should employ that [substance] for various tasks upon the body of iron. (RA_16.92.2) One part each of gold-mercury (*hemābhraka*) and two parts of *sūtaka* (mercury); likewise, one part each of silver-mercury (*tārābhraka*) and two parts of *sūtaka*. (RA_16.93.2)
One should prepare a paste with that and bind it with the fetter;
in the crucibles, there is binding with the paste, the ball, and the fetter.
O Goddess of the Gods, I shall further explain another method for the binding of the powder.
Having added flour and borax, it should be thoroughly rubbed with the juice of *dvipadī*.
Once it has become a fine paste (*naṣṭapiṣṭa*) and dried, one should heat it and cook it in a *puṭa* vessel.
O Goddess of the Lord of Gods, one should enclose it within a ball and secure it with a chain.

One should apply gentle heat to the powder on the ground using a fire of chaff and grain-husks for one day and night or three nights; thus the powder becomes excellent. Due to the absence of the state of being bound in a *saṃkalikā*, the solvent (*vedhaka*) becomes twofold.
Furthermore, I shall describe another method for binding the silk ribbon that is very difficult to obtain:
(99) green vitriol, borax, alkali, rock salt, sulfur, mica, (100.1) and mercury, ground together with citron juice for the duration of one *yāma*. (RA_16.100.2)
Having prepared a pill (*golaka*) from tin, silver, mercury, *rasaka*, and the milk of the *snuk* plant,
one should wrap it in birch bark and enclose it with a cloth thread.
Then, having placed cow dung above and below it, one should heat it in the middle of the earth.
One should perform rubbing and sweating in this very manner three times.
According to local custom, one should apply a paste and rub with molasses and sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
Then, one should place [the substance] inside a crucible smeared with the juice of *dhattūra*.
O Goddess, having sealed the mouth of the crucible, one should apply a sealing compound (*saṃdhilepa*).
One should place the crucible inside salt and the large outer crucible outside it.
Then, having bound the mouth of that crucible with salt-clay (*loṇamṛd*), [one proceeds].

One should apply mild heat to the ground using a fire fueled by husks and grain-chaff for one day and night or for three nights; such are their various properties. One should perform this procedure in this very manner seven times.

Those who are bound both within and without become pure in Dharma. (RA 16.107) Mercury struck by sulphur, along with potassium carbonate, green vitriol, rock salt, *snuhī*, *arka*, borax, and *guñjā*, ground together with the milk of the sun-plant (*ravikṣīra*), [is used for purification]. (RA 16.108.1–2)
They quickly become ancient [mantras], bestowing virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation.
One should cause the five parts of copper and two parts of lead to be fashioned into the form of petals, and should coat them according to the previous procedure.
For in this way the lord of mercury is indeed colored; thus the processes of *sāraṇā* and so forth must be performed.
Tell me that, O Goddess of the Gods; what else do you wish to hear? (16.110.1–2) 17
The Goddess said:
"I have heard about the liquefying and the coloring of mercury;
you should now explain, in due order, its solidification and its transmutative power."
Śrī Bhairava said:

(2.1) Having fashioned a crucible (*mūṣā*) shaped like a cow’s teat and resembling the flower of the *dhattūra*, one should fill it with oil to half its capacity and cast in the colored mercury. (2.2–3)
One should cause [the substance] to be treated externally with fire from chaff and grain within a crucible;
having combined it with one-twentieth part of lead, one should cast it as a *samāvarta* bolus.
By means of long tongs alone, one should drop it [into the crucible], and it will become *sārita*.
From that, by means of double the amount of gold, *pratisārita* is produced;
then, by means of triple the amount of gold, *anusārita* is produced.
One should digest [the mercury] again and again using the *viḍa*-mixture as before.
By this method, O Goddess, one becomes a twofold piercer (*vedhaka*).
Mercury, *bhūlatā*, blood, mica, poison, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and mercury— [these],
along with *tāpya* [calamine] ground together with breast milk, constitute a transmuting agent (*krāmaṇa*) for both casting and smearing.
Indragopa, poison, *kānta*, cinnabar, and blood, as well as *rasaka* and sesame oil, are used for the process of *krāmaṇa* in both casting and smearing.
(7.1) For *krāmaṇa*, there are *bhūlatā*, honey, mica, borax, blood, and poison. (8.1)
Crow dung, breast milk, the wax from the ears of a buffalo,
asafoetida, and *rāmaṭha*, O Maheśānī, are used for the purpose of transference (*krāmaṇa*) in casting and anointing.
For transference, there are *bhūlatā*, *lāṅgalī*, *śṛṅgī*, crow dung, and *śailaja*.

Viṣṇukrāntā, beeswax, blood, and the dust of dvipadī; (RA_17.9.2) surasā, brahmasomā, gṛdhrakarṇī, and lakṣaṇā—these, along with the ear-secretion of a buffalo, serve for the purpose of causing [the victim] to step forward, whether by casting or by smearing. (RA_17.10.1–2)

The supreme transmuter of mercury (*rasasaṃkrāmaṇa*) consists of *gaṇḍola* poison, the saliva from the mouth of a frog, and the impurity from the eyes of a buffalo, combined with blood. (11.1) The mercury-transmuting poison (*rasakrāmaṇa-viṣa*) consists of cochineal insects (*surendragopa*), yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and bdellium (*guggulu*). (12.1)
When combined with these, along with women’s breast milk, the mercury penetrates the metal.

(12.2) Through the penetration of mercury by means of sandalwood, the resin of the *nimba* tree, women’s breast milk, poison, and borax, when joined with cow’s ghee, the mercury penetrates the metal. (RA 17.13.1–2)
Upon the destruction of the group of enemies, tin and lead are the two supreme transmuters (krāmaṇa).
(14) Mother’s milk, crab, and the impurity produced within a conch shell, as well as the exudation of the wood-apple (kapittha), are the supreme transmuters of mercury. (RA_17.15.1–2)
One should administer the *krāmaṇa* of the king of essences (*rasarāja*) at the time of transmutation (*vedha*).
For one who does not know the *krāmaṇa*, his labor is fruitless.
Hereafter, I shall explain the gold and silver foils. (17)
Lead and mercury, rubbed together and combined with the twelve fragrant substances, (18.1) should be rubbed in the juice of *dhattūra* to form a pill the size of a chickpea.
(RA_17.18.2) Four parts of silver (*tāra*) and likewise three parts of copper (*śulva*). (RA_17.19.1)
Having properly rotated it, O Goddess of Gods, one should cast a single pill [into the crucible].
By this sequential yoga, one should process the copper in silver until the silver becomes red; of this there is no doubt.
Two parts of this [mercury] should be taken, along with five parts of *tāra* (silver).
When combined with one part of gold and melted, it becomes eight parts of gold.
Copper struck by sulfur and joined with *darada* (cinnabar) [is likewise transformed]. (21.1–22.1)
One should grind ginger, radish, dry ginger, garlic, asafoetida,
and honey with citron juice and smear it upon the leaves of *nāga* (leadwort). By means of a *puṭa* (sealed crucible), the lead is killed, becoming as red as vermilion.
When that gold is processed three times with *tārā* (silver), it becomes seedless (*nirbīja*) gold.

With mercury, sulfur, realgar, orpiment, iron, copper, and *sūtaka*, (25.1) increasing the parts in sequence and mixed with honey and clarified butter, one should apply [the paste] in a fifth part. (25.2)
Through *puṭanā* and *śuṣkapuṭanā*, the two-fold blackness of the *tāra* [silver] is removed.
(RA 17.26) Smeared with a paste of yellow sulphur and *pālāśa* resin, by the application of three *puṭas*, silver becomes gold. (RA 17.27.2)

Silver: *rañjana* (coloring). To remove whiteness, one should take a well-ground powder of yellow, black, and red minerals as they are available, (28.1) saturate it with cow’s ghee, and apply it by sprinkling onto the silver; this destroys the white color.
(RA_17.28.2) Furthermore, a mixture of red, yellow, and black minerals with abundant goat’s milk... (29.1)
One should keep it in *tāra* for seven days; this increases passion from the moment of infusion (*niṣeka*).
When, through sowing and infusion, it has the luster of a cat's eye, that *tāra* is called "petal" (*dala*) and is considered the supreme union.
One should color copper with mercury so that it becomes black like bell-metal. Then, one should mix two parts of that copper with one part of silver;
this is considered the supreme method for the union with that lord of mercury.
O Goddess of the Suras, one should pierce [the mercury] with pure mercury in the proportion of one hundredth part.

(RA_17.32.2) One should grind gold, honey-iron (mākṣika), and salt with honey and clarified butter until it takes on the luster of saffron; then one should cook it in a *nāgapuṭa* [furnace]. (RA_17.33.2)
Then an equal amount of copper should be added;
that copper, having been applied to a silver leaf, should be purified three times, whereby it becomes a pure gold leaf.
Tin, lead, likewise iron, copper, and silver—these five [are to be used].
Having applied [the reagents] three times, it should be purified; thus the gold-leaf becomes pure.
(35.2) Having smeared tin with realgar, sulphur, honey, borax, and poison, combined with *mātuluṅga*, one should cook it in a sealed crucible (*puṭa*). (RA_17.36.2)
Having smeared with cinnabar, sulphur, honey-gem (mākṣika), rock salt, and poison, along with citron juice, one should heat the sharp iron in a closed crucible (puṭa).
(37.1–2) Realgar, sulphur, honey-gem, rock salt, and poison... (38.1)
Having smeared *nāgaloha* with *mātuluṅga*, one should cook it in a sealed crucible (*puṭa*).
All of this should be applied to a gold leaf; one should pierce the gold with [the resulting] bound [alloy].
When the parts of gold and *karin* are equal, the *tīkṣṇa* [iron] should indeed be double that amount.
When it is smelted with red minerals and sprinkled [with mercury], that silver becomes gold.
(40.2) Having treated copper with *tāpya* (calamine), one should color it with excellent lead (*nāga*).
One should process that lead into the silver until it becomes a leaf of gold. (RA_17.41.2)
Take mercury equal in weight to poison (*viṣa*) and sulphur (*gandha*), combined with three times that amount of collyrium (*añjana*).
Having ground these for three days with an acidic liquid (*amla*), one should mix equal parts of silver (*tārā*) and copper (*arka*).
After cooking it with the five earths (*pañcamṛd*), one should fire it in a sealed crucible (*puṭa*) until only the silver remains.
In this manner, one should dye the excellent *tāra* three times.
[One should take] four separate portions of *bhujaṅga* and copper (*śulva*),
twelve separate portions each of oil, and of both *rītika* and *tāra*.

O Goddess, a single part of gold, with the remainder consisting of silver, should be a superior golden leaf, shining like the eye of a cat. Eight parts of silver, four parts of copper, two parts of lead, and one part of gold [should be used].
Then, everything sprinkled with the red powder becomes gold, leaving only the dross behind.
One should prepare equal parts of rājāvarta, fourthly darada, and coral, combined with gold and honey. (RA_17.47.2)

One should grind three parts of *rasaka* with the milk of a female sheep (*meṣī*). Then, one should form it into pills and dry them in the shade. Subsequently, combined with the five fluxing agents (*drāvaka*), one should grind it on a stone slab.
One should combine the *tārāriṣṭa* with this prepared paste (*kalka*):
in the first [preparation], with an equal amount of paste; in the second, with half that amount;
and in the third, with a quarter part—thus the *tārāriṣṭa* is produced.
When it undergoes heating, scratching, and cutting upon the leaf, that gold becomes imperishable.

(RA_17.51) Taking mercury (*sūtaka*), cinnabar (*darada*), pyrite (*tāpya*), sulfur (*gandhaka*), and realgar (*kunaṭī*), one should apply them in successive increasing proportions to the leaves of copper. (RA_17.52.1–2)
Having ground it with the fresh juice of *cāṅgerī*, one should administer five *puṭa* applications.
One should then process that powder in silver; this shall become the extraction of gold (*hemākṛṣṭi*).
O Goddess, one should apply it to gold, and from that it shall become black in color.
Having ground turmeric with cow urine and melted copper, one should sprinkle it;
by purifying it in this manner a hundred times, it becomes gold-like in luster.
Alternatively, O beloved, [one may use] copper extracted from bell-metal or *āroṭa*.
Then the wise one, having purified it with a sixfold amount of *nāga*,
should dissolve half a hundred [parts] of *sindhuvāra* into its juice;
thereafter, he should cause it to be administered seven times in the juice of *kuṣmāṇḍa*.
Likewise, one should cause [the metal] to be repeatedly heated and quenched in buttermilk mixed with *niśā* (turmeric).
When it has become as bright as a parrot's beak or a *kiṃśuka* flower, and is red when cut and soft,
then that entire copper (*śulva*) should be smeared with *tāpya* (calamine) until it acquires a blackish tint (*kālikā*).
O beautiful lady, one should grind cinnabar, the juice of *kiṃśuka*, red *citraka*, the two types of *haridrā*, and goat’s urine together.
One should then apply this as a sprinkling upon copper seven times; of this there is no doubt.
The *śulva* should be the color of vermilion, and the excellent *hemadala* should be of gold.
One should employ two parts each of *tīkṣṇa* and *bhujaga*, along with *ghoṣa* and *kṛṣṇa*.
Alternatively, according to the smith’s method, one may use one, two, or three *palas* in sequence.
Three *pañcaka*s of *nāga* and likewise one *pala* of copper,
when smelted, that which remains shall resemble refined gold (*tapanīya*).
[The herbs] *lāṅgalī*, *citraka*, *śigru*, *nirguṇḍī*, and *karavīraka*.

O Goddess, one should prepare a liquor combined with the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, tamarind, sour [substances], and *vajra-kanda*, along with the milk of a buffalo. One should smear copper plates with the milks of *snuhī* and *arka* and salts.
When the first-mentioned liquor has been prepared for one day,
one should repeatedly sprinkle it with liquor until it becomes red-hot like fire as before.
One should then cause it to be turned over many times using excellent shells (*varāṭaka*).
One should sow with *sarjikā*, *sindhu*, and *datta*, and employ them in ritual acts.
(RA_17.67) One *pala* of mercury (*rasaka*), combined with gold-ore (*hemamākṣika*), half a *pala* of rock salt (*saindhava*), and combined with the sour juice of *mātuluṅga*. (RA_17.68.1–2)

Thereafter, one should cause it to undergo digestion until it smells like saffron and resembles the indragopa insect; one should digest the paste through the application of a *puṭa* (sealed crucible).
That paste, combined with honey and mixed with sugar and *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax), [should be consumed].
Then, having combined and thoroughly rubbed them together, one should cook [the mixture] with cow’s milk.
First, one should dye purified copper with the juice and paste;
one should dye it three times, and beautiful gold is produced.

One should cultivate *munipuṣpa*, *karavīra*, and *manaḥśilā*. First, copper is dyed with that [mixture] and likewise combined with the mineral; when heated in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), it becomes beautiful gold.
One should prepare a paste of silver using that very same juice and paste; by sprinkling it with *kaṅguṇī* oil, that [silver] shall become divine gold.
[The plants are: *arjunī*, *lāṅgalī*, *padmacāriṇī*, and *śakravāruṇī*.
O Pārvatī, when a copper leaf is smeared with medicinal herbs, gold-ore, and red chalk, and then subjected to the *niṣeka* process, it becomes gold. Likewise,
[the same occurs with] *mayūragrīva*, blue vitriol (*tuttha*), saffron, and *rasaka*.
One should take the dung of a young calf and the Hālāhala poison,
as well as the powder of red *citraka*, and have them made in equal parts.
One should grind them with sour gruel and then dry them in the shade.
Having mixed it with honey, one should smear the *nāgapattras* [leaves].
When heated in a sealed crucible (*mūkamūṣā*), the lead (*nāga*) is colored in an instant.
One should sprinkle it seven times with the juice of *śāka* leaves alone.

Or, by immersing it twenty-eight times in oil derived from *bhūnāga*, that *nāga* becomes divine, serving as an ornament for the gods. Alternatively, one may take equal parts of powdered *bhūlatā* and powdered *nāga*.
One should heat it in an *andhamūṣā* crucible and pour it into hot oil;
when this is done seven times, it becomes sixteen-fold pure (*ṣoḍaśavarṇaka*).
Then, [one should add] the dung of a young calf, lac, red ochre, and sandalwood.
Realgar known as haṃsapāda, the pulp of the bilva fruit, and jaggery,
along with rājāvarta and kaṅkuṣṭha, [should be used] with the water of young śāka leaves; by sprinkling it one hundred times, one can turn a serpent into gold.
Mañjiṣṭhā, the two types of rajanī, kāṅkṣī, gold, mākṣika,
kausumbha, poison, sindhūttha, darada, and red sandalwood,
combined with the leaves of śāka, pālāśa shoots, and flowers. (RA_17.84.1)
By sprinkling it one hundred times, O beloved, one pleases the Nāga. One should likewise saturate kaṅkuṣṭha, sulphur, and the two types of turmeric seven times with the juice of *cāmīkara*.
If it is poured into *śiṃśapā* oil and re-coated seven times,
it quickly dyes the *nāga* gem, and once dyed, the color becomes inexhaustible. If coral, cinnabar, or steel is likewise re-coated with this [mixture], [the same result follows].

One should sprinkle [the serpent] with the juice of *mañjiṣṭhā* and *kiṃśuka*, as well as with vegetable broth. Sprinkled and treated in this sequence, the serpent attains the state of gold; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
O Goddess, the golden leaf has been described; now hear about the excellent silver leaf.
White mica, steamed in sour gruel (*kāñjika*) three times and then subjected to *puṭa* firing, should be cast into purified copper along with a small amount of borax and tin.

One should pierce that *tāra* and *tāla* mixed with a fifth part [of mercury]; one should join that *tāla* to the *tāra* and quickly pierce it with the liquid. One part each of mercury and rock salt (*saindhava*), and two parts each of sesame and *sarjī*.
One *ṭaṅka* [of mercury] should be rubbed with liquid gold for three days.
A copper leaf smeared with that should be heated and then rolled back again.
One should grind *iṅguda* and *tālamūla* with sour curd.
In the midst of that, one should immerse copper seven times so that it becomes leaf-like;
O Supreme Goddess, one should mix it with a third part of the seed.
Lāṅgalī, Citraka, Dantī, Hayaghna, and Uttaravāruṇī—(95.1)
Godhāvatī, vajravallī, śvetārka, and śakravāruṇī; viṣṇukrāntā, aśvagandhā, śigru, pañcāṅgulī, as well as punarnavā, apāmārga, iṅgudī, and cakramardaka.
Guḍūcī and hiṃsrā, [applied] on the first, second, third, and fourth days;
when the infusion is performed after seven days, O beloved,
the purification of copper occurs.
One should smear the copper leaves with a sixteenth part of *tāla* (antimony).
Having placed them in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), one should melt them three times again.
The white group consists of the three alkalis: conch-shell, rock salt, and *sarjikā*.
Ivory, cowrie shells, conch shells, mother-of-pearl,
and copper filings— this is one part which, when treated with wine-soakings, becomes as white as a fingernail.
There should be three parts of magnetite and likewise two parts each of silver and copper.
There should be ten parts of tin; one should pierce it by means of piercing with silver (*tāravedha*).
Silver should be twice [the amount] of iron, and magnetite (*kānta*) four times [the amount] of silver.
Tin should be eight times [the amount] of magnetite; one should pierce it by means of piercing with silver.
Having made the mercury and the *tāla* equal and rubbed them with the milk of the *vajrī*, one should apply a *puṭa* and [heat it] with a press; thus the essence falls out beautifully.
O Goddess of Gods, having melted tin, one should grind it with the milk of the *vajrī*.
The purification of tin twenty-one times is the best method.
One should cause that tin to digest mercury in equal amounts, or in proportions starting from double and so forth,
using the oil of *bhallātaka* and black mustard, conch-shell powder, and *viḍa* salt.
Through that, lead and tin become equal by means of amalgamation with tin;
likewise, by the sprinkling of alkaline water, the seed [of the metal] is transformed in many ways.
I shall explain that method by which softness is produced.

For softening [the teeth], clarified butter, curd, milk, and honey, along with the juices of *bilva* and *jambīra*, mixed with jaggery and sesame seeds, act as a softener when used for sprinkling. (108.1–2) Elephant tusks, horse hooves, and the horns of both sheep and buffalo... (109.1)
One should sprinkle it seven times with a mixture of camphor resin;
the leaf, though split into a thousand pieces, attains softness.
[This is done] in the oil of *jyotiṣmatī* or *kusumbha*, or even in *kārañja* oil.
The wise highly praise the refining of gold;
even if it is being repeatedly processed with silver, if it is not yet pure, it will quickly attain purity by the application of glass and borax. (111.2–112.1)
To soften *candrārka* (mica): with licorice, honey, goat-fat, *saurāṣṭrī*, jaggery, and rock salt;
(113.1) when combined with vinegar, conch-shell, and wine, *candrārka* becomes soft.
(RA_17.113.2) Furthermore, by sprinkling it with honey, oil, and ghee, and [immersing it] in cow urine, (114.1) [it becomes soft].
Even from the leaves of the *khara* plant, softness is produced.
Through the juice of the *ciñcā* tree, with sea-salt, milk, and the heat of the sun,
the silver becomes purified, resembling a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon.

If it is not stainless, then one should cook it again in that same manner; this procedure is declared as the honored method for the rite of purification (*tārakarma*). Gold-dyeing: red *kaṅguṇī* oil, *mañjiṣṭhā*, the two types of *haridrā*, and saffron.
By means of this impregnation (*niṣeka*), one produces gold with a luster like that of the rising sun.
Having added half a part of sulfur (*gandhaka*) and half of that amount of killed mercury (*mṛtasūtaka*) to the molten metal (*śulva*),
one should grind it for three days with the fresh juice of *cāṅgerī*.
One should smear the pale gold with the *pluta* [solution] consisting of various juices;

O Goddess, having cooked it with the five-fold clay (*pañcamṛd*), this is the supreme method for the excellence of gold. One should cause gold, copper (*śulva*), and steel (*tīkṣṇa*) to be made in equal parts.
When heated in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), it instantly becomes a *khoṭa*.
Taking one part of this *khoṭa* combined with mercury and gold,
one should cook it with *anujāmla* until it resembles saffron in color.
By that very same hundredth part, one should pierce pale gold;
divine gold is produced, and there shall be an excellence of two colors.
One should smelt it with salt-ash until it becomes pure.
It should be poured into red oil, and beautiful gold is produced. Sulfur and realgar are rubbed with mustard oil;
alternatively, rājāvartaka and honey [are rubbed] with the acid juice of *mātuluṅga*.
Alternatively, by means of *puṭapāka* (encapsulation), vit, *kapota*, *rājāvartaka*, and *saindhava* produce white gold with the luster of saffron. Furthermore,
the powder of *rājāvartaka* [processed] with the juices of *śirīṣa* flowers...

Copper that has been processed many times and mixed with one-eightieth part [of the additive] bestows color. Copper melted a hundred times in *kaṅguṇī* oil, along with an equal amount of gold and infused with honey, produces color when added in a one-hundredth part.
With cotton seeds, realgar, blue vitriol, rock salt, and red ochre; with leaf-juice, lac, mañjiṣṭhā, red sandalwood, and coral; combined with jaggery, bhallātaka, oil, cow dung, and brick.
Through the process of *āvāpa*, white gold arises, resembling the sun.

[In the case of] *varṇapuṭa*, there are eight parts of red [cinnabar] and three parts each of [mercury] produced from the ocean. A *puṭa* prepared with the juice of white *arkapattra* leaves bestows color.
Having made red and yellow [mercury] equal, and adding honey equal to those two,
one should stir it with *karañja* oil and heat it in a sealed crucible (*mūkamūṣā*).
By heating it once with a tenth part of yellow [mercury], ten times with a hundredth part of yellow [mercury], and so on— (RA_17.131.2) (RA_17.132.1)

One hundred [parts] pierced by one thousand [parts] of *pīta* and half a *koṭi* [of parts] pierce [the metal]. Furthermore, salt that has been processed hundreds of times with the juice of *kiṃśuka*, along with *ṭaṅkaṇa*, when subjected to cupping (*puṭa*), will bestow an excellence of color.

Take three parts of iron powder and twice that amount of red ochre; one should sprinkle these with the decoction of madhuka and kumuda flowers, as well as with urine. One should grind them together with kodrava grain and then cast the mixture into the middle of a cow-pen.
This [gold] becomes color-bestowing when reduced by one-eightieth part through smelting (*vāpa*).
One should flux the gold exceeding the [required] wire (*śulva*) using an *andhamūṣā* crucible;
at that time, immersion (*niṣeka*) in sea-mineral water is recommended.
When smeared with ocean-born red ochre, the liquefied [metal] attains softness.
One should apply a plaster of that [ochre] mixed with cow-dung ashes in equal proportions.
The gold, exceeding the copper, shall attain purity through the *puṭa* process.
Having smeared the crucible with a paste of powdered naga-bone ashes, the wise [alchemist] should place it within a blind-crucible (*andhamūṣā*); thus, it will always become gold-leaf.
Then, the wise one, having spread it out with gentle hammering, [should proceed].
It should be heated repeatedly and poured [into the crucible] until it attains softness.
Having smeared it with a paste of marine mineral (sāmudra-dhātu), the skillful practitioner,
having placed it upon a palāśa leaf, should burn it with a gentle fire.

The wise one should cook it until it reaches a state of purity; then, having allowed it to cool, he should extinguish it in water. This procedure should be performed exactly until the desired color has been attained.
Then one should heat that again, combined with powdered cow-dung.
Once heated by the fire, the wise man should cast it into the salt.
Then he should melt the excellent gold with salt and red ochre.

Having thoroughly purified it again and again, the wise practitioner should apply coatings and perform *puṭapāka* in order to produce the [desired] color. O Goddess of Gods, one should cook the *tārāriṣṭa* with red oil.
One should sprinkle it a hundred times; thus protected, the leaf becomes colored.
One should extract the group of mercury and the secondary minerals (uparasa) into lead and tin;
furthermore, one should extract lead and tin into copper, and copper into silver.
O Goddess of gods, when silver is repeatedly poured into red oil,
auspicious gold is produced, free from all defects. The residue of the mercury, when combined with half the amount of gold, is highly praised.
Divine gold, equal to the *mātṛkā* and most excellent, is produced.
One should cause tin, mica, white *tāpya*, or *śaila* to be sown into white [silver];
for that, when added in a tenth part to silver (*tāra*), bestows an excellence of color.
O Pārvatī, ninety-eight parts of the *tārāriṣṭa* constitute the hundred-fold process (*śatāṃśavidhi*).
Each single part of mercury and gold is known as a "hundred-fold penetration" (*śatavedha*). By this sequential application, it becomes a penetrator by the thousand-fold part (*sahasrāṃśa*).
Having fashioned a crucible shaped like a cow's udder, firm and filled with leaf-fragments,
one should heat it until that leaf becomes stainless and opened.
Then, having applied the mercury combined with a transmuting agent (*krāmaṇa*), one should perform the piercing (*vedha*).
A leaf of *dalapatra* smeared with mercury and placed inside a copper vessel,
coated on top with clay, and heated over a gentle fire;
having thus processed it together with the seed-mantra, the wise man should always maintain it.
One should quench [the mercury] with borax and sesame powder while it is cold. Having prepared the gold with the essence, one should leave it on the ground for one fortnight.
O Goddess of the Gods, having lifted it up and opened it again, that may be sold.

Furthermore, I shall explain another method of how the transmutation by mercury (*rasavedha*) occurs: one should provide two *pala* of the powder of *tila* and mustard seeds, and two *pala* of turmeric; these should be ground together in a single vessel. (RA 17.159)
One should crush five *pala* of the serpent-plant in an earthen vessel;
one should sow it with the perfected mercury (*siddhasūta*) and stir it with a rod.
One should continue sowing it again and again until it reaches a state of hardness.
That divine nāga is born, possessing a luster equal to Jāmbūnada gold.
I shall describe the opening [of the vessel] and the serpent [mercury] processed with rasa.
One should join the copper that has been drawn by sound with a sixteenth part [of the mercury].
Having combined and thoroughly stirred them together, one should sprinkle them with goat’s urine.
Thus, the gold becomes beautiful and entirely freed from all defects.
O Goddess of the Suras, this is known as *lohavedha* in its detailed application.
Just as it is with metal, so should the elixir (*sūtaka*) always be applied to the body;
O Goddess, entering both the body and the metal, it makes them equal.
One should first test it on the metal, and thereafter apply it to the body.
Therefore, tell me that, O Goddess of the Gods; what else do you wish to hear?
(RA_17.166.2) 18 The Illustrious Goddess said: (1.1)

"O God, regarding those 'piercings of iron' which have been described by you, please explain that 'piercing of the body' by means of which the state of moving through the sky (*khecarī-gati*) may be attained. Śrī Bhairava said: (2.1) "The piercing of iron has been explained by me; now listen to the piercing of the body. (RA_18.1.2–3) [Note: The provided text contains only the first half of verse 2.1.]
First one should purify the body, and afterwards one should employ the medicinal paste (*kalka*);
otherwise, there will be no success in either mercury (*rasa*) or elixir (*rasāyana*).
At the beginning, one should drink ghee and rock salt every morning for three days.
Thereafter, one should drink the decoction of *ketakī* flowers for three days.
Having performed fomentation (*svedana*) according to the prescribed method with barley-alkali and sugar,
O Goddess worshipped by gods and asuras, one should drink the decoction of *varā* for three days.
Once purgation has been properly induced, one should drink a decoction of *kaṭukarohiṇī* for three days and eat barley-gruel mixed with ghee.
By consuming a sweetmeat (*modaka*) made from *palāśa* seeds, *jantughna*, and *guṇa*, [the desired result is achieved].

Then one should effect the casting down of the insect with water desired by crows. For three days, [one should take] a powder made from *vacā*, black pepper, rock salt, turmeric, *kaṇā*, ginger, *dhātrī*, jaggery, and *viḍaṅga*.
Having thus purified the *śāli* rice with milk, mung-bean water, and barley-gruel,
one should then, having regained strength,
practice the rāsa-āyana regimen with the juice of the *dhātrī*, ghee, honey, and milks produced from the celestial trees (*surataru*).
O Goddess of the gods, having extracted the oil from [the mineral] containing two, four, or six *pala*s,
one should drink it daily for three months according to the small, medium, or superior measures. Thereafter, one should consume *āroṭa*, and once that has been digested, [one should proceed further].
Then, having made the body a field, one should increase that which is to be consumed.
Having purified it with the two [substances] of space and fire, and immediately thereafter having cast it down,
one should grind *taṇḍulīyaka* and *bhṛṅgarāja* and sow the resulting juice.

One should first employ *āroṭa* for the sake of achieving bodily perfection (*dehasiddhi*). [This concludes] *rasāyana*. Alternatively, having been reduced to ashes six times through the application of a paste, one should utilize that *āroṭaka* for a full year.
One who consumes bitumen, honey, viḍaṅga, ghee, iron, abhayā, mercury, and gold-leaf will replenish the depleted tissues of a weak body within fifteen nights, just like the moon.
(14.1–14.2) [This is achieved] with the juice of *bakakanyā*, honey, the two types of turmeric, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and jaggery. (RA_18.15.1)

Having consumed the mercury reduced to a paste, combined with *vyoma*, *kānta*, honey, and clarified butter, one shall attain immortality; this is the supreme method for making the body a sacred field (*kṣetrīkaraṇa*).
Then, [one may consume] the powder of the essence of mica (*abhraka*) or of *kāntaloha*.
Or, O Great Goddess, for one who is sharp-witted, it should be saturated with a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) until it resembles collyrium;
then, having purified it while covered by cloth,
[one should treat it] with the essence of *bhṛṅga* and *āmalaka*, and with the juice of turmeric.
Encased in a seal, combined with mercury, and mixed with honey and ghee, it should be placed inside a metal casket and kept for a month among grain.
One should lick it with ghee and honey; this is the supreme method for making the field [of the body] receptive.
By practicing this for a year, a man shall attain a lifespan of a thousand years.
Prior to the mastery of mercury (*rasasiddhi*), one should consume gold the size of a *guñjā* seed every day for the sake of bodily perfection; thus, the mastery of mercury is produced.

One should first lick a preparation consisting of the essence of beautiful mica, mixed with honey and ghee, and slightly alloyed with gold; this is the supreme method for "consecrating the field" (*kṣetrīkaraṇa*).
One should consume it in this manner for a year, or half a year, or even beforehand.
O Goddess, mercury digested by *vajra* is proclaimed as the most excellent;
that digested by gold is middling, O Dear One, while that digested by silver is inferior.
When the ash-born mercury is digested by gold and consumed, one attains the state of Rudra.
When *tāra* has been digested, one attains the state of Viṣṇu; when *bhāskara*, the state of Brahmā.
When *tīkṣṇa* has been digested, one becomes the Lord of Wealth; and when *capalālaya*, one attains the state of the Sun.
When *vājara*, one attains the state of the Moon; and when *rohaṇa*, the state of Fire.
In general, however, by means of a sharp [substance], a man may attain the state of Śakra.
Likewise, he who consumes the ash-mercury that has been digested by iron will become water-like through water and attain the state of dry land through dry land.
Likewise, fire is superior to fire, and [the practitioner] is more powerful than even the wind.
He is the destroyer and the creator, manifestly the one who bestows both curses and favors.
Wherever the practitioner may discard urine or feces, [that place becomes sacred].
There, stone and clay clearly become gold.
His perspiration would pierce the eight types of metals;
all that becomes pure gold once twelve *pala* have been consumed.
O Great Goddess, you who bring about freedom from old age and death, one equal to Rudra [is attained].
One should consume sixteen *pala* of mercury processed with ash (*bhasmasūta*) along with silver (*tāra*);
or else, one should consume the ash-mercury that has been digested by silver.
Copper and tin, through its sweat, attain the state of silver.
Alternatively, one should consume the ash of mercury that has been processed with *tīkṣṇa* iron;
when tin is touched by its urine, it attains the state of silver.
By each single application of the *niṣeka* rite, the immobilization (*stambhana*) of lead and tin occurs.
O Goddess, one should consume mercury in a dose of one *guñjā* that has been digested by gold;
two *guñjās* for that which has been digested by silver, and three for that which has been digested by copper.

One *māṣa* of sharp *abhraka* (mica) and one *guñjā* of *drāvika* (liquefier) shall be prepared. One should consume [the medicine] processed with *vajra* and *vaikrānta*, combined with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*).
Lead, tin, mercury, and ash, combined with poisons and secondary poisons (*viṣopaviṣa*), [should be used].
Then, one should consume the elixir (*rasāyana*) in the prescribed measure;
thus, gold, silver, and likewise *kānta* iron gradually become fire-resistant.
And this bound king of mercury (*rasarāja*) shall bestow the perfection of the body (*dehasiddhi*).
With *vajra*, magnetite (*ayaskānta*), *mākṣika*, *vaikrānta*, mica (*abhra*), and gold—
when these have been digested according to their availability, mercury is praised for the practice of *rasāyana*.
One should also process exactly six secondary minerals (*uparasa*) for the purpose of consumption.
Having digested one *tīkṣṇa* [dose], one should consume one *pala*;
he lives with a vajra-body for ten thousand years.
Likewise, one should consume twelve *palas* once the *tīkṣṇa* has been digested.
Thus one may live for a great kalpa, and at the end of the dissolution, one shall go to Śiva.
From one *pala* of well-digested ash, the lifespan is one hundred thousand years;
from two *palas*, the lifespan is ten million years; and from three *palas*, the lifespan is equal to that of Brahmā.
With four *palas* of *vaiṣṇava-āyus*, and with five *palas* of *rudra-āyus*,
when the sixth *pala* is attained, he lives for a *mahākalpa*.
With one *pala* of gold that has been digested by *bhasman*, one attains the lifespan of Brahmā.
With two *pala* one attains the lifespan of Viṣṇu, but with three *pala* the lifespan of Rudra;
with four *pala*, O Goddess of the Gods, a man shall attain the state of Śiva. When three *pala* of the digested ash-elixir of gold have been consumed in due order, [the result follows].
Eighty-eight thousand yoginīs, arrogant in their power, stand as his servants; a man shall become able to assume any form at will. Whatever form he contemplates, he shall come to bear that very form.
One should consume the gold ashes in a dose of eleven *mitas*.
O Goddess of the Gods, having ascertained one’s own digestive capacity, one should take a single *guñjā* at a time;
then, coating it with ghee and honey, one may enjoy betel leaf and the company of beloved women.
For there is this one subtle defect when the *bhasmasūtaka* has been consumed: O lady of excellent limbs, for three weeks the man becomes blinded by passion;
indeed, within a single day he might agitate a thousand women.
O lady of excellent hips, from union with a woman, impurity spreads through the body.
O lady of excellent hips, from union with a woman, indigestion arises for him.
When the semen has been discharged through sexual intercourse, [the following occurs] sequentially over a period of three times seven days.

A risk to one's life arises from that; therefore, one should abandon sexual intercourse with her. One may engage in conversation with a young woman and massage her limbs—she whose mere touch causes the vital essence (*rasa*) to waste away within the body.
Just as desire arises from gazing upon the form of a beautiful woman,
O Goddess of the Gods, so too does that seminal flow (*sūtaka*) proceed from there in due course.
She whose vulva (*bhaga*) is auspicious, even, and resembles a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree—
O Goddess, sexual union with such a woman is indeed a vessel for alchemy (*rasāyana*).
Furthermore, one whose vulva is fleshless, elongated, and possesses dry veins—
one who always brings about poverty— should be avoided in the practice of alchemy.
One should constantly satisfy [the deities] with the *arghya* offering and present fish and meat.
Having worshipped the lords of yogins and the yoginīs with mantras, one should ask for their forgiveness.
One should, however, abandon the group of eight *kakāra* [foods], as well as pungent, sour, and salty [tastes].
By one *pala* of processed mica (*abhra*), one is not overcome by diseases;
in the second [dose], there is an increase of semen; in the third, one becomes strong.
In the fourth, it destroys gray hair; in the fifth, it conquers wrinkles.
In the sixth [month], one becomes a retainer of what has been heard and eloquent; in the seventh, a conqueror of eye diseases.
In the eighth, one possesses the vision of Tārkṣya, the lifespan of Brahmā, and the prowess of Brahmā. By the consumption of nine *palas*, one becomes a gatherer of gods (*suramelāpaka*).
With a dosage of ten *palas*, the second [type] becomes Śaṅkara.
To protect the flavor and potency, one should offer an oblation day by day;
by reciting the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, the perfection of mercury (*rasasiddhi*) is produced.
O Supreme Goddess, the man who consumes the *rasa* when it has become pure and digested shall live for ten thousand years. When it has become doubly pure and digested, he lives for one million years.
When it has been digested three times over and is pure, one lives for ten crores [of years].
O Goddess, when it has been digested four times over, the mercury leads to the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratā*).
Then, when it has been digested five times over, the great mercury becomes a penetrator by touch (*sparśavedhī*).
Just as it is with pure, aged [mercury], so it is with gold-beetle [mineral];
O Goddess, he obtains that fruit and lives by its potency.
Furthermore, I shall describe another elixir: the mercury of diamond-ash (*vajrabhasma-rasāyana*).
O Goddess praised by the gods, one should first cause sulfur to be digested within mercury.
One should then add three times as much *tīkṣṇa* iron and an equal amount of gold to the mercury.
With that very [mixture] in which the gold has been digested, one should coat the diamond-gem (*vajraratna*).
Then, one should wrap that vajra with the dung of a young calf;
having bound it in a small pouch, one should subject it to *puṭapāka* (sealed heating).
At that very moment, it turns to ash, resembling a conch shell, jasmine, or the moon.

O fortunate one, one should prepare that vajra-ash to the consistency of a paste; then, one should rub that powder from the mercury-ball until it has permeated the body [of the substance]. Furthermore, that powder from the ball should be mixed with the dung of young calves.

One should apply a coating to the crucible using that very [substance] in half-and-half portions. One should heat that [substance], which has been processed with mercury (*vajra*) and rendered malleable (*mūrchita*), in a blind-crucible (*andhamūṣā*). By means of a thousand puffs of breath, it becomes ash in an instant.
Half of that half becomes ash resembling cow’s milk, O beloved. When the medicinal paste (*kalka*) held in oil is combined with *kaṅguṇī* oil,
O woman of excellent hips, purification of the body occurs after three weeks.
One *tila* measure of vajra-ash and an equal amount of gold ash,
smeared with *dhatura* juice and heated, destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
Eight *pala* of pure gold combined with an equal amount of dead mercury [is likewise effective].
One should grind it with sour gruel, and in an instant it becomes a ball.
O Dear One, half of it is obtained as ash resembling cow’s milk.
One part of the dead vajra and four parts of the ball [are to be used].
One should rub it with a heated mortar until the mercury is reduced to ash.
One should kill it in a *bhūdhara* machine through the process of seven successive coatings (*saṅkalikā*).
Then, that ash should again be rubbed with sour gruel (*madhyamāmla*).
One should carefully apply the *puṭa* [sealing] three hundred and sixty times;
O Goddess, that ash becomes like the reddish hue of vermilion (*sindūra*).
One should lick one *pala* of that ash mixed with honey and clarified butter.
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on a diet of milk should lick [the medicine] in this manner seven times.
On the second and seventh [days], one should consume two *pala*s;
by this progressive increase, one should consume it for seven weeks.
Through its increase, one becomes perfected; the man shall possess divine splendor.
His lifespan shall equal that of Rudra, and he will undoubtedly attain the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*).
By means of his urine and feces, the eight metals as well as gold [are produced].
One pala of that ash, when combined with a transmuting agent (*krāmaṇa*),
produces divine gold fit for the ornaments of the gods from twelve thousand palas of base metal.
Eight *pala*s of *kānta* powder and eight *pala*s of mercury,
having combined and thoroughly rubbed them together, one should then grind them with the juice of *bījapūra*.
By rubbing [them] with a heated mortar, they become a ball (*golaka*) in an instant.

One part of dead-vajra and four parts of bola, having combined these and then thoroughly rubbed them together, the mercury is reduced to ashes. One should kill [the mercury] in a *bhūdhara* yantra through the sequence of seven *saṅkalikās*.
One part of its ash and one part of sulphur,
when heated in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), instantly becomes a solid bolus (*khoṭa*).
[Then], thirty-two parts of the dead bolus and twenty parts of pure gold...
Silver, copper, *vyomasattva*, and *kāntasattva* as the fourth—each of these should be twelve parts; one should cause them all to be combined into one.
When placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heated, it instantly becomes a *khoṭa*.
One should cause thirty-two *khoṭas* to be ground into a fine powder.
(89.2) That fine powder of *khoṭa*, when combined with the juice of *āroṭa*, should be rubbed with a moderate acid; in an instant, it becomes a ball (*golaka*). (RA_18.90.1–2)
Two *pala* of *golaka* and an equal amount of *mṛtakānta*,
having combined these and then ground them with the juice of *meghanāda* and the juice of *munipuṣpa*, one should grind them for one day.
O Goddess, one should have three hundred and sixty pills prepared.
Among them, a man should eat one pill daily for one year, combined with ghee, triphalā, and honey; thus he attains the lifespan of Brahmā.
If one subsequently consumes them all, that person shall possess the lifespan of Rudra.
Furthermore, O Amarasuṃdarī, if a single pill is held in the mouth,
it will forcibly destroy all diseases as well as gray hair.
I shall explain the ritual application (*upacāra*) regarding the elixir (*rasāyana*) of Vajrasattva.
O Goddess, that mercury which is bound by the *vajra* brings about the state of a *vajra*.
Those bodies which are bound by it become bodies possessing the form of a *vajra*.

O Goddess, by [taking] a quantity of the essence the size of a sesame seed, one lives for the lifespan of Brahmā; O Goddess, by [taking] a quantity of the essence the size of a barley grain, he lives for ten million lifespans of Viṣṇu;
but by [taking] a quantity the size of a *guñjā* berry, O Mistress of the Gods, one shall possess the lifespan of a great kalpa.
O lady of excellent hips, even one who possesses qualities equal to mine would become like a mere bean [in comparison].
O fortunate one, he shall not be accessible to one devoid of mantra;
for him, there is no accomplishment of siddhi even in hundreds of millions of births.
Deprived of his family lineage and its teachings, this person wanders with a deluded mind.
O Goddess of the Suras, gods and dānavas, as well as goddesses who travel through the sky and those who move upon the earth, create thousands of obstacles for him. (RA 18.101–102)
Having worshipped him in a dream, those [female spirits] carry away his semen and blood;
by that very path of the semen, they carry away the essence that has been consumed.
O Goddess, the planets beginning with the Sun roar in their own forms.
In the form of a kṣatriya, the gods indeed roar;
in the form of a vaiśya, the piśācas; and in the form of a śūdra, the rākṣasas.
Others, in human form, attend upon him during the interval between sleepings.
O beautiful goddess, they devour bones and flesh in dreams;
at the end of a dream, a human being generally experiences delusion and sees [visions].
At the end of a dream, they indeed carry off the ashes of the vajra and cause agitation.
When it has been consumed, those who are pure as gold flee in the ten directions—
the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, śākinīs, guhyakas, and the rest.
This applies to those who deal with the killing of diamonds, or with metals, or with mercury.
Listen, my dear, to those [methods] which, when employed, must be avoided with great effort.
(108.2) As for the various types of reasoning employed by those who provide such reasoning, beings and others speak in this way to terrify that man. (109.2)
The *rañjaka* is that which causes passion; the *krāmaṇa* is beneficial for the act of attraction. The *bandhaka* and *dṛḍhakāra* are likewise known as those that bring about nourishment.
One should consume semen, blood, feces, and urine in various ways.
That [elixir], which causes leprosy when tainted by lead and tin,
[is neutralized by] triphalā, jāti, and kaṅkola mixed with the juice of camphor.
One should consume the essence of khadira ground with an equal amount of water.
Having rubbed *kaṭuka* with milk, it is an excellent, wholesome *krāmaṇa* [agent].
O Goddess of the Gods, this is not to be eaten when rubbed with breast-milk or with gold.
Through the consumption of *alambuṣā*, magnetite (*ayaskānta*), and *tālaka*, [the desired result is achieved].
The lord of mercury moves within the body; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

Mercury necessarily moves [through the body] during union with a woman; this is the supreme transmutation (*krāmaṇa*). Or else, through celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the yogi should always employ the mercury (*sūtaka*).
Samādhi is its cause, and that is considered the supreme means of transference.
One should consume the mercury at dawn, when two watches [of the night] have passed;
one must not let three watches elapse, nor should one eat at midday.

One should avoid excessive drinking, overeating, excessive sleep, and staying awake too long; one should also avoid excessive attachment to women and traveling too great a distance. One should avoid excessive anger, excessive joy, excessive greed, and excessive longing.
One should avoid empty talk, playing in water, and excessive anxiety.
[One should also avoid] the eight "ka" fruits: the *kūṣmāṇḍa*, the *karkaṭī*, the *kāliṅga*, the *kāravellaka*, the *kusumbhaka*, the *karkoṭa*, the *kadalī*, and the *kākamācikā*.
One who consumes the *rasa* should indeed avoid these eight syllables beginning with "ka.
One must not commit a sin and should avoid association with the uninitiated (*paśu*).
One should not step over the shadow of a *liṅga*, nor likewise the shadow of a woman.
One should not go to a crossroads, nor should one step over excrement or urine.
O Goddess, one should avoid reviling the gods and should refrain from disparaging women.
One should speak truthful words and should not utter speech that is unpleasant.
One should avoid horse gram, linseed oil, sesame seeds, mung beans, and lentils;
one should also avoid pigeon meat, rice with sour gruel, and boiled rice with buttermilk. One should likewise avoid that which is pungent, sour, sharp, salty, slimy, or bile-inducing.
One should avoid sesame oil, curd, milk, grapes, *kola*, and *parūṣaka*;
as well as *badara*, *cirabilva*, mango, and *suvarcala*;
and one should also renounce orange, *kāñcanāra*, and *śobhāñjana*.
One who is afflicted by hunger should not remain [without eating], nor should one cause indigestion to occur. One should not engage in debate or idle chatter, nor should one sleep during the day.
One should never consume food offerings (*naivedya*), and one should always avoid camphor.
One should avoid anointing oneself with saffron and avoid dancing on the ground.
One should not touch fire with the foot, nor cows, nor Brahmins.
One should not strike a young girl, and one should also avoid those who are insane.
One should recite the mantra day and night, and bathe every single day.
(RA_18.130) Beneficial food consists of mung beans, milk-rice, and *śāli* rice, consumed with a concentrated mind.
(131.1) O Goddess, there should also be *paunarnava* greens, *meghanāda*, and *vāstuka*. (RA_18.131.2)

One should consume rock salt (*saindhava*), dry ginger (*nāgara*), nut-grass (*mustā*), and lotus roots. (131.3) The woman whose nipples have emerged becomes dark-complexioned, beautiful, fortunate, auspicious, endowed with divine luster, and her power of desire is increased. (RA_18.132.1–2)
She should be kept in close proximity and protected by the elders.
One should never consort with a woman who is dark-skinned, pale, excessively aged, or of immoral character.
[One should avoid using] the *tilaka* mark, saffron, perfumes, and charming musk.

Fragrant flowers, comfortable beds, and desired food—these are said to constitute pleasant dwelling; furthermore, the "intoxicating" (*krāmaṇa*) rite for the newborn is performed. One should engage in discourse on self-knowledge and especially perform worship of Śiva.
O blessed lady, one must not transgress these rules regarding the consumption of mercury (*rasa*).
Should they be transgressed, its various effects and characteristics are described as follows:
O beloved, when the king of essences (*rasarāja*) is undigested, this sign shall appear.

Fainting, grief, dizziness, trembling, vomiting, delusion, and likewise fever; (137.2) hiccups, shivering, pains, sleepiness, lethargy, and loss of appetite; (RA_18.138.1) stiffness of the limbs, diarrhea, coughing, labored breathing, and yawning. (RA_18.138.2)

Burning sensations arise in the ears, mouth, eyes, flanks, scrotum, abdomen, and head; there is a loss of digestive fire and danger to all the limbs. One should observe other great diseases as well when the *rasa* is undigested.

One should drink *kāñjika* (sour gruel) mixed with *sarjikākṣāra* (alkali of wood-ash), saturated with the juice of *kāravallī*, combined with cow’s urine and *saindhava* salt; this is its transference. O Goddess, [one should also take] the juice of *mokṣaka* and the juice of *rājakoṣātakī*.

A person suffering from indigestion of meat (*rasājīrṇa*) should drink *sindhuka* salt mixed with black cow's urine and saturated with the juice of *kāravallī*, combined with *sauvarcala* salt. One who suffers from indigestion of meat will not survive; he dies—of this there is no doubt.
When the elixir (*rasāyana*) has been well-digested, everything is accomplished by means of it.
When [the practitioner] is asleep, his limb should be rubbed with the breast of a woman;
he should likewise massage it with his left hand. In this way, the mercury (*sūta*) transmutes without distress.
In a windless, secluded place, such as an undisturbed underground chamber,
free from cold and heat, eating wholesome food and consuming light meals,
one shall attain accomplishment within the stated number of days; of this there is no doubt.
One shall attain accomplishment in twice as many days by consuming all types of food;
by practicing while enduring cold and wind, one attains it in three times as many days in succession;
and by means of the practices of the *atimārga*, one attains it in four times as many days.

In this regard, I shall explain the piercing (*vedha*), preceded by the perfection of the body (*dehasiddhi*). Out of affection for you, O Goddess of Gods, I have indeed taught this elixir (*rasāyana*). First, O Goddess, is the piercing of the skin; second is the piercing of the flesh.
The third is the piercing of the blood, while the fourth is the piercing of the bones.
The fifth would be the piercing of the marrow, and the sixth is the piercing of the channels.
The seventh is the piercing of the constituents (*dhātu*), and the eighth is that of the armor.

O Goddess of the gods, by piercing the skin, the serpent becomes crooked; O fortunate one, by piercing the flesh, the crooked becomes gold. O Goddess of the gods, by piercing the bone, even the sharp [metal] attains the state of gold.
O beautiful lady, by piercing the marrow one should pierce the eight metals;
by the piercing of the armor, gold shall appear in the earthen vessel;
and when the pure gold is pierced, gold is produced from the marrow.
O Goddess of the Suras, one should pierce silver with mercury that has been processed;
likewise, in the case of *alaka*, *vimala*, *tāpya*, *tīkṣṇa*, silver, and *bhāskara*,
there should be buttermilk, sugar, and honey as the *krāmaṇa* (transmuting agent).
O Goddess, that buttermilk from a tawny or black cow is indeed for the purpose of *rasāyana* (rejuvenation).
Cow's buttermilk is *sāttvika*, while that produced from a crane is *rājasa*.
Buffalo buttermilk is *tāmasa*; it must never be given for *rasāyana*.

O Goddess, the juice of ginger as well as areca nuts, when rubbed with fresh butter, constitute the supreme method for the transference (*krāmaṇa*) of the essence. That derived from vegetables and roots is inferior; that born from fruits and roots is middling.
O Goddess of the gods of gods, *rasaka* is indeed supreme for the practice of alchemy (*rasāyana*).
Through piercing with *tīkṣṇa*, it becomes blue in luster; through copper, it possesses a reddish glow;
through silver, it resembles the moon; and through gold, it is like pure gold.

One who observes smoke, when placed in the mouth, leads to the state of a sky-walker (*khecaratā*) within a month; one that effects penetration by touch, when placed in the mouth, bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*) within two months.
By three months, [one attains] a hundred crores, and by four months, ten crores.
With five [repetitions], there is penetration of five *koṭis*, and with six, one becomes a piercer of a *koṭi*.
(160.2) Thus, by performing it in this sequence, one makes the body free from old age and death;
the sovereignty of the qualities such as *aṇimā* arises, and the perfection of command (*ājñāsiddhi*) is produced. (RA_18.161.1–2)
With seven months [of practice], one becomes a piercer of a hundred thousand; with eight, furthermore, ten thousand;
with nine months, a thousand; and with ten months, again, a hundred.
By means of his urine, feces, phlegm, and bodily impurities, (RA 18.163.1)
Through the application of medicinal paste (*lepāt*), stones and other materials on the earth attain the state of gold.
By means of a sixty-fourth part [of mercury], there is penetration (*vedha*) in one month; by ten such penetrations, it becomes a "ten-fold penetrator.
That which possesses a thirty-second part of penetration, however, shall penetrate the body after a year.
She whose hair has curled ends, who is dark-complexioned with lotus-like eyes,
whose hips are broad and whose chest is narrow;
that young woman in whom the appearance of menses occurs during the dark fortnight— (RA_18.165.1–2).
She is declared to be a "kāminī" and the most excellent in the practice of *rasāyana*. Through embracing, touching, sexual intercourse, and even conversation with her,
one becomes free from all diseases and devoid of wrinkles and grey hair.
He cannot be cut by weapons nor burned by fire;
possessing the speed of the wind and great majesty, he is like another Kāmadeva.
By his own will, he becomes visible, and indeed, he becomes invisible.
By its mere touch, all metals become gold.
In that terrible single ocean, where all moving and stationary beings have perished,
and where even the gods are dissolved, there the Siddha likewise dissolves.

This supreme secret has been proclaimed by me, O Mistress of the Gods. Those who know the essence of virtuous and noble people and are devoted to the practice of refining mercury are truly called "alchemists" (*rasavādī*); others are merely "haters of discourse" (*dveṣavādinaḥ*).

Furthermore, I shall describe another pill that is difficult for mercury to attain. Mercury is prepared by alchemists when combined with tin, lead, copper, mica, gold, and silver, and joined with diamonds, iron, and so forth.
Having gathered all those together and placed them within a crucible, one should blow upon them;
a divine pill is produced, named Vajrāṅgasundarī. When held in the mouth, it is said to bestow accomplishment and destroy old age and death.
He is a hero victorious in battle, possessing a vajra-body and great strength;
he is eternally beloved by all the world and likewise fortunate among women.
Vajra, vyomaja, sattva, sakana, candra, ravi, kāntaka, nāga, vaṅga, and ayas—when these are made into a very firm *sūta* (mercury), it becomes equal to that [vajra].

The mercury-ball (*rasagolaka*), situated in the mouth, produces pleasure, grants all aims, and removes heat; in one year it destroys the accumulation of defects, and one becomes possessed of a lifespan of a kalpa.
(178.2) O Goddess, one should add a quarter-part of gold to the previously perfected mercury;
one should then add the essence of space (*vyomasattva*) along with a part of a *pala* of "dead" (*mṛta*) vajra. (RA 18.179.1–2)
Having ground it according to the prescribed method with milk, a silken cloth, water, and the juice of *suradālī*, one should reduce it to a fine powder (*naṣṭapiṣṭa*). Then,
adding a minute portion (*truṭi*) of *kāntaloha* powder, one should heat it in a sealed crucible (*mūkamūṣā*).
A divine pill is produced which, when held in the mouth, bestows all accomplishments.
One should prepare equal parts of auspicious honey, mica, and vajra, as well as gold, copper, and silver.
The pill, bound with the vajra, when held in the mouth, bestows all accomplishments.
It consists of *bhrāmaka* and *mākṣika*, combined with the three metals,
joined with the seed-syllable of Śakti, and endowed with the three seed-syllables.

Having combined the mercury crushed with *tridaṇḍī* into a single ball (*golaka*), one should place it inside a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heat it; then, one should perform the re-melting (*samāvarta*). Having performed worship, O Dear One, if one places it in the mouth, after six months he shall become [an immortal].
Fearless toward all enemies, he possesses a vajra-body and great strength.
Nandikeśa, Kumāra, and others—who used to carry away those being devoured—now have their shadows vanished and are no longer seen; they hold only ashes in their hands.
But with a deluded mind, he did not see the essence being carried away by them.
He said to all the beings: "I have achieved no success in alchemy;
yet in my mind, I believed in the perfection of alchemy, and for that reason, such hardship was endured by me. (RA 18.187.2–188.1)
This loss of wealth was brought about by me, a person of evil intellect and deluded mind.
He did not realize that such a deed, performed by me, was devoid of scriptural authority;
for the most wicked corrupt the sacred texts and do not recognize their own actions.
O Goddess, a rasa devoid of the prescribed ritual will never attain perfection;
O Mistress of the Gods, O fair-faced one, for one who lacks the scriptural tradition, there is no success whatsoever.
The lineage does not succeed through any inauspicious actions.
In the science of alchemy (*rasaśāstra*), one would not succeed; such a guru would not be found. (191.2) One would not obtain such an empowerment (*ājñā*), nor such knowledge (*jñāna*).
O fair-faced one, one would not find such a woman who is single-mindedly devoted. (RA 18.192.1–2)
He did not obtain the flavorful [elixir] nor that queen Rasāṅkuśī;
for him with whom Śiva himself is pleased, there is success in the elixir of alchemy.
Furthermore, I shall describe another supreme method: the binding of the cow (*golabandhana*).
By merely consuming which one indeed becomes free from old age and death.
Having combined sulphur, mica, magnetite,
and gold with an equal amount of sharp iron, and having bound it with mercury (rasendra), one should form a pill (golaka).

One should mix five palas of the king of mercury with equal parts [of the other ingredients] and grind them with the juice of seven jambīra fruits into a ball. Once that ball has been dried in the shade, it brings about the state of the moon.
All of this, including the mercury (*sūtaka*) and the *golaka*, should be ground together.
One should then apply a gentle fomentation (*mṛdusveda*) upon the earth using a fire of dried cow-dung (*karīṣāgni*).
This *golaka* placed within the mouth bestows immortality.
The fruit of one born from a *sūta-golaka* cannot be described;
he brings about the restoration of complexion through alchemy (*rasāyana*) and bestows success in the mastery of mercury (*rasasiddhi*).
[He enjoys] fragrant ointments, betel, musk, saffron, and aloe-wood.
One should cause sandalwood, musk, kaṅkola, and nutmeg,
as well as other fragrant substances, to be offered for bathing and drinking.
She whose hair has curled ends, who is dark-complexioned, and lotus-eyed— (RA_18.201.1)
She whose hips are broad but whose heart is narrow;
she for whom the appearance of menses occurs during the dark fortnight— that young woman is declared a *kāminī*, and she is the most excellent for the practice of *rasāyana*.
Through embracing, touching, and even through sexual conversation,
one becomes completely free from all diseases and devoid of wrinkles and gray hair; moreover,
if these are held within the mouth, the hundred diseases shall perish.
One shall live for three hundred years with a body of incomparable measure.
O Goddess of the Gods, I shall now describe the qualities that arise when sixteen [leaves] are held within the mouth for sixteen years.
He cannot be cut by weapons nor burned by fire;
possessing the speed of the wind and great majesty, he is like another god of love.
By his own will, he becomes visible, and indeed, he becomes invisible.
By the mere touch of it, all metals become gold.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, I shall further describe another [mantra], the Vajrabandha.
One who has deficient limbs, or extra limbs, or is afflicted by disease, or is hunchbacked and bent over—
With his feet bent, his speech faltering, and his senses numbed by old age,
though he is dull, stammering, mute, and likewise deprived of movement,
he remains alive, freed from the skin of his conch-like neck.
When, by the power of this bound [mercury], a circular revolution occurs,
one should take mercury that pierces ten million [parts] and combine it with six *piṇḍas*.
The wise man should then have a pill prepared, with each [ingredient] situated in the center of one [pill].
There are five counted pills, and the sixth is indeed the fifth;
the mass should be sixfold, in a very beautiful copper vessel. The height should be one man's measure, and the mandala half a man's measure.
One should offer a piece of wood carved with four faces upon it;
one should smear it with equal parts of ghee and great oil (*mahātaila*).
Having worshipped the cauldron, one should likewise worship the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*).
Thereafter, one should worship the maiden and likewise offer a bali-oblation in the cardinal directions.
One should perform the fanning there very slowly in the four directions. It should be made thoroughly heated until it becomes smokeless.

Then, having bowed to the Guru and the God, as well as the planets such as the Moon and the Sun, and having fully worshipped the lunar mansions, one should dissolve oneself therein. [One should contemplate:
"Earth, water, fire, air, and space..."
One should know it to be very difficult to attain; one should apply the form of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Everything becomes the *kalala* stage, and first one should cast forth water.
One should know it to be red in color; one should join fire with fire.
There, a mass of flesh should be formed; one should deposit the wind right there.
Then, that which has a lovely color should be made, and one should deposit space within the skull.
Blowing [upon it], making it resemble gold, one should then reduce it to the state of ash.
Having uttered there a great roar, the *huṃ* syllable worshipped by the gods,
he rises up without a doubt, with limbs well-nourished like the sun,
possessing divine splendor, a massive body, divine vision, and great strength.
It was well-honored, with the sound of bells extending for a hundred yojanas;
divine, made of radiant gold, and adorned with precious rubies;
rich with flower garlands and banners, and decorated with a network of tinkling bells.
Mounted upon a supreme celestial chariot, accompanied by the sounds of conchs and trumpets,
with the songs and instrumental music of *apsarases* and enchanting dances;
adorned with divine ornaments and graced with celestial garlands.
Endowed with the beauty of collyrium at the corners of her eyes, beautiful in form, and intoxicated with passion,
a celestial maiden approaches as foretold— of this there is no doubt.
Having taken hold of the lord of practitioners, she shall thereafter dwell in the world of the Siddhas.
He enjoys divine baths and drinks, and divine ornaments,
together with a hundred thousand Siddha maidens who are afflicted by love.
While that single, terrible ocean exists, in which all moving and non-moving beings have perished—
Where the gods dissolve away, there the Siddha likewise dissolves.
This fierce one is described as the "Destroyer of the Past and Time.
O Great Goddess, in reality, when this [state] cannot be brought about, [then it occurs].
By this very body, accomplishment will then be attained.
